World.title: Brazil Court Orders Retailer Casas Bahia to Rehire Workers
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Key Facts — The ruling Judge Katarina Roberta Mousinho de Matos, of Brasilia’s 11th Labor Court, suspended the August mass layoffs on August 18, 2026.

— The deadline the retailer has five days to put the dismissed staff back on the payroll, and 48 hours to switch health plans back on.

— The penalty R$500 (about US$97) per day for each worker left out, plus R$10,000 (about US$1,930) for any new Phase 2 dismissal without union talks.

— The headcount the company told the bankruptcy court that about 3,000 jobs went in August, while the CNTC labor confederation counts about 1,900.

— The wider retreat roughly 11,600 jobs and about 355 stores have gone since 2023, including 298 stores closed this month.

A day later. A second judge in Sao Paulo gave the chain only part of the shelter from creditors it had asked for.

Illustrative photo: a Casas Bahia store in Sao Lourenco, Minas Gerais. The chain closed 298 stores in August 2026 before a labor judge suspended the accompanying mass layoffs. (Photo: ZeroTwoAndHiroWW2, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

A labor judge in Brasilia has ordered Casas Bahia, Brazil’s best-known furniture and appliance chain, to reverse its August mass layoffs. The company must put the dismissed staff back on the payroll within five days.

Because it filed for court protection from creditors days earlier, the retailer is now fighting on two fronts at once.

What the Judge in Brasilia Ordered

The injunction came on the evening of Tuesday, August 18, 2026. Judge Katarina Roberta Mousinho de Matos, of the 11th Labor Court of Brasilia, signed it.

She suspended the effects of the collective dismissals and ordered the contracts provisionally restored. In addition, health plans and other assistance benefits cancelled because of the firings must be switched back on within 48 hours.

The court gave the company five days from formal notice to return the staff to the payroll. That clock started once the ruling was served.

Why the Layoffs Were Blocked

Brazilian law treats mass firings differently from ordinary ones. Under a Supreme Court precedent known as Tema 638, a company must talk to the unions before it dismisses a large group.

The judge found that step missing. As a result, she froze the round rather than cancelling it outright.

Leaving the door open for the company to redo the process properly. The rule is about process, not permission.

Unions have no veto, and no collective agreement has to be signed, yet the talks must genuinely happen first.

What Grupo Casas Bahia does. Grupo Casas Bahia S.A., together with its subsidiaries, operates as an omnichannel retailer in Brazil. The company provides consumer electronics, home appliances, furniture, and other domestic items. It also engages in the manufacture, industrialization, and sale of wood-based furniture; ownership and management of equity interests; management of logistics operations; and provision of…

Who Brought the Case

The action was filed by the CNTC, Brazil’s national confederation of commerce workers. It is an umbrella body for retail unions across the country.

The confederation argued that the cuts were pushed through without the bargaining the law requires. Therefore it asked for an urgent order, and it got one the same week.

How Many Workers Casas Bahia Must Take Back

The decision does not name a single headcount. Instead, it covers everyone dismissed on August 13 and 14.

Plus later exits through August 17 that formed part of the same operation. That leaves two competing tallies.

The CNTC counts about 1,900 people cut on those two days. While Casas Bahia told the bankruptcy court that roughly 3,000 jobs went during the August round.

So the true number sits somewhere between the two. It will only be fixed once the company files its own list with the court.

The Fines Attached to the Order

The penalty is not a lump sum. If the company misses the deadline, it owes R$500 a day for each affected worker.

Roughly US$97 at the August 19 rate of R$5.17 to the dollar. That amount is capped, at least for now, at the equivalent of ten months of pay per employee.

Even so, spread across thousands of people it adds up quickly. A second penalty covers fresh cuts.

Any new Phase 2 dismissal made without prior union involvement carries a fine of R$10,000, about US$1,930, per worker.

A Second Courtroom, a Second Ruling

The very next day the story moved to Sao Paulo. On Wednesday, August 19, Judge Taina Maria Leonardo de Oliveira, of the city’s 2nd Bankruptcy and Judicial Recovery Court.

Ruled on the company’s plea for shelter from creditors. She granted the emergency requests only in part.

Crucially, she did not yet admit the reorganization itself, so the full protection the retailer wants is still pending.

What Sao Paulo Granted and What It Held Back

The judge barred the group’s roughly 28,000 creditors from calling in contracts early purely because a recovery request had been filed. Suppliers must also deliver goods already in transit to stores and distribution centres.

In addition, essential contracts must keep running. That list covers water and power utilities, technology and security providers, and the leases on the shops themselves.

She also blocked unusual seizures of receivables outside the normal contract flow. Breaching any of these points carries a fine of R$50,000 a day, close to US$9,700.

The limits matter as much as the grants. She set no end date for the shelter.

Yet ruled that the time used will be deducted from the 180-day freeze the company would get if the reorganization is admitted.

An Inspection Before Anything Else

Before deciding whether to admit the case, the judge ordered an on-the-ground check. A court-appointed administrator must verify that the group really operates as its filing describes.

The report is due within 30 days. Meanwhile, the company has ten days to hand over paperwork it left out of the original filing.

Three Years of Shrinking

August was not the first round. The transformation plan launched in 2023 closed 55 loss-making stores and removed about 8,600 posts.

This month added 298 store closures and, by the company’s own count, about 3,000 more jobs. Taken together, that is roughly 11,600 positions and around 355 shops gone since 2023.

Folha de S. Paulo, working from quarterly filings, puts the staff cut at 11,749 people, or 28 percent of the workforce.

Headcount fell from 41,866 in June 2023 to 30,117 by mid-2026.

The Debt Behind the Crisis

The reorganization filing lists about R$17.3 billion in debt, near US$3.35 billion. It names roughly 28,000 creditors.

The biggest single claim belongs to insurer Zurich Minas Brasil, at R$1.97 billion. An investment fund is next with R$1 billion, followed by Samsung’s Brazilian unit on R$937.6 million.

Household names fill the rest of the top of the list. Electrolux, Whirlpool, LG and Motorola are all owed hundreds of millions of reais.

What the Company Says

The retailer’s response to the labor ruling was short. It told the news outlet Poder360 that it had learned of the decision and was weighing the terms and its next steps.

An appeal remains available. Nothing so far suggests a higher labor court has touched the injunction, so the five-day clock still runs.

What Happens Next

Two timetables now overlap. The labor deadline is measured in days, while the Sao Paulo court’s inspection runs for up to a month.

For staff, the immediate question is pay and health cover. For suppliers and lenders, it is whether the reorganization is admitted at all.

Shoppers with pending orders sit in between. Until the court rules on admission, the company keeps trading under a patchwork of temporary orders.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which court blocked the layoffs?

The 11th Labor Court of Brasilia, part of the 10th Regional Labor Court, or TRT-10. Judge Katarina Roberta Mousinho de Matos signed the injunction on August 18, 2026.

Is the daily fine R$100,000?

No. The labor injunction sets R$500 a day per affected worker, about US$97. A separate Sao Paulo ruling sets R$50,000 a day, near US$9,700, for breaching creditor-protection measures.

Are 3,000 or 1,900 workers going back?

The order does not fix a number. It covers everyone cut between August 13 and 17 in the same operation.

Has the judicial recovery been approved?

Not yet. As of August 20.

Sources: G1; Poder360; O Globo; Folha de S.Paulo; Metropoles; UOL.

World.title: Mexico’s Government Websites Went Dark for Nearly Two Hours
World.content:
Mexico · TECHNOLOGY

Key Facts Date the afternoon of 19 August 2026.

the afternoon of 19 August 2026. First reports around 16:58 local time.

around 16:58 local time. Restored shortly before 18:43 local time.

shortly before 18:43 local time. Duration close to one hour and forty-five minutes.

close to one hour and forty-five minutes. Stated cause a connectivity cut, per the federal digital agency.

For most of a working afternoon, Mexico’s federal government had no website at all.

Every federal government website on Mexico’s gob.mx domain went down on the afternoon of 19 August 2026. Service returned shortly before 18:43, close to an hour and three quarters later.

The agency responsible blamed a connectivity cut, without giving further technical detail.

What went down

The gob.mx domain carries the websites of Mexico’s entire federal public administration. When it failed, effectively all of them failed together.

That includes the portals where the public consults budgets, contracts and official documents. Ministries named in coverage include Hacienda, the finance ministry, and the energy ministry.

Reports of the interruption began circulating around 16:58. Service came back shortly before 18:43.

That works out at close to one hour and forty-five minutes.

Any figure of about ninety minutes understates it.

The domain has been the single address for federal government websites since the mid-2010s. Almost nothing federal sits outside it.

What the government said

The Agencia de Transformación Digital y Telecomunicaciones posted that the gob.mx sites were temporarily disabled because of a connectivity cut. It said they would be back in 25 minutes.

They were not. The actual outage ran roughly four times that estimate.

The agency said it would give notice as soon as service returned. It did not publish a fuller technical account.

As of the following day it had not clarified whether the cut was an infrastructure failure, a provider problem or something else.

The statement was posted publicly rather than sent to the press. It is the only official account of the outage.

Mexican outlets reproduced its wording in full.

Why a single domain is a single point of failure

Mexico consolidated federal government websites onto gob.mx more than a decade ago. The aim was consistency, cheaper hosting and a single front door for citizens.

The trade-off is exactly what happened on 19 August. Consolidation means one failure takes everything with it.

Countries that keep ministry sites on separate infrastructure lose less in any single incident. They also spend more and confuse users more.

There is no obviously correct answer to that trade-off.

Consolidated government websites are the international norm now. The United Kingdom and Singapore run the same model.

Each of them has had comparable outages.

What was actually unavailable

Public information portals were the most visible loss. Journalists and researchers use these to check contracts and budget lines.

Transactional services also sit behind gob.mx. Appointment booking, tax formalities and document requests run through the same front door.

Anyone mid-way through an online formality during those hours would have lost the session. There is no published guidance on what happened to those.

The agency has not said whether any data was affected.

Nothing in its statement suggests it was.

Timing made it worse. Late afternoon is when most people deal with administrative tasks.

What this means for foreign residents

If you live in Mexico on a residency permit, several routine tasks run through government websites. Immigration appointments and tax filings are the common ones.

An outage of under two hours is an inconvenience rather than a crisis. Deadlines are rarely that tight.

It is still worth keeping paper or PDF copies of confirmations. Systems that fail once tend to fail again.

Screenshots of a completed submission are worth more than a memory of one.

Immigration and tax portals are the two that matter most to foreign residents in Mexico. Both sit on the affected domain.

Neither published a separate notice during the outage.

How unusual this is

Total outages of the federal domain are not routine in Mexico. Individual ministry portals go down more often and attract less attention.

What made this one notable is that it took everything at once, in the middle of a working afternoon. That is when usage peaks.

The agency’s own 25-minute estimate suggests it initially expected a small problem. The gap between the estimate and the outcome is the part worth noting.

Public bodies rarely revise a published estimate mid-incident.

Mexican government websites were unavailable for the duration across the whole federal administration. Partial outages are far more common than total ones.

The transparency question

The digital agency has not published an incident report. There is no obligation on it to do so.

Without one, the phrase connectivity cut is doing a lot of work. It could describe a fibre break, a provider outage or a configuration error.

Mexican outlets noted the absence of detail the following day. That absence is the only substantive criticism in the coverage.

We would report a fuller explanation if one were issued.

The agency is a relatively new body with a broad brief over federal digital services. Its incident communication practice is still being established.

What to do if it happens again

Check whether the whole domain is down or only one site. If gob.mx itself will not resolve, waiting is the only option.

Government websites in Mexico do not generally have mirrors. There is no alternate address to try.

For time-sensitive formalities, physical offices continue to operate during a web outage. Queues get longer.

Most deadlines in Mexican administrative practice fall on a date rather than an hour.

Keep a note of the time you attempted a submission. That record is occasionally accepted where a deadline is disputed.

Government websites in Mexico do not issue outage certificates.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long were Mexico’s government websites down? Close to one hour and forty-five minutes, from around 16:58 to shortly before 18:43 on 19 August 2026. What caused it? The Agencia de Transformación Digital y Telecomunicaciones said it was a connectivity cut. It has not published further technical detail. Which sites were affected? All federal public administration sites hosted on the gob.mx domain, including portals for the finance and energy ministries. Was any data lost? Nothing in the agency’s statement suggests data was affected, and no incident report has been published. Was it a cyberattack? The agency described a connectivity cut and gave no indication of an attack. It has not ruled anything in or out publicly.

World.title: Chile Fines a Santiago Broker for Faking Its Own Accounts
World.content:
Chile · REGULATION

Key Facts Fine 6,000 unidades de fomento, about US$266,000.

6,000 unidades de fomento, about US$266,000. Firm Nevasa Corredores de Bolsa, a Santiago brokerage.

Nevasa Corredores de Bolsa, a Santiago brokerage. Regulator the Comisión para el Mercado Financiero.

the Comisión para el Mercado Financiero. Reason false information on its financial position and solvency.

false information on its financial position and solvency. Reported 19 August 2026, under CMF Resolution 8334.

A brokerage made its own balance sheet look healthier than it was. The regulator noticed, two years later.

Chile’s financial regulator has fined the brokerage Nevasa 6,000 unidades de fomento for supplying false information about its financial position. That is about US$266,000.

Chile’s CMF supervises every brokerage licensed to trade on the Santiago exchange.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

What the regulator found

The Comisión para el Mercado Financiero sanctioned the Santiago brokerage Nevasa. It found the firm had provided false information about its financial situation.

The CMF also said the firm altered the calculation of the indicators used to measure its equity and solvency. Those indicators are the ones supervisors use to judge whether a broker can meet its obligations.

The finding was reported on 19 August 2026, citing CMF Resolution 8334. Three Chilean outlets carried it.

The regulator’s own resolution text sets out the detail.

We have not seen that document directly and are reporting the press account of it.

Emol, Biobiochile and Diario Financiero all reported the sanction on the same day. Their accounts agree.

How the accounts were altered

According to the reporting, Nevasa recorded a badly issued cheque as if it had been collected. That single entry made its liquid equity and financial ratios look better than they were.

It also used a current account to make unpaid debts appear to be current. Both moves point in the same direction.

The cheque entry relates to August 2023. The current account misuse is dated between January and August 2023.

So the sanction lands roughly three years after the conduct.

Neither entry is complicated. Both are the kind of thing a supervisor finds by reconciling reported figures against bank records.

Nevasa has not published a public response in the coverage we have seen.

What the fine is worth

The fine is 6,000 unidades de fomento. The UF is Chile’s inflation-indexed accounting unit, revalued daily.

At the UF value of 40,859.28 on 20 August 2026, that is about 245.2 million Chilean pesos. Chilean press reported it as close to 245 million pesos.

Converted at the Banco Central de Chile observed dollar rate of 920.26 on 20 August 2026, the fine is about US$266,000.

The arithmetic checks out at each step. We verified it before publishing.

The peso figure quoted in the press is journalistic. The legally binding amount is the one stated in UF.

Why fines are set in UF

Chile prices long-dated obligations in unidades de fomento rather than pesos. The unit rises with inflation, so a UF-denominated fine keeps its real value.

A fine set in pesos in 2023 would be worth less by 2026. A fine in UF is not.

Mortgages, rents and insurance contracts in Chile use the same unit. Foreign residents encounter it quickly.

It is one of the more useful pieces of Chilean financial infrastructure.

The UF stood at 40,859.28 on 20 August 2026. It moves by a few pesos a day.

How big a penalty this is

About US$266,000 is not a large sum for a brokerage. It is not intended to be ruinous.

The reputational cost is the larger part. A public finding of false financial reporting follows a firm through every client due-diligence process.

The CMF has not announced a licence suspension for Nevasa. The sanction as reported is monetary.

Nevasa’s response, if any, has not been published in the coverage we have.

Chilean regulatory fines are modest by international standards. The CMF’s deterrent rests more on disclosure than on amount.

What solvency ratios are for

A brokerage holds client assets and takes positions of its own. Regulators require it to keep capital against both.

Liquid equity and solvency indicators are the tests of whether it can absorb a loss without touching client money. Understating a problem in those numbers is a supervisory offence, not an accounting slip.

That is why the CMF treats false reporting more seriously than a poor result. A weak but honest broker can be supervised.

A broker whose numbers are wrong cannot be.

The conduct dates to 2023, when Chilean markets were under strain. Brokers were being watched closely at the time.

What this means if you invest through a Chilean broker

Foreign residents in Chile often hold local investments through a corredora de bolsa. The CMF publishes its sanctions publicly.

Checking whether your broker appears in that record is worth the ten minutes it takes. Resolutions are listed on the regulator’s own site.

This case involves the firm’s own balance sheet rather than client accounts. No client loss has been reported.

That distinction matters, and the coverage does not suggest otherwise.

Client assets at a Chilean brokerage are held separately from the firm’s own. That segregation is what the solvency rules are meant to protect.

The wider supervision picture

The CMF was created in 2017 by merging Chile’s securities and banking supervisors. It covers banks, insurers, brokerages and the securities market.

Its sanction record is public and searchable. That is not the case everywhere in the region.

Chile’s regulatory transparency is one reason foreign investors treat it as the region’s most predictable market. Cases like Nevasa are evidence of the system working rather than failing.

A three-year gap between conduct and sanction is the fair criticism.

Nevasa remains licensed as far as the reporting shows. A fine is not a withdrawal of authorisation.

What to watch

Nevasa can appeal a CMF resolution through the Chilean courts. Whether it does will become visible in the case record.

The regulator may publish further detail on the investigation. Resolution 8334 is the reference to look for.

We will report an appeal or a further sanction if either appears.

For now the fine stands as issued.

Chilean sanction records stay public permanently. The finding will remain searchable regardless of any appeal.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much was the fine? 6,000 unidades de fomento, about 245.2 million Chilean pesos. That is roughly US$266,000 at the Banco Central de Chile observed rate of 920.26 on 20 August 2026. What did Nevasa do? The CMF found it provided false information about its financial situation and altered the calculation of its equity and solvency indicators. How were the accounts altered? Reporting says a badly issued cheque was recorded as collected, and a current account was used to make unpaid debts appear current. The conduct dates to 2023. Did clients lose money? No client loss has been reported. The findings concern the brokerage’s own balance sheet and regulatory reporting. What is a unidad de fomento? Chile’s inflation-indexed accounting unit, revalued daily. Fines, mortgages and rents are commonly denominated in it so their real value holds.

World.title: Paraguay Wants a Quarter of Mercosur’s EU Export Quotas
World.content:
Paraguay · TRADE

Key Facts Position an equal 25 percent share for each Mercosur member.

an equal 25 percent share for each Mercosur member. Stated by Paraguay’s foreign minister, Rubén Ramírez.

Paraguay’s foreign minister, Rubén Ramírez. Reported 18 to 19 August 2026, via EFE.

18 to 19 August 2026, via EFE. Status no agreed methodology among the four members.

no agreed methodology among the four members. Context the EU-Mercosur association agreement quotas.

The EU deal gives Mercosur a fixed volume of tariff-free exports. Nobody has decided who gets how much.

Paraguay says it wants an equal quarter of the export quotas Mercosur negotiated with the European Union. Its foreign minister set out the position on 18 August 2026.

Beef is the quota line that matters most to the smaller Mercosur members.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesMarkets, currencies and the economy › RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. × Markets today The currency Rates & inflation Economy outlook Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

What Paraguay said

Paraguay’s foreign ministry relayed comments by Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez at a meeting with private sector groups. The subject was how the EU export quotas should be divided.

The ministry said Paraguay maintains its defence of an equitable distribution of 25 percent of the quotas among Mercosur members. In plain terms, an equal quarter each.

It also said Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay have not reached agreement on the methodology for distributing the quotas. That is the actual news.

EFE carried the account and Infobae republished it.

There is no Mercosur decision allocating quotas on this basis.

The EU export quotas are the central commercial prize in the agreement for South American farmers.

What quotas are being fought over

The EU-Mercosur association agreement gives the South American bloc tariff-rate quotas on a set of agricultural products. A tariff-rate quota is a fixed volume that enters at a reduced tariff.

Technical commentary describes a combined beef quota of 99,000 tonnes a year, entering at a preferential 7.5 percent EU tariff. A sugar quota of 180,000 tonnes a year is also described.

Paraguay’s statement does not name a product. It refers generally to the quotas foreseen in the agreement.

We are separating the two: the political position is Paraguay’s, the tonnage figures come from technical analysis of the deal.

A tariff-rate quota is not a right to sell. It is a right to sell a fixed volume at a lower tariff than everyone else pays.

Sugar and poultry lines are also in the agreement. Beef is the one that generates the argument.

Why the split matters so much

Brazil and Argentina are far larger beef exporters than Paraguay and Uruguay. Under a market-share method, they would take most of the EU export quotas.

An equal split would hand Paraguay four times what its market share would justify. That is why it wants one.

For a country of about seven million people, a guaranteed volume into the European market is transformative. For Brazil it is a rounding error.

This is the classic small-member problem in any customs union.

Paraguay is the smallest economy in Mercosur. It also has one of the region’s largest cattle herds relative to its population.

That combination is why the EU export quotas matter more there than anywhere else in the bloc.

Where the other three stand

Commentary on the negotiations describes Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay favouring an allocation based on market share. Paraguay has been pushing for an equal split.

None of the other three has published a formal position in the material we could verify. The reporting describes their preference rather than quoting it.

Uruguay is in an awkward middle position. It is small like Paraguay but a much larger beef exporter.

That may be why no methodology has been agreed.

Market share allocation is the more common international practice. Equal allocation is the more common demand from smaller members.

Why this is not settled yet

The EU-Mercosur agreement has taken more than two decades and is still not fully in force. Internal allocation is one of several unresolved pieces.

Quota distribution is a Mercosur matter, not an EU one. Brussels sets the total; the bloc decides the split.

That means the argument is between four governments with directly opposing interests. There is no external arbiter.

Deadlock is the default outcome in that structure.

The agreement has been signed but is not fully ratified in Europe. Several EU member states remain opposed on agricultural grounds.

What it means for Paraguayan producers

Paraguayan beef currently sells largely to Chile, Russia, Taiwan and Brazil. European access at a reduced tariff would open a higher-priced market.

The EU applies strict traceability and deforestation rules to imported beef. Paraguay has been building systems to comply.

A quota share without compliance is worth nothing. Both have to arrive together.

That is a longer project than the allocation argument.

Paraguay has been building satellite-based traceability and deforestation monitoring. Those systems exist to satisfy European rules.

How this fits Paraguay’s wider position

Paraguay set an export record earlier this year. It has also published a mining and energy plan targeting large-scale investment.

The country’s strategy has been to make itself the cheap, low-tax option inside Mercosur. Winning an outsized share of the EU export quotas would fit that.

It has limited leverage to force the point. Mercosur decisions are taken by consensus.

Consensus is exactly what is missing.

Its residency and tax regime has drawn foreign residents for the same reason. Paraguay competes on cost within the bloc.

What to watch

A Mercosur decision published in the bloc’s official gazette would settle it. None exists.

Watch also for the agreement’s ratification timetable in Europe. Allocation becomes urgent only once the quotas are real.

Paraguayan cattle groups will keep the pressure public. That is how a small member negotiates.

We will report a decision when one is published.

Until the split is agreed, the EU export quotas exist on paper only. No exporter can plan against them.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Paraguay asking for? An equal 25 percent share of the EU export quotas Mercosur negotiated, rather than a split based on market share. Who said it? Paraguay’s foreign minister, Rubén Ramírez, in comments relayed by the foreign ministry and reported through EFE on 18 to 19 August 2026. Which products are covered? Paraguay’s statement refers generally to the quotas in the agreement. Technical commentary describes a combined beef quota of 99,000 tonnes a year and a sugar quota of 180,000 tonnes. Has anything been agreed? No. Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay have not agreed a methodology for distributing the quotas, and no Mercosur decision exists. Why does Paraguay want an equal split? It is a much smaller exporter than Brazil or Argentina. A market-share method would leave it with a small fraction of the volume.

World.title: Three in Ten Uruguayans Feel Poor Even as New Money Arrives
World.content:
Uruguay · ECONOMY

Key Facts Subjective measure about 31 percent say they feel poor.

about 31 percent say they feel poor. Headcount more than 1.1 million people.

more than 1.1 million people. Official income poverty 16.6 percent of the population.

16.6 percent of the population. Source the INE household survey, reported 19 August 2026.

the INE household survey, reported 19 August 2026. Same week two foreign investment announcements in Montevideo.

Uruguay’s official poverty rate and how Uruguayans describe their own situation are two very different numbers.

More than 1.1 million Uruguayans say they feel poor, according to a subjective measure in the national household survey. The official income poverty rate is 16.6 percent.

Uruguay has the highest income per head in South America and a persistent perception gap.

The number and what it measures

Uruguay’s Instituto Nacional de Estadística runs the Encuesta Continua de Hogares, its continuous household survey. The survey now includes a subjective module.

That module asks people whether they consider themselves poor. More than 1.1 million said yes, which the reporting puts at 31.1 percent of the population.

A second figure in the same coverage says 31.3 percent said they feel poor. The two are close but not identical, and we could not establish which cut each refers to.

We are reporting the measure as about three in ten rather than picking one decimal.

The exact survey question wording has not been published in the coverage we have.

Subjective poverty modules are increasingly common in national statistics. They sit alongside income measures rather than replacing them.

Why it differs from official poverty

The official income poverty rate in Uruguay is 16.6 percent. That is calculated by comparing household income against a defined basket of goods.

The subjective figure is roughly double. That gap is the whole story here.

An income threshold measures whether you can buy a fixed basket. Asking whether you feel poor measures something else entirely.

Both are real measurements. Neither is a correction of the other.

Uruguay’s income poverty measure is one of the most reliable in the region. Its household survey has run continuously for decades.

The subjective module is a newer addition.

What the gap usually means

A large gap between measured and felt poverty tends to appear where costs have risen faster than the poverty line. It also appears where people compare themselves against a visible richer group.

Uruguay has the highest income per head in South America. It also has some of the region’s highest consumer prices.

Someone above the income poverty line in Montevideo may still be unable to afford what their neighbours have. That is what makes people say they feel poor.

Housing costs are the usual driver in a country like this.

Rent and utilities have risen faster than the poverty line in Montevideo. That is the mechanical part of why people feel poor.

Money still arriving

The same week produced two investment announcements. Banco Santander launched a green finance programme in Uruguay called Impulso Verde.

The bank said it would direct US$100 million to financing sustainable projects across the country. The scope covers renewable energy, energy efficiency, sustainable mobility, agriculture, industry and real estate.

Loans can be made in dollars or in unidades indexadas, Uruguay’s inflation-linked unit. No time horizon for the US$100 million was published.

That matters. A commitment with no period attached is not the same as an annual budget.

Santander is the largest private bank in Uruguay by assets. A green finance line of this size is a strategic commitment rather than a marketing exercise.

An Argentine developer buying in

IRSA, the Argentine property group, is advancing a large mixed-use project in Uruguay. It is called Distrito Calcagno and sits near Lago Calcagno, close to Parque Roosevelt and the Carrasco airport.

The masterplan covers 230,000 square metres, of which 190,000 are buildable. It is divided into 14 mixed-use macro-lots with more than 1,900 housing units planned.

The reported investment figure is more than US$10 million. That number looks small against 1,900 homes, and most likely describes IRSA’s own outlay rather than total project cost.

The report does not clarify which. We are flagging it rather than presenting US$10 million as the value of the district.

No IRSA filing confirming the figure has been published.

Argentine capital has moved into Uruguayan property for decades. Punta del Este is the best-known example.

A claim we could not stand up

The project has been described elsewhere as a scheme revived after fifteen years. We could not find a source tying a fifteen-year delay to this Uruguayan project.

A separate IRSA project, Ramblas del Plata in Buenos Aires, broke ground this year decades after the land was divested. That is a different site in a different country.

Conflating the two is easy and wrong. We are not repeating the fifteen-year framing.

If IRSA publishes a project history we will update.

Press coverage of property projects frequently borrows detail from a developer’s other schemes. Checking which site a figure belongs to is basic work.

The dispute at the state oil company

Fancap, the union at the state oil company Ancap, struck at the La Tablada plant in mid-August. The union said the stoppage would not seriously affect supply.

A meeting was scheduled at the Ministry of Labour with Ancap, the union, the economy ministry and the planning and budget office. It was set for the following Wednesday.

Reports of a government threat to declare the work an essential service are not confirmed in the material we could verify. Nor is the formal label of a dialogue table.

We are reporting the strike and the scheduled meeting, and nothing beyond them.

Ancap holds a legal monopoly on fuel refining and import in Uruguay. Any stoppage there is politically sensitive.

The union said supply would not be seriously affected.

How to read all of this together

Uruguay is a country where the macro numbers look good and a third of people say they feel poor. That combination is not unusual in middle-income economies.

Foreign money keeps arriving because the institutions are stable and the currency is manageable. That is a separate question from household experience.

For a foreign resident, the practical implication is cost. Uruguay is expensive relative to its neighbours, and the subjective poverty figure is one measure of that.

For an investor, the implication is political. Governments do not survive long when a third of voters feel poor.

The two numbers in this story are both from the same statistics office. They are not in conflict; they answer different questions.

The share who feel poor is the one politicians will be watching.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many Uruguayans say they feel poor? More than 1.1 million people, about 31 percent of the population. The figure comes from the subjective module in the INE household survey, reported on 19 August 2026. What is the official poverty rate? 16.6 percent, measured against household income and a defined basket of goods. That is roughly half the subjective figure. Why is there a gap? An income threshold measures whether a fixed basket is affordable. The survey question asks how people see their own situation, which reflects costs, comparison and expectations. What is Santander’s Uruguay commitment? US$100 million for sustainable projects under a programme called Impulso Verde, covering renewables, efficiency, mobility, agriculture, industry and real estate. No time period was published. How big is the IRSA project? 230,000 square metres of land, 190,000 buildable, 14 macro-lots and more than 1,900 planned homes. The reported investment of more than US$10 million most likely refers to IRSA’s own outlay rather than total project cost.

World.title: Honduras Puts 75 Municipalities on Red Alert Over Drought
World.content:
Honduras · CLIMATE

Key Facts Red alert 75 municipalities, declared 19 August 2026.

75 municipalities, declared 19 August 2026. Yellow and green alerts 71 and 88 municipalities respectively.

71 and 88 municipalities respectively. Total under alert 234 of the country’s 298 municipalities.

234 of the country’s 298 municipalities. Declared by COPECO, the national risk management agency.

COPECO, the national risk management agency. President’s estimate the crisis runs to March or April 2027.

Almost eight in ten Honduran municipalities are now under some form of drought alert.

Honduras has declared a red alert in 75 municipalities because of drought linked to El Niño. The declaration was made on 19 August 2026.

Honduras sits in Central America’s Dry Corridor, which suffers first in an El Niño year.

What has been declared

COPECO, the Honduran risk management agency, declared a red alert in 75 municipalities. The reason given is drought associated with El Niño.

A further 71 municipalities are on yellow alert and 88 on green. Together that is 234 municipalities.

Honduras has 298 municipalities in total. So 234 is 78.5 percent of them.

Wire coverage rounded that to 80 percent of the country, including the capital. Both descriptions come from the same underlying count.

The red alert was declared for an indefinite period, with some reports citing a 120-day validity on the initial decree.

Infobae reported the total of 234 municipalities affected. Prensa Libre carried the COPECO declaration itself.

What a red alert means

Red is the highest of the three levels in the Honduran system, and the Honduras drought has now reached it. It unlocks emergency powers and budget reallocation for the affected municipalities.

Yellow and green are lower tiers, indicating preparation rather than active emergency. All three appear in the same declaration.

The alert level is a measure of administrative response, not of rainfall. It does not tell you how much rain has failed to fall.

That distinction is worth keeping in mind when comparing across countries.

The Honduras drought declaration covers meteorological drought specifically. It is separate from any flood or storm alert.

What is actually happening on the ground

Wire reporting describes El Niño scorching harvests and livestock dying of thirst. Those are the visible effects.

Honduras sits in Central America’s Dry Corridor, a belt running from Guatemala through El Salvador and Nicaragua. It is the region that suffers first in an El Niño year.

Subsistence maize and bean farmers are the most exposed to the Honduras drought. They have no irrigation and no financial buffer.

Coffee, the country’s main export crop, grows at higher altitude and is affected differently.

The Dry Corridor is one of the most climate-exposed farming regions in the Americas. It has suffered repeated failed harvests over the past decade.

El Niño years are consistently the worst of them.

How long the president expects it to last

President Nasry Asfura said the crisis will take the country until March or April next year. That was reported on 19 August 2026.

That timeline matches the forecast El Niño cycle. Meteorological agencies have put the odds of a strong event over the coming Northern Hemisphere winter above 90 percent.

A drought that runs to March covers the entire dry season. It also covers the planting decisions for next year’s first harvest.

That is the part with the longest economic tail.

Asfura’s estimate is a political statement rather than a meteorological forecast. It happens to align with the seasonal outlook.

The other thing that happened this week

On the same day, Asfura met representatives of Standard & Poor’s at the presidential palace. The stated purpose was to review the economic situation and the fiscal, financial and institutional outlook.

S&P moved Honduras from a negative to a stable outlook in March 2026. It kept the long and short-term sovereign ratings at BB-/B.

Those are letter grades rather than monetary figures. BB- sits below investment grade.

Meeting a rating agency the same week you declare a drought emergency is a coincidence of calendar rather than of substance.

It is also a reminder that emergency spending and sovereign ratings pull against each other.

The meeting took place at Casa Presidencial in Tegucigalpa. The account comes from the presidency.

The fiscal problem underneath

The Honduras drought emergency costs money that has not been budgeted. Honduras has limited room to absorb that.

The country returned to ICSID, the World Bank’s investment arbitration body, this month. It has also been reworking its power sector with European support.

Those are the moves of a government trying to restore external confidence. An unbudgeted Honduras drought response complicates them.

None of the reporting quantifies the cost of the emergency.

A sovereign at BB- has limited access to cheap external borrowing. Emergency funding usually comes from multilateral lenders instead.

What it means for the region

The Honduras drought sits in a corridor where dry years drive migration. That link is well documented across previous El Niño cycles.

Honduras is already a major origin country for migration north. A failed harvest season increases the pressure.

Food prices in the region rise with a maize and bean shortfall. Neighbouring countries import from the same market.

The Panama Canal is separately restricting ship draft over the same El Niño forecast.

Guatemala, El Salvador and Nicaragua share the same corridor. None has declared an emergency at this scale so far this season.

The Honduras drought is the first formal declaration of the cycle.

What to watch

The first thing is whether the Honduras drought alert is extended beyond its initial 120 days. That decision would come around December.

The second is the primera harvest assessment, usually published in the autumn. That gives the first hard number on crop losses.

The third is any international appeal. Emergencies of this scale usually generate one.

We will report figures on the Honduras drought as agencies publish them.

COPECO publishes municipality-level alert changes as they happen. Those are the most current source.

The alert levels can be lowered as well as raised.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many municipalities are affected? 234 of Honduras’s 298 municipalities are under some level of alert: 75 red, 71 yellow and 88 green. That is 78.5 percent of the total. Who declared the alert? COPECO, the Secretaría de Gestión de Riesgos y Contingencias Nacionales, on 19 August 2026. How long will the drought last? President Nasry Asfura said the crisis will run until March or April next year. Forecasters put the odds of a strong El Niño through the coming winter above 90 percent. Why do reports say 80 percent of the country? That is the rounded share of municipalities under alert. The precise figure from the counts published is 78.5 percent. What did the S&P meeting concern? The president met Standard & Poor’s representatives on 19 August to review Honduras’s economic situation and fiscal outlook. S&P rates Honduras BB-/B with a stable outlook.

Connected Coverage Panama Canal marks 112 years with El Nino draft limits

World.title: Izzi and Megacable Have Taken 1.2 Million Phone Lines
World.content:
Mexico · TELECOMS

Key Facts Net gain 1,199,072 lines, all postpaid, to July 2026.

1,199,072 lines, all postpaid, to July 2026. Received from others 1.93 million numbers in total.

1.93 million numbers in total. Share from incumbents 94.2 percent came from three operators.

94.2 percent came from three operators. Biggest source Telcel, at 1,270,453 lines received.

Telcel, at 1,270,453 lines received. Data source the IFT historical portability database.

Two companies better known for home internet have quietly built a mobile business out of other people’s customers.

Izzi and Megacable have a combined net gain of 1,199,072 mobile lines through number portability. Every one of them is a postpaid line.

Mexican users can move their number between operators without changing it.

What the numbers say

Izzi Telecom and Megacable together hold a net positive balance of 1,199,072 mobile lines gained through number portability. The count runs from the start of their records as mobile operators to July 2026.

All of those lines are postpaid. That is the contract market rather than the prepaid market where most Mexican mobile users sit.

They received 1.93 million numbers from operators other than themselves. Of those, 94.2 percent came from Telcel, AT&T and Movistar.

The underlying data is the historical number portability database maintained by the IFT, Mexico’s telecoms regulator.

El Economista published the analysis on 19 August 2026.

Izzi belongs to Grupo Televisa. Megacable is a separate listed operator based in Guadalajara.

Where the lines came from

Telcel is by far the largest source. It lost 1,270,453 numbers to the two cable companies and won back 426,579.

AT&T gave up 339,919 numbers and received 80,422, for a stated net loss of 259,497. Movistar gave up 210,911 and received 102,592, for a net loss of 108,319.

The Telcel net figure is not printed in the reporting. Subtracting the two published numbers gives 843,874, and we are labelling that as our arithmetic rather than as a published figure.

All three are described as balances to July 2026.

Movistar is the Mexican arm of Telefonica. AT&T Mexico is the third national network operator.

Between them the three hold almost the entire Mexican mobile market.

A gap worth explaining

Add the three incumbent nets together and you get 1,211,690. The stated overall net gain is 1,199,072.

The difference is about 12,618 lines. That is not an error.

It means Izzi and Megacable have lost roughly that many lines net to everyone else in the market. Smaller operators and virtual networks account for the rest.

We ran the arithmetic specifically to check whether the headline figure held up. It does.

The gap is the interesting part rather than a problem with the data.

Mexico has a growing set of virtual operators including Bait, which sells through Walmart stores. Those account for the outflow.

What number portability is

Number portability lets a subscriber move to a different operator and keep the same phone number. Mexico has had it since 2008.

The IFT keeps a record of every port, which is why this data exists at all. Few countries publish it in this detail.

The process in Mexico is fast by international standards. A port typically completes within a day.

For a challenger operator, that speed is the whole business model.

The regulator publishes the database as a matter of course. It is one of the few genuinely open competition datasets in Mexican telecoms.

Why cable companies are winning

Izzi and Megacable are cable operators. Their core business is home internet and television.

Both entered mobile as virtual operators, buying wholesale network capacity rather than building their own towers. That keeps costs down.

The sales pitch is bundling. A household already paying for cable is offered mobile lines at a discount.

That approach targets postpaid households specifically, which is why the entire net gain is postpaid.

Neither company built a national mobile network. That would have cost billions and taken years.

Renting capacity turns a fixed-line customer base into a mobile one almost immediately.

What it means for Telcel

Telcel remains the dominant operator in Mexico by a wide margin. Losing 1.27 million numbers over several years is not existential.

It is, however, concentrated in the contract market. Postpaid customers are worth several times a prepaid customer over their lifetime.

Telcel has been recovering some of these lines, taking 426,579 back over the same period. Churn runs in both directions.

The net direction has been steady, and it has not favoured the incumbent.

Telcel is part of America Movil, controlled by the Slim family. It has been subject to asymmetric regulation in Mexico for over a decade.

Number portability was one of the tools introduced to loosen its grip.

What this means if you live in Mexico

If you are on a postpaid plan, number portability means switching costs you your loyalty rather than your number. That is worth knowing before you renew.

Bundled cable and mobile offers are usually cheaper per line than a standalone contract. They also tie you to one supplier for both.

Coverage differs. A virtual operator rides on somebody else’s network, and quality depends on which one.

Ask which host network an offer uses before switching.

Porting requires an NIP code obtained by text message from your current operator. The process is free.

How to read the 1 million shorthand

Some coverage describes this as a million postpaid lines taken from the incumbents. The precise figure is a net gain of 1,199,072 lines.

The rounding undercounts, and it also blurs what the figure is. This is a net balance across the whole market, not a total taken from three companies.

The share taken from the incumbents is 94.2 percent of 1.93 million lines received, which is about 1.82 million. That is the gross figure.

Net and gross tell different stories here, and both are useful.

The precise figure is the one the IFT database supports. The rounded one travels further.

What to watch

The IFT updates the portability database monthly. The July 2026 cut-off will move.

Whether the incumbents respond on price is the open question. Postpaid discounting in Mexico has been restrained so far.

Number portability gives the regulator a clean measure of competition. Few other markets have one this direct.

We will revisit the figures when the next quarter’s data is out.

Prepaid remains the larger market in Mexico by subscriber count. Nothing in this data speaks to it.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many lines have Izzi and Megacable gained? A net 1,199,072 mobile lines to July 2026, all postpaid, according to the IFT portability database as reported by El Economista. Where did most of them come from? Telcel, AT&T and Movistar accounted for 94.2 percent of the 1.93 million numbers the two companies received from other operators. Do the individual figures add up? Almost. The three incumbent nets sum to 1,211,690, about 12,618 more than the stated total. The two companies lost roughly that many lines net to other operators. What is number portability? The right to change operator while keeping your phone number. Mexico has had it since 2008, and ports usually complete within a day. Are these prepaid or contract customers? All postpaid, which is the contract market. Postpaid customers are worth considerably more per line than prepaid ones.

World.title: Costa Rica flood emergency keeps 473 schools closed and 1,300 people in shelters
World.content:
If you were thinking of or had plan to go to Caribbean side or in the Northern Zone this week, the heavy rain may have stopped but the disruption has not. Classes remain suspended at 473 schools, and more than 1,300 people are still living in 23 temporary shelters four days after Tropical Wave #33 pushed already-swollen rivers past their banks. Emergency crews are still reaching communities they could not get to over the weekend.

The Education Ministry closure list covers seven education regions. Sarapiquí accounts for 138 schools closed outright, Guápiles for 131 on partial suspension and Sulá for 110, with smaller numbers in Turrialba, Zona Norte-Norte, Limón and Cartago. That is a sharp drop from Monday, when 990 schools were shut. The ministry says the list changes daily and asks families to check its official channels rather than secondhand reports, because a school can reopen and close again within hours.

The rain itself has eased. The National Meteorological Institute expects only isolated showers on the Caribbean coast and variable downpours in the Northern Zone through the morning, with scattered afternoon rain reaching the Central Valley, the Central Pacific and the South Pacific, and possible showers on the Nicoya Peninsula.

The risk that remains is in the ground, not the sky. Soil across the Caribbean and the South Pacific is saturated, which means an ordinary afternoon shower can now trigger a landslide or push a river back up with almost no warning. A hillside that held all season can fail on a rainfall total that would normally pass without incident.

The weekend produced some of the heaviest rain on record. Nine weather stations set 24-hour precipitation records between 7 a.m. Sunday and 7 a.m. Monday, according to preliminary Institute data, with eight of them on the Caribbean slope.

Roxana de Pococí recorded 263.4 millimeters (10.4 inches) in a single day. For comparison, a heavy Costa Rican downpour typically drops around 60 millimeters (2.4 inches) over three hours. The Fundación Neotrópica station in Sierpe de Osa, on the Pacific side, logged 134.6 millimeters (5.3 inches).

Across 48 hours, the Caribbean and parts of the Northern Zone took between 200 and 360 millimeters (7.9 and 14.2 inches). At some stations a single weekend delivered half of what August normally brings in a full month, and monthly totals elsewhere have already reached between 100 and 170 percent of the historical average with almost two weeks still to go.

The National Emergency Commission is still supplying communities it cannot reach by road. A helicopter has been running food deliveries to the indigenous territories of Tayní Cabécar and Alto Chirripó in Limón, and to communities in Sarapiquí, where damaged roads and bridges have cut off vehicle access.

People in shelters are receiving meals, bedding, hygiene kits and medical checks. The count has stayed above 1,300 since Monday and will keep shifting as some families go home and others are evacuated. Route 32, the main link between San José and Limón, was closed Tuesday afternoon after material fell onto the roadway, and the Public Works Ministry scheduled an inspection for first thing Wednesday. Whether it reopens depends on what crews found.

If you need to reach the Caribbean, Route 10 through Turrialba is the alternate and is open to all vehicle types, though it has taken closures of its own during this rain cycle. Check the ministry’s channels before you leave rather than after you are on the road, because the Zurquí stretch can shut again within minutes of a downpour.

Do not drive through standing water, however shallow it looks. Moving water just 30 centimeters (12 inches) deep can float a car, and on a flooded road you cannot see whether the surface underneath is still there. If you have anything booked or scheduled in Sarapiquí, Tortuguero, Cahuita, Puerto Viejo or Guápiles, call ahead. Access varies community by community, and people on the ground will know whether the road to their door is open well before any official list catches up.

The forecast calls for lighter rain in the days ahead. But with the ground this saturated and most of the rainy season still to come, conditions on the Caribbean slope can change a good deal faster than the forecast suggests.

World.title: Brandon Nakashima Saves Three Match Points to Stun Daniil Medvedev at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Brandon Nakashima saved three consecutive match points before completing a dramatic comeback against Daniil Medvedev on Tuesday at the Cincinnati Open. The 27th-seeded American defeated the fourth seed 6-7(3), 7-6(4), 6-1, advancing to the round of 16 after two hours and 51 minutes.

Nakashima appeared headed for elimination when he served at 4-5, 0-40 in the second set. Medvedev had already taken the opening set in a tiebreak and stood one point away from closing the match on three occasions. Instead, Nakashima attacked. He saved the first match point with a forehand approach and volley, survived an 18-shot rally on the second and used serve-and-volley to erase the third. He eventually held serve before forcing another tiebreak.

“Down match points, I was just trying to tell myself to keep fighting for every point,” Nakashima said during his on-court interview. The American carried that momentum into the tiebreak, winning it 7-4 to force a deciding set. Medvedev never recovered. Nakashima broke early in the third and pulled away as the former Cincinnati champion became increasingly frustrated.

Nakashima closed the final set 6-1 to earn his first victory over Medvedev in four career meetings. Medvedev had won their previous encounter in the Brisbane final in January. The result continued an impressive North American hard-court run for Nakashima. The 25-year-old reached the semifinals in Washington before advancing to his first Masters 1000 final in Montreal, where he lost to fellow American Ben Shelton.

Now ranked a career-high No. 22, Nakashima has won 20 hard-court matches this season. Only Jakub Mensik, with 21, has recorded more on the ATP Tour. Tuesday’s victory was also Nakashima’s fifth against a top-10 opponent. It came against a player who has traditionally produced some of his best tennis on hard courts and won the Cincinnati title in 2019.

Nakashima will next face Portugal’s Nuno Borges, who produced another upset by defeating 13th-seeded Andrey Rublev 6-3, 6-4. Borges entered that match having lost all five of his previous meetings with Rublev. The winner will advance to the Cincinnati Open quarterfinals as the tournament moves closer to its August 23 championship match.

World.title: Burrell Boom man out on bail after allegedly taking cellphone from friend who was giving him a ride but got stuck in ditch
World.content:
Burrell Boom man out on bail after allegedly taking cellphone from friend who was giving him a ride but got stuck in ditch

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 28-year-old Burrell Boom man is out on bail after being accused of stealing a cellphone from a motorist while he was reportedly assisting him after his vehicle became stuck in a ditch.

Roy Frederick Tillett, a barber and construction worker, appeared in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court, where he was charged with theft of a black Android cellphone valued at $450, which belonged to a man he knows.

Tillett pleaded not guilty to the charge and denied stealing the phone.

With no objection from the prosecution, the Magistrate granted him bail in the sum of $2,000 plus one surety in the same amount.

As conditions of his bail, Tillett must remain at least 100 yards away from the complainant and must not interfere with him or any other prosecution witnesses.

According to police, the complainant reported that on August 11 he was driving along an unnamed street in Burrell Boom when he picked up Tillett, whom he knew.

The complainant said his vehicle subsequently became stuck in a ditch, prompting him to exit and inspect it. He reportedly left his cellphone between the driver’s and passenger seats while Tillett remained nearby.

The complainant told police that he later asked Tillett to go and purchase something for him. After Tillett left, the complainant noticed that his cellphone was missing.

He reportedly waited for Tillett to return so he could question him about the missing phone, but Tillett did not return.

The man told investigators that no one else had entered his vehicle during that period and subsequently requested court action against Tillett.

Tillett is scheduled to return to court on October 14, 2026.

World.title: Burrell Boom man pleads guilty to possession of cocaine but Judge gives him time served for month already served on remand
World.content:
Burrell Boom man pleads guilty to possession of cocaine but Judge gives him time served for month already served on remand

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Burrell Boom resident who spent nearly a month on remand for possession of 0.13 grams of cocaine walked free from the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday after changing his plea from not guilty to guilty.

Eyon Ramirez, 20, appeared in Court #5 around midday, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug. In sentencing him, the Magistrate took into account the three weeks and six days Ramirez had already spent at the Belize Central Prison and sentenced him to time served.

Ramirez, who had been unable to post bail following his arraignment, expressed relief at being released and said he was happy to be going home. He is expected to celebrate his 21st birthday on Sunday, August 23.

Ramirez was first arraigned on July 24, 2026, following his arrest a day earlier.

According to police, officers conducting motorcycle patrol on Euphrates Avenue near Allenby Street observed Ramirez acting suspiciously and allegedly attempting to evade them. Police said that as officers approached to conduct a search, Ramirez removed a white substance from his pocket and dropped it to the ground before attempting to flee.

Officers reportedly detained Ramirez and recovered the substance, which was later weighed at 0.13 grams and identified as cocaine.

Ramirez was subsequently charged with possession of a controlled drug and remanded to the Belize Central Prison, where he remained until Wednesday’s court appearance.

World.title: Cop accused in Kevin Depaz Caye Caulker murder receives 145 pages of disclosure
World.content:
Cop accused in Kevin Depaz Caye Caulker murder receives 145 pages of disclosure

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police Constable Lionel Rodolfo Urbina, who is on interdiction and remanded on charges stemming from the 2025 stabbing death of 19-year-old Kevin Matthew Depaz on Caye Caulker, returned to the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Wednesday.

Urbina was brought from the Belize Central Prison under a special security escort and appeared unrepresented in Court #3, where he was provided with 145 pages of disclosure, including seven DVDs containing evidence in the case.

The matter was adjourned to October 21, 2026, when Urbina is expected to appear in the San Pedro Magistrate’s Court for the commencement of his preliminary inquiry. He was further remanded to the Belize Central Prison.

Urbina was arraigned on January 22, 2026, on one count of murder in connection with Depaz’s death, as well as two counts of attempted murder and two counts of use of deadly means of harm in relation to injuries allegedly inflicted on Neesean Allen and Julian Canul. Reports identified Urbina as a 20-year-old police constable when he was charged.

The charges arose from a violent altercation on Caye Caulker during the early morning hours of June 30, 2025. Depaz, Allen and Canul became involved in a confrontation with off-duty Police Constables Urbina and Darneak Swasey after an earlier incident near Munchies Fast Food on Luciano Reyes Street. Depaz suffered a stab wound to the abdomen and later died at the Caye Caulker Health Centre, while several others involved in the confrontation were injured.

Following an investigation and directives from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, Urbina was charged in January. Swasey was not charged with Depaz’s murder.

Urbina remains on remand awaiting the preliminary inquiry.

World.title: Why Belize keeps speaking on Palestine, the century behind yesterday’s statement
World.content:
Why Belize keeps speaking on Palestine, the century behind yesterday’s statement

By Horace Palacio:

Yesterday, from Belmopan, the Government of Belize issued a statement about violence in a land more than twelve thousand kilometers away. It condemned escalating attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian civilians in the West Bank, called on Israel as the occupying power to protect the population, and reaffirmed that the occupation itself is unlawful and must end.

And somewhere in Belize, somebody read that and asked the honest question. Why does a small country with potholes to fix keep raising its voice about a war on the other side of the world?

Today I will answer that question properly. First the facts of this moment, then the century of history behind them, told fairly, and finally why this quarrel touches Belize far more directly than most Belizeans realize.

Start with what is happening right now, because the numbers are staggering. United Nations officials told the Security Council this month that the West Bank has reached a breaking point. Settler violence stands at the highest levels since UN monitoring began twenty years ago, more than 1,400 documented attacks this year across 260 communities, an average of six attacks every single day, dozens of Palestinians killed, roughly 3,800 driven from their homes in 2026 alone, among them more than a thousand children. UN investigators describe a repeating pattern, an outpost rises beside a Palestinian village, the harassment begins, the wells and grazing lands are cut off, the attacks come, and when the families finally flee, the land is taken. Israeli lives have been lost in this spiral too, and Belize’s statement mourned all civilian victims, as it should.

But none of this began this year. To understand it, you must walk back a century, and you must walk fairly, because this is the story of two peoples and one land, and each carries a wound the other rarely sees.

The Jewish people trace three thousand years of history, faith, and longing to that land, and by the late 1800s, fleeing massacres and hatred across Europe, a movement arose to rebuild a Jewish homeland there. In 1917, Britain, then conquering the region from the Ottomans, promised support for that homeland in a territory whose population was overwhelmingly Palestinian Arab, people rooted in those hills and orchards for countless generations. One land, promised in different ways to two peoples. Nearly everything since flows from that.

Then came the Holocaust, six million Jews murdered in Europe, and with it an unanswerable case for refuge. In 1947 the United Nations voted to partition the land into two states, one Jewish, one Arab. Jewish leaders accepted. Arab leaders rejected what they saw as the carving up of their homeland. War followed. In 1948 Israel declared independence and survived invasion by its neighbors, and in that same war some 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven from their homes, a catastrophe they call the Nakba, creating a refugee people whose descendants number in the millions today. One event, two memories, a state born and a homeland lost, both true at once.

The hinge of everything came in 1967. In six days of war, Israel captured the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza. And here is the plain meaning of the word that fills every news report, occupation. It means the Palestinians of those territories have now lived for nearly sixty years under a military authority they did not elect and cannot vote out, while Israel began moving its own civilians into the captured land, the settlers, whose communities now hold hundreds of thousands of people. International law is not vague here. Moving your population into occupied territory violates the Geneva Conventions, and in July 2024 the International Court of Justice, the world’s highest court, ruled that the occupation and the settlements are unlawful and must end. Belize made formal submissions in that very case, and the court’s opinion is the foundation of yesterday’s statement.

There were moments of hope. In the 1990s, the Oslo Accords brought mutual recognition and a promised path to a Palestinian state beside Israel. That hope bled out through an assassin’s bullet that killed Israel’s peacemaking prime minister, through terror bombings that shattered Israeli buses and cafes, through settlement growth that ate the map faster than negotiators could draw it, and through failed summits and a second uprising. Gaza spiraled into its own tragedy, an Israeli withdrawal, a Hamas takeover, a blockade, and war after war.

Then October 7, 2023. Hamas fighters stormed southern Israel and killed about 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and dragged roughly 250 hostages into Gaza, the deadliest single day for Jews since the Holocaust. Israel’s response engulfed Gaza in a war in which Gaza’s health authorities report tens of thousands killed and whole cities pulverized, a war that brought genocide proceedings before the ICJ, a case in which Belize formally moved to intervene last year. A fragile ceasefire finally took hold in late 2025. But while the world watched Gaza, the West Bank burned hotter each year, and that is the fire yesterday’s statement addresses.

Now, Belize’s record, and note something remarkable about it. This is one of the very few foreign policy questions on which red and blue have stood in one line. It was the Barrow government that recognized the State of Palestine in 2011. It was the National Assembly, in 2022, that passed resolutions on the character of the occupation. It was the Briceño government that suspended diplomatic ties with Israel in November 2023 over the bombardment of Gaza, that argued before the world court, that welcomed the 2024 opinion, and that filed to intervene in the genocide case in 2025. Fifteen years, two parties, one consistent voice. Whatever else divides Belmopan, this has not.

Why? Here is the answer, and it sits closer to home than Jerusalem. It sits on our own western border.

Belize is a small nation living beside a larger neighbor that has claimed, in our lifetimes, a vast portion of our territory. We did not answer that claim with an army we do not have. We answered it with law, taking the dispute to the International Court of Justice, the same court, the same law, the same principles now being tested in Palestine. The deepest rule of the modern world order, written in blood after the Second World War, is that territory shall not be acquired by force. That rule is not an abstraction to Belize. That rule is Belize. It is the legal ground beneath every square mile of this country.

So understand what is truly at stake when settlements devour occupied land and the world shrugs. Every time force creates facts and law fails to undo them, the shield that protects every small nation rusts a little more. If occupation can be normalized there, annexation can be normalized anywhere, and the countries that should tremble first are not the great powers. They are the small ones whose only armor is the rulebook. When Belize stands at the United Nations and insists that international law must govern, it is not meddling in a distant quarrel. It is paying the premium on its own insurance policy.

And there is something older than law in it too. We are a people who know what it is to be colonized, to have our land promised over our heads, to win nationhood against the appetite of the powerful. A nation with that memory recognizes the story when it sees it, and loses something of its soul the day it looks away.

Yesterday’s statement called for the protection of all civilians, Israeli and Palestinian alike, and for peace grounded in law, justice, and mutual security, two peoples, two states, side by side. That is not radical. That is the world’s own stated solution, endorsed again by more than 150 nations, waiting only for the courage to enforce it.

Small countries cannot send armies, Belize. We send principles. And in a world where might keeps testing the fence, a small nation’s loudest weapon is its refusal to accept that might makes right.

Yesterday, Belmopan fired that weapon again.

It should never holster it.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Higher light bills as BEL adds 1.5 cents per Kilowatt-hour in August
World.content:
Higher light bills as BEL adds 1.5 cents per Kilowatt-hour in August

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Electricity customers across Belize will pay more on their light bills this month as Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) applies a new Cost of Power Adjustment (COPA) of 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour, following a final ruling by the Public Utilities Commission (PUC).

The adjustment is the first under a new regulatory sandbox introduced by the PUC to monitor BEL’s actual cost of purchasing power. BEL reported that its actual power costs over the past six months were 4.3 cents per kilowatt-hour higher than the reference cost approved by the PUC.

However, customers will not be required to cover the full difference at once.

Under the new system, monthly COPA adjustments are capped at 1.5 cents per kilowatt-hour. For August, customers who are not enrolled under the Social Rate will therefore pay an additional 1.5 cents for every kilowatt-hour consumed. The charge will appear separately on electricity bills and is not subject to GST.

The PUC said the adjustment will be reassessed monthly based on verified information provided by BEL, meaning future COPA charges could increase, decrease, remain at zero or result in a rebate.

World.title: International News: Colombia quake losses estimated at $9.6 billion
World.content:
International News: Colombia quake losses estimated at $9.6 billion

By Zoila Palma: Colombia’s President Abelardo De La Espriella has estimated that the economic losses from last week’s powerful earthquake could reach 30 trillion pesos, or approximately $9.6 billion.

The preliminary assessment includes damage to buildings and infrastructure across affected areas, Reuters report.

De La Espriella said around 24.5 trillion pesos in losses were linked to buildings, while another 5.5 trillion pesos involved infrastructure. “Just imagine the scale of the disaster,” the president said.

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake caused widespread damage across western Colombia, including in the major cities of Cali and Pereira.

The disaster has reportedly killed 280 people, injured more than 4,000 and left another 143 people missing.

The earthquake represents the first major crisis facing De La Espriella, who took office only days before the disaster.

World.title: 30th Anniversary of National Pesticide Training & Certification Programme 1996 – 2026
World.content:
30th Anniversary of National Pesticide Training & Certification Programme 1996 – 2026

The Pesticides Control Board (PCB) has been dedicated to training and awareness-raising in pesticide life-cycle management since 1988 when the PCB Secretariat was established, and a nationwide awareness campaign launched in anticipation of the Pesticides Control Act, Chapter 216 of the Laws of Belize, coming into effect. The Pesticides Control Act, which came into effect on 31 December 1988, allowed for the phased implementation of the provisions dealing with the certification of users of restricted use pesticides.

On 17th August 1996, the Certified Users Regulations, S.I. No. 112 of 1996 came into effect. The Regulations require users of Restricted-Use Pesticides to be able to extract information from the label to follow dosage, application and precautionary directions; understand general principles of safe and effective pesticide use, storage and disposal; differentiate pesticides according to use and hazard; accurately and safely prepare the mixture to be applied; calibrate and maintain a knapsack sprayer, and understand responsibilities toward fellow workers and the public.

The Pesticides Control Board (PCB) has been dedicated to training and awareness-raising in pesticide life-cycle management since 1988 when the PCB Secretariat was established, and a nationwide awareness campaign launched The PCB’s National Pesticide Training and Certification Programme was thus launched in 1996, targeting an initial 10,000 farmers for training and certification in the first two years of programme implementation.

The Training and Certification Programme has evolved over the years and is currently implemented by a cadre of five inspectors/trainers. The training modules in pesticide life-cycle management are adaptable to different target groups and training approaches.

The programme is carried out nationally on an ongoing basis, with training sessions carried out routinely at centralized locations, and by request from partners and stakeholders.

From 2020 – 2025, almost 6,000 Certified Applicator licenses were issued to persons who were trained and certified as farm and trade applicators under the PCB’s National Pesticides Training and Certification Programme.

The Pesticides Control Board takes great pride in showcasing its flagship programme and its dedicated team of trainers who continue the legacy of PCB pioneers who laid the foundation for the PCB’s enduring mission in responsible pesticide management.

World.title: International News: Traffic in Strait of Hormuz slows as uncertainty over waterway persists
World.content:
International News: Traffic in Strait of Hormuz slows as uncertainty over waterway persists

By Zoila Palma: Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz slowed today as uncertainty continued over the status of the key waterway following a blockade during the Iran war.

Vessel-tracking data showed that many shipowners remained reluctant to use the strait amid conflicting signals about whether it has fully reopened to shipping, Reuters report.
