We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has unveiled plans to reduce income tax rates for an estimated 3.5 million people earning around or slightly above average salaries. The costs of the cuts would be covered by increasing the tax rate for large companies and individuals with the highest earnings. The changes, which Prime Minister Donald Tusk says are intended to “provide relief and assistance to the growing middle class”, would come into effect from next year – when the government is facing re-election. However, the proposals still require approval from parliament, where Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, has a majority, and President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. 📊 Nowa skala PIT będzie lepiej dopasowana do rosnących wynagrodzeń. Do 130 tys. zł pozostaje stawka 12%, między 130 a 150 tys. zł pojawi się 24%, a 32% zacznie obowiązywać dopiero powyżej 150 tys. zł. 💰 #WięcejWPortfelu pic.twitter.com/1S2MpSkVoC — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 19, 2026 The main elements of the proposed changes, which were outlined by Tusk and finance minister Andrzej Domański on Wednesday, are an increase in the earnings threshold at which the lowest rate of income tax is paid and the introduction of a new rate between the lowest and highest earnings brackets. Currently, there are two income tax brackets: the first taxes earnings of up to 120,000 zloty (around €27,800) at a rate of 12%; the second taxes earnings above that level at a rate of 32%. There is also a tax-free allowance for earnings of up to 30,000 zloty. Meanwhile, anyone who earns more than 1 million zloty a year pays an additional “solidarity levy” (effectively a third tax bracket) of 4% on income above that amount. Under the new proposals, the threshold for the first 12% tax bracket would be raised to 130,000 zloty. For earnings between 130,000 and 150,000 zloty, a new tax bracket of 24% would be introduced. Then earnings above 150,000 would be taxed at 32%. Tusk noted that, since his government took office, wages in Poland have increased by around 30%, bringing increasing numbers of people into the higher tax bracket. According to figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, in June this year, average monthly earnings at companies employing more than nine people were 9,401.58 zloty, the equivalent of almost 113,000 zloty a year. “We’re not talking about millionaires here; we’re talking about a growing middle class…on whose shoulders the financing of state security, defence spending, etc. rests to a large extent,” said Domański. “We want to change this…so that those who work hard to earn their average wage can clearly feel the relief,” added Tusk. “And we want this to be financed by the wealthiest companies and the wealthiest individuals, who have the lowest tax burden.” The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Therefore, in order to finance the middle-class tax cuts, Tusk and Domański announced that the government would seek to increase corporate income tax from 19% to 22% for firms and tax capital groups that generate annual revenues above €50 million. Meanwhile, the solidarity levy for individuals earning over 1 million zloty a year would be increased by one percentage point, to 5%. “I am absolutely convinced that this will make our tax system more equitable,” declared Tusk. However, he also conceded that raising the income-tax-free amount from 30,000 to 60,000 zloty – as his Civic Platform (KO) party promised to do within its first 100 days in office – would not be possible for budgetary reasons, in particular the need to finance high defence spending. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) tax free. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build savings and channel money into the domestic financial market https://t.co/1xDHHJGYKX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 14, 2026 The prime minister said that the planned tax changes would be discussed further this week at a cabinet meeting devoted to next year’s state budget, which is currently being prepared. The relevant legislation will subsequently be submitted to parliament, with the aim of bringing it into force in 2027. However, Tusk acknowledged that there is a strong possibility of a veto by Nawrocki, who has blocked dozens of government bills, including fiscal measures. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increase in the tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. Last month, he effectively blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits by sending it to the constitutional court for review. However, he did approve a law increasing the corporate income tax rate for banks. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 Next year’s budget will be closely watched given that Poland’s fiscal situation has become increasingly problematic in recent years. In 2024, the European Union placed Poland under its excessive deficit procedure, requiring Warsaw to commit to measures to bring down the deficit. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. Given that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in autumn 2027, it is unlikely that either the government or Nawrocki – who will be supporting the right-wing opposition – will be keen on any fiscal measures that either raise taxes or reduce spending in areas such as social policy and defence. Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to promote itself internationally and attract more tourists from “key European markets” and the United States. The new initiative, which has the slogan “Poland. More than you expected”, features global Polish icons such as football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, and Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, who received Polish citizenship last year. A series of videos, the first of which was released Tuesday, will aim to present Poland as “modern, safe, diverse and authentic”, as well as “defying stereotypes”, says sports and tourism minister Jakub Rutnicki. Commissioned by his ministry and launched by the Polish Tourism Organisation (POT), the campaign will be conducted in Germany, Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States. The first video promotes Warsaw, Poland’s capital, and features Lewandowski, Rubik and Eisenberg appearing near the city’s landmarks. Polish actor Nikodem Rozbicki, meanwhile, plays the role of renowned 19th-century Polish composer Fryderyk Chopin. In the 30-second spot, Chopin’s character declares that Warsaw is “where my heart is” – a reference to the fact that Chopin’s heart, preserved in cognac, was brought back to the city from Paris by his sister shortly after his death in 1849 and is now immured in a pillar in the city’s Holy Cross Church. Lewandowski, who recently joined US football team Chicago Fire, tells viewers that Poland offers “more than you expected”, a reference to the campaign’s main slogan, which suggests to viewers that Poland may surprise them positively. “Research shows that people who have visited Poland rate it much more favourably than their previous perceptions or media reports suggested,” notes POT in its press release. Magdalena Krucz, the head of POT, adds that she believes the campaign “will be as surprising to audiences as Poland itself is to tourists who come to us for the first time”. However, the slogan is not new: it has been used by POT to promote Poland since 2021. The new campaign will also feature Nobel Peace Prize winner and former president Lech Wałęsa, who led the Solidarity movement that brought down Poland’s former communist regime. POT notes that he remains “one of the most recognisable symbols in the world of the fight for freedom and democracy”. The music is arranged by Radzimir Dębski, better known as Jimek, a Polish composer and conductor who has regularly performed with US rap legend Snoop Dogg. This year, Time Out magazine rated Kraków the 16th best city in the world. World.title: Warsaw Uprising veteran and activist Wanda Traczyk-Stawska dies aged 99
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Wanda Traczyk-Stawska, a veteran of the Warsaw Uprising against Nazi-German occupation during World War Two, has died aged 99. Traczyk-Stawska, who survived imprisonment in German camps after the uprising, in her later years became a vocal advocate for the rights of women and disabled people. “Warsaw has lost someone extraordinary,” wrote Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, announcing her death on Wednesday. “A heroine, a soldier…but above all a teacher who, throughout her life, taught us what matters most: courage, dignity, and responsibility for our fellow human beings.” Odeszła Pani Wanda. Trudno w to uwierzyć. Warszawa straciła kogoś wyjątkowego – Bohaterkę, żołnierkę Powstania Warszawskiego, Honorową Obywatelkę miasta. Ale przede wszystkim nauczycielkę, która przez całe życie uczyła nas tego, co najważniejsze: odwagi, godności i… pic.twitter.com/uSNcsZ7c1P — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) August 19, 2026 Traczyk-Stawska, born in Warsaw in 1927, was only 12 years old when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. She initially became involved in the Grey Ranks (Szare Szeregi), an underground resistance movement associated with the Polish scouting movement, participating in sabotage operations. She later joined the Home Army (AK), Poland’s main resistance force, and, at the age of 17, served as a riflewoman and liaison during the Warsaw Uprising, taking the nom de guerre “Pączek” (meaning “Bud”). Traczyk-Stawska was seriously injured while fighting in the uprising. After the revolt was defeated, she was taken prisoner and subsequently held in various prisoner-of-war camps in Germany until the end of the war. After returning to Poland, Traczyk-Stawska earned a degree in psychology and began working as a teacher of disabled children in Warsaw. At the same time, she became an active figure in commemorating the uprising and its participants. In her final years, Traczyk-Stawska also became politically active. In 2018, she visited parliament to support a protest by disabled people and their carers, who were seeking more state support. Two years later, at the age of 93, she and another female uprising veteran, Hanna Stadnik, joined the mass Women’s Strike protests that broke out in response to the introduction of a near-total ban on abortion under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. “We women will not relent this time,” she told broadcaster TVN at the time. “In the uprising, we fought for our freedom, because there is no dignity without freedom. If we are currently treated like incubators, we have the right to fight for our dignity…We will fight – unarmed, but to the last woman – not to be treated like objects.” Traczyk-Stawska was also among a group of female Uprising veterans who that year criticised PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński for wearing, during a speech condemning the Women’s Strike protests, a badge featuring the anchor symbol that was used by the Home Army during the war. She was also an advocate for women’s rights more broadly. In 2023, in a speech at the 79th anniversary of the uprising, Traczyk-Stawska noted that, “at the beginning, the generals shouted: ‘Why do we need so many women?'” But, by the time the uprising ended, “we had been given the same rights as boys. And we won’t get rid of these rights. Because everyone, whether a man or a woman, is a citizen of this country and has equality written into the constitution”. Her speech then became overtly political, saying that “this [PiS] government needs to be completely changed, as it doesn’t remember that women have their own position enshrined in the constitution. That we are equal to men.” In both the 2020 and 2025 presidential elections, Traczyk-Stawska expressed support for the candidacy of Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that is PiS’s main opponent. However, in both elections, Trzaskowski lost to PiS-backed candidates. Odeszła Wanda Traczyk-Stawska ps. „Pączek” – Bohaterka, Patriotka, wzór odwagi i niezłomności. Pokazywała, że prawdziwy patriotyzm to budowanie wspólnoty, empatia i otwartość na świat. Cześć Jej pamięci! 🕯️🤍 Najgłębsze wyrazy współczucia dla Bliskich. pic.twitter.com/nY0ijDSBlJ — Monika Sikora ⚡️ (@Moni_Sikora) August 19, 2026 Following news of Traczyk-Stawska’s death, many prominent figures paid tribute to her, in particular from the current KO-led ruling coalition. “Farewell, heroine,” wrote KO leader and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, sharing a photo of himself with Traczyk-Stawska and quoting one of her statements: “Do not stand, do not watch when evil happens, but react immediately, for that is your duty.” While she had fought against German occupation, Traczyk-Stawska later called for reconciliation. In her 2023 speech, she called Germany “our best neighbour” and said that the two countries must now “stand together”, including supporting Ukraine against Russian aggression. Today, Germany’s ambassador to Poland, Miguel Berger, expressed his “great sadness” at Traczyk-Stawska’s death, calling her an “advocate of dialogue in the process of Polish-German reconciliation and a passionate champion of peace, freedom, and human dignity”. „Nie stój, nie patrz, gdy się zło dzieje, tylko reaguj natychmiast, bo to jest twój obowiązek." – Wanda Traczyk-Stawska Żegnaj, Bohaterko. pic.twitter.com/MhfqlszVcI — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, says that they are “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia. Last week, judicial authorities in Poland confirmed that they had received a letter purportedly from Romanowski, who is wanted in Poland for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. In the document, Romanowski claimed to be in Transnistria and requested safe passage back to Poland. However, as the authenticity of the letter had not been confirmed, some media outlets speculated that the politician may not, in fact, be in Transnistria. Meanwhile, the Moldovan authorities quickly announced that they had no record of Romanowski travelling to Transnistria, which is a landlocked territory that only has borders with Moldova and Ukraine and operates no commercial passenger flights. A former government minister who fled criminal charges in Poland appears to be in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. Marcin Romanowski's whereabouts have been unknown since he left Hungary earlier this year https://t.co/MPWroFVbMe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 13, 2026 Speaking on Tuesday morning, Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, said they have “still not confirmed” the veracity of Romanowski’s claim to be in Transnistria, reported broadcaster RMF. However, shortly afterwards, speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said he wanted to address the issue given there has been “a great deal of speculation and misinformation regarding Mr Romanowski and his whereabouts”. “I can say that the intelligence services of other countries in the region with which we cooperate have confirmed to us the information that Mr Romanowski is 99% certain – I say that just in case – to be in Transnistria, in Tiraspol,” he continued, referring to the capital of the breakaway region. "Pan Romanowski znajduje się na 99 procent w Naddniestrzu. Chyba nie trzeba tu komentarzy" Donald Tusk podczas posiedzenia rządu ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/muVQVKrOTs — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 18, 2026 Transnistria is a narrow strip of land in eastern Moldova that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s as the Soviet Union collapsed, fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Its flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. Various experts and former intelligence officials have noted that it would be impossible for Romanowski to enter without Russia’s approval. The fact that Romanowski appears to be hiding there has led to criticism of PiS, the party Romanowski still technically serves as an MP and which publicly takes a strongly anti-Russian position. “If it is true that [Romanowski] is in Transnistria, a republic not recognised by anyone, de facto controlled 100% by Russia, then it must have happened through and with the participation of Russia,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last week. “Escaping under the Russian umbrella is the worst possible thing, because not only are they cowardly, but they are also joining the enemy of Poland,” he added. In his remarks today, Tusk said that Romanowski’s likely presence in Transnistria “speaks for itself regarding not only Mr Romanowski but the entire political group that covered up for and benefited from such people, and continues to cover up for them”. PiS politicians have largely avoided commenting, noting that it has not been confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. However, deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek last week admitted that, if Romanowski did trael there, he would have “crossed a line”. Nie wyprzedzajmy faktów – powiedział poseł PiS Zbigniew Kuźmiuk, pytany, czy Marcin Romanowski może zostać zawieszony w partii.https://t.co/IQzuS8Ad7O — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 14, 2026 Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government from 2019 until 2023, when the party lost power to a new ruling coalition led by Tusk. In 2024, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 11 crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group and using crime as a source of income. However, he instead fled to Hungary, where he was granted asylum by the then-government of Viktor Orbán, a PiS ally. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, his successor, Péter Magyar, promised to extradite both Romanowski and Zbigniew Ziobro, the former PiS justice minister who had also fled criminal charges in Poland and been granted asylum by Orbán. However, as Magyar was sworn in as the new prime minister, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains, and Romanowski disappeared, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians deny the accusations against them and claim to be victims of political persecution by Tusk’s government. Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges. He denies wrongdoing and calls the case political revengehttps://t.co/BXdQgWm61q — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In his comments on Tuesday morning, Nowak said that prosecutors had found “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. Polish prosecutors are still, however, attempting to confirm Romanowski’s whereabouts and secure his extradition to Poland to face justice. He is subject to a European Arrest Warrant. However, that applies only in EU countries, and Moldova is not a member of the bloc. The European Commission has granted approval for a consortium led by American transportation conglomerate FedEx to take over Polish delivery giant InPost in a deal worth €7.8 billion (33.7 billion zloty). InPost, which operates in France, Spain, the UK, Portugal, Italy and the Benelux countries, as well as in its home market, confirmed on Tuesday that it had received the green light from the EU for the deal, which was announced in February. If it goes through, the takeover will see a consortium made up of FedEx along with existing InPost investors, Advent, A&R, and PPF, purchase all of the company’s shares at a price of €15.60 each. Konsorcjum inwestorów, w którym jednym z uczestników jest amerykański @FedEx, uzyskało bezwarunkową zgodę KE na nabycie wszystkich akcji @InPostPL @RBrzoska https://t.co/F4AleTCViO — WNP.PL (@wnppl) August 18, 2026 The group behind the deal says the aim is to help InPost continue its recent rapid expansion. The firm will retain its name, branding and Polish headquarters. Founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska will remain in place, as well as being a major shareholder through A&R, which is his investment vehicle. The deal will see Advent, an American private equity firm, and FedEx each hold 37% of InPost. A&R would have 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. Currently, PPF holds 28.75%, A&R 12.49%, and Advent 6.5%. The initial offer period for the consortium’s takeover was due to end on 27 July. However, on 22 July, it was extended until 18 September due to the fact that antitrust proceedings in the EU and Vietnam were still ongoing. In its announcement today of EU approval, InPost noted that it is still awaiting a green light from the Vietnam Competition Commission but expects a decision to be made by 8 September. Although the Polish company has no operations in Vietnam, FedEx has been present on the market since 1994. InPost has grown rapidly in recent years through its pioneering use of parcel lockers, first in Poland and then across western Europe. In the UK, it has established a network of over 14,000 parcel lockers, including in branches of the British Post Office. In June this year, French President Emannuel Macron thanked InPost for its latest investment in France, where the firm – which operates there through its subsidiary Mondial Relay – is planning to spend a further €500 million to expand its presence. In the first quarter of 2026, InPost saw its revenue rise 31% year-on-year to reach 3.9 billion zloty. That included 121% growth in the UK, 28% in the Eurozone and 9% in Poland itself. However, the group’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA), a measure of profitability of business operations, were down 4% to 902 million zloty. World.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among those to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. World.title: Students in Czech Republic Face Higher Rents as Housing Costs Rise
World.content:
Students looking for private accommodation in Czech university cities this year are facing higher rents, with prices for some types of housing up by as much as 14 percent compared with 2025.

The increase comes as demand for student accommodation reaches its annual peak ahead of the winter semester.

Data from several Czech property platforms show that the busiest period started earlier this year, meaning students who have not yet found accommodation may face a more limited and expensive selection in September.

Those unable to secure a place in a student dormitory generally have three alternatives: renting a small apartment alone, taking a private room in a shared apartment, or renting a bed in shared accommodation.



The most expensive option is usually a small one-bedroom apartment with a kitchenette, typically around 30 square meters. According to the REMAX network, monthly rents for these apartments range from more than CZK 7,000 in Ústí nad Labem to around CZK 14,000 in Prague.

Prices have not increased evenly across the country. Brno recorded the sharpest rise, with rents for small apartments increasing by 12 percent year on year.

Prague saw a 4 percent increase, while rents in Hradec Králové and Pardubice rose by almost 9 percent. Olomouc was one of the few exceptions, with prices falling by slightly more than 2 percent.

Rent is not the only expense students need to consider. Utilities, water and maintenance charges can add another CZK 1,000 to CZK 2,000 a month, according to property platforms.

Private rooms offer a cheaper alternative

Many students instead rent individual rooms in shared apartments, with properties ranging from smaller 2+kk and 2+1 layouts to larger 4+kk and 4+1 apartments. Czech property portal Sreality.cz puts the average cost of a private room in university cities at between approximately CZK 5,700 in Opava and CZK 11,500 in Prague.

In Prague, private rooms listed on Sreality.cz were around 10 percent more expensive than during the same period last year. Prices in Brno, meanwhile, remained roughly unchanged.

Shared housing remains the cheapest option

For students on a tighter budget, sharing an apartment and renting a bed rather than an entire room remains the least expensive choice. The more people share a property, the lower the individual housing costs tend to be.

Even this option, however, has become more expensive. According to UlovDomov.cz, the cost of renting a bed has increased by several hundred Czech crowns compared with last year.

Prague remains considerably more expensive. A bed in a two-bedroom apartment costs almost CZK 5,500, about CZK 1,200 more than a bed in a three-bedroom apartment.

World.title: 58 Years Since Warsaw Pact Troops Invaded Czechoslovakia
World.content:
On August 21, 1968, Soviet troops and their Warsaw Pact allies invaded Czechoslovakia to bring an end to that country’s brief period of political liberalization, called the Prague Spring.

People still recall waking up on that fateful morning to find that Soviet-led Warsaw Pact tanks had rolled into the country, crushing all hope of implementing the democratic reforms of the Prague Spring. Shocked citizens took to the streets in protest of the invasion.

About 500,000 troops were involved in the invasion and occupation, during which 137 Czechoslovaks died and some 500 were wounded.

One of the key battles was for the control of Czech Radio, similar to the one that took place at the end of the Second World War.

The invasion ended the political and economic reforms led by Alexander Dubcek and reasserted dominant Soviet and Communist authority in Czechoslovakia.

It also helped establish the Brezhnev Doctrine, which Moscow said allowed the U.S.S.R. to intervene in any country where a communist government was under threat.

Within the following year, resistance faded, Dubček was removed from office, his reforms were undone, and a more Soviet-controlled government was installed.

World.title: From Munich to Prague: Enrique Paredes on the Future of International Education
World.content:
FAST FACTS

Enrique Paredes

Marketing & Enrollment Manager, AAU

MBA – International Marketing

4 countries / 2 continents

International marketing + Customer Experience + Digital transformation

At AAU:

56.8% increase in lead-to-enrollment conversion

26% reduction in acquisition costs

53.1% increase in local enrollment

AAU #1 University in Europe based on student reviews

From Corporate Munich to Academic Prague

After building a career in international marketing, customer experience, digital transformation and commercial strategy across the US, Europe and Latin America, Enrique Paredes now leads marketing and enrollment strategy at Anglo-American University in Prague.

Having lived in four countries across two continents, Paredes believes Prague has become one of Europe’s most attractive destinations for international students, not only because of its affordability, but also because of the academic, professional, and personal opportunities the city offers.

His journey into higher education was not originally planned. Originally from El Salvador, he completed his MBA in Munich with a specialization in International Marketing, an experience that gave him firsthand insight into the challenges and opportunities international students face when building their lives abroad.

After graduating, an opportunity with a major international company brought him to Prague, where he has now lived for almost eight years. He describes the move as both a significant career opportunity and a step in the direction he wanted his professional life to take.

Moving from the corporate world into higher education required a shift in mindset, but not in ambition.

“One thing that’s driven me throughout my career is ambition, purpose, and above all, determination to achieve. That’s what has kept me motivated to reach where I am today.”

Prior to entering higher education, Paredes held international marketing, project management, and customer experience leadership roles at Anheuser-Busch InBev, where he led digital initiatives across Europe. Earlier in his career, he worked on enterprise solutions at SAP and contributed to market insights and research projects for Volkswagen Group (VAG) in Germany.

That corporate background continues to influence how Paredes approaches higher education. He views recruitment not simply as marketing, but as a combination of customer experience, data, commercial strategy and long-term relationship building.

From Marketing to Enrollment Leadership

Although his title is Marketing & Enrollment Manager, Paredes’ responsibilities extend well beyond marketing and student recruitment. His role covers marketing strategy, recruitment and enrollment initiatives, decision making that shapes the organization, as well as projects that influence the broader prospective and student journey.

For him, supporting students starts long before they arrive in Prague.

“These are young people who are stepping away from home, often for the first time, to become independent. We understand how challenging that can be, and we try to support them in every way we can.”

Since joining AAU, Paredes has helped transform marketing and student recruitment into a more data-driven, commercially focused operation, redesigning elements of the recruitment funnel, digital acquisition strategy, CRM processes and cross-departmental collaboration. That shift has translated into measurable results, including a 56.8% increase in lead-to-enrollment conversion, a 26% reduction in acquisition costs, and a 53.1% increase in local enrollment, among other results.

His philosophy is simple: attracting students is only the beginning. The goal is to ensure they have a smooth transition academically, professionally, and personally, while creating an experience that stays with them long after graduation.

Recruitment Is About Fit, Not Just Volume

For Paredes, effective recruitment is not simply about generating as many leads as possible. It is about understanding what prospective students actually want and determining whether the institution can genuinely meet those expectations.

“The goal isn’t to convince everyone. It’s to understand the student, understand what they need and show them honestly whether we are the right fit. If we’re not, we should be transparent about that and focus our efforts on students where we can create real value.”

The Case for a Dual-Accredited Degree

One of the strongest advantages Paredes sees at AAU is its dual accreditation.

The university holds both US and Czech accreditation, giving students the opportunity to earn a degree recognized internationally while studying in Prague, one of Europe’s most affordable major capitals.

For students comparing the cost and experience of studying in the United States with studying in Europe, Paredes believes the model offers significant value.

AAU’s US accreditation comes through the same institutional accreditor used by universities including Stanford and UC Berkeley. This allows students to pursue an internationally recognized US-accredited education while benefiting from the lower cost of living associated with studying in Prague.

For Paredes, the dual accreditation also provides students with flexibility as they consider where they want their careers to develop.

Students who are unsure whether their future lies in Europe or the US can use their university years to explore different opportunities before making that decision.

As he puts it, students have “another three years to discover where you want your career to take you.”

Small Classes, Real-World Learning

Paredes believes universities should prepare students for the workplace, not simply help them pass exams.

He contrasts AAU’s approach with traditional university environments, where lecture halls can contain hundreds of students and learning may focus heavily on taking notes, memorizing information, and preparing for exams.

At AAU, classes average between 17 and 20 students, allowing for more direct interaction with professors, many of whom bring professional experience from industry.

Learning is centered on discussion, collaboration, and solving practical problems, including challenges sometimes presented by real companies, rather than relying solely on theoretical knowledge.

“That’s what students will encounter outside university. We want them to graduate already understanding how to solve real-world challenges.”

Paredes also points to the importance of practical experience. Every AAU student completes an internship before graduation, giving them an opportunity to gain professional experience while still studying.

A More Diverse Student Community

AAU’s recruitment strategy has also evolved in recent years.

According to Paredes, the university has intentionally expanded its visibility across multiple markets, helping create a more balanced student population between Czech and international students while welcoming students from more than 80 countries.

He sees this diversity as one of the university’s greatest strengths.

“When students work every day with classmates from different cultures and perspectives, they naturally develop communication skills, adaptability, and a global mindset that employers increasingly value.”

For Paredes, international education is therefore not only about what students learn in the classroom. The people they meet and the environments in which they study can also shape how they approach their future careers.

AI Is an Intern, Not a Replacement

Asked how universities should respond to the rapid development of artificial intelligence, Paredes offers a simple analogy.

“I personally treat it as an intern. I wouldn’t give a task to AI that I would not give an intern. It’s help. It’s not a solution.”

Rather than resisting AI, he believes universities should teach students how to use the technology effectively while strengthening the skills that remain uniquely human, among them:

Critical thinking

Leadership

Communication

Creativity

Ethical decision-making

“You can use AI to support research or analyze data, but when it comes to making important decisions, that responsibility should always remain human.”

For Paredes, the challenge for universities is therefore not simply deciding whether students should use AI, but teaching them how to use it responsibly and critically.

Why Prague?

Having lived in four countries, Paredes believes Prague offers a combination that is difficult to find elsewhere. He highlights the city’s safety, affordability, history, international atmosphere, and quality of life.

One everyday moment particularly stood out to him after moving to Prague: seeing children walking home safely at night.

“It’s something I don’t take for granted because it’s not something I’ve experienced in every country I’ve lived in.”

For international students, he believes these everyday realities matter just as much as the academic experience. Studying abroad means building a life in a new city, and factors such as safety, affordability, transport, culture, and opportunities outside the classroom can all influence that experience.

Advice to Future International Students

For students considering studying abroad, Paredes encourages them to think beyond earning a diploma.

International education, he says, is ultimately about personal growth and the experiences that come from stepping into an unfamiliar environment.

“Everything good in life happens outside your comfort zone.”

He points to his own international experiences, including building a business with a friend in Switzerland, as examples of how studying and working abroad can create opportunities that extend far beyond graduation.

For him, choosing where to study is therefore also a decision about the environment in which students will develop personally and professionally.

Final Quote

Asked to summarize what AAU represents in one sentence, Paredes offers a final thought:

“Choosing a university isn’t only about where you’ll study for the next three years. It’s about where you’ll build the skills, network, and experiences that shape the next thirty.”

World.title: Prague’s Groovy Market Fest Returns After a Successful Debut
World.content:
A new urban festival is aiming to become a regular fixture on Prague’s cultural calendar after attracting 1,200 visitors to its first edition in Riegrovy sady.

Groovy Market Fest, held on August 1, brought together food, design, music and local brands in a format inspired by European city markets.

According to the organizers, around 85% of visitors were tourists or foreign residents of Prague, highlighting the event’s appeal beyond the Czech-speaking audience.



The festival will return to Riegrovy sady on September 5, with further editions planned for October, November and December.

From Barcelona to Prague

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food culture.

Their interest in international gastronomy also led them to compete in Spain. In 2025, they won first place in the Cooking The Street competition, where their dish was judged by a professional panel that included chefs Beñat Ormaetxea and Jon Kepa Aurrecoetxea.

After returning to Prague, they decided to develop their own event, drawing inspiration from markets such as Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market.

The First Edition

Food Garden focused on gastronomy, while Palm Street featured local products and handmade goods. The Design Zone presented Czech brands working in fashion, design and art.

Rather than filling the site with as many vendors as possible, the organizers selected a smaller number of participants. They say the approach was intended to create a more coherent experience for visitors.

Music was another part of the programme, with live performances and DJ sets throughout the event. Visitors could also attend a masterclass focused on preparing the festival’s signature Groovy cocktail.

Additional editions are scheduled for October 3, November 7 and December 5, all at the same location.

Tickets for upcoming editions are available through GoOut.

World.title: Faster Than the Metro. New Bus is Now Linking Prague 8 and Prague 6
World.content:
A new bus service running through Prague’s Blanka tunnel has begun operating, offering a direct connection between the northern part of the city and Dejvice.

Bus line 145 connects Čimice and Kobylisy in Prague 8 with Hradčanská and Dejvická in Prague 6. The journey takes around 15 minutes, according to Prague’s public transport authority ROPID.



The same trip by metro requires a change between lines C and A in the city centre and takes around 22 minutes.

Including the time spent walking through stations and using escalators, the journey can take about half an hour.

The first day of operation brought mostly positive results, with many buses arriving on time or even ahead of schedule. The real test will come during regular weekday traffic, when congestion around Prague is heavier.

Where the new bus runs

In the direction from Čimice to Dejvice, line 145 serves:

Sídliště Čimice – Čimice – Libeňská – Řepínská – Podhajská pole – Čimický háj – Písečná – Služská – Kobylisy – Okrouhlická – Vychovatelna – Hradčanská – Vítězné náměstí – Dejvická

The return route follows the same corridor in the opposite direction.

The key feature of line 145 is its use of the Blanka tunnel, allowing buses to avoid the city centre and provide a direct connection between Prague 8 and Prague 6.

The new route is expected to make commuting easier for residents of Čimice, Kobylisy and surrounding neighbourhoods, while providing an alternative to the metro for journeys towards Dejvice and Hradčanská.

World.title: Leo Express to Launch Direct Prague–Brno Trains in December
World.content:
Leo Express is set to begin operating direct trains between Prague and Brno in December, marking the private carrier’s first direct connection between the two cities.

The company has already been serving passengers in the South Moravian Region, but its trains have so far bypassed Brno.

Over the past year, travellers from towns such as Hodonín and Břeclav have been able to use Leo Express services to reach Prague, travelling via Přerov and Olomouc.



The new Prague–Brno service will change that, putting the carrier directly on one of the Czech Republic’s busiest rail routes.

There is, however, one limitation for passengers travelling to Prague.

Leo Express trains do not serve Prague Main Station. In Prague, passengers must use Praha-Libeň station, which may be less convenient for those travelling to the city centre.

Leo Express was founded by businessman Leoš Novotný and has operated passenger trains in the Czech Republic since 2012.

The company has gradually expanded its network in the Czech Republic and abroad, competing with established operators such as České dráhy and RegioJet.

The Prague–Brno connection is expected to become another important part of the company’s Czech network from December.

World.title: Romanian Community to Celebrate Culture and Traditions in Prague
World.content:
The Romanian community in Czechia will come together in Prague on September 6 for the 12th edition of the Romanian Celebration, an annual event highlighting Romanian culture, traditions and the community’s ties with Czech society.

The main event will take place at the Ethnographic Section of the National Museum of the Czech Republic in Kinský Park, Prague 5.

The program will bring together Romanian music, dance, food, literature and activities for children.



Organized by the Association of Romanians in the Czech Republic (ARRC), the event is part of a wider cultural project running from March 1 to November 30, 2026.

Visitors can expect traditional music and dance performances, educational activities for children, cultural exhibitions, book presentations and Romanian gastronomy.

The event is aimed at members of the Romanian community, Romanian-speaking families, children and young people, as well as Czech residents interested in Romanian culture.

According to ARRC, the project aims to preserve and promote Romanian cultural and linguistic identity among Romanians living in the Czech Republic while creating opportunities for greater interaction between the Romanian and Czech communities.

“Through this project, we aim to offer the Romanian community, Romanian speakers, and lovers of the Romanian language a space for meeting, dialogue, and celebration of our cultural values, while also contributing to the consolidation of intercultural relations between Romania and the Czech Republic,” the ARRC leadership said.

World.title: Czech Fish Farmers Take Emergency Measures Amid Prolonged Drought
World.content:
Fish farmers reduce or suspend supplementary feeding to lower oxygen consumption, reports say.

Fish farmers in the Czech Republic have begun taking emergency measures as a prolonged drought, worsened by high temperatures across Europe, strains water supplies.

Facing water shortages, fish farmers have reduced or suspended supplementary feeding to lower fish oxygen consumption, while ponds are being regularly aerated, according to the report.



Several ponds have also been netted earlier than usual.

In the Třeboň area, which delivers tons of carp for the Czech Christmas table, part of the 200-hectare Koclířov pond has been drained and the fish moved to holding tanks.

More than a third of the water is missing from the region’s famous system of fish ponds due to the drought. The water level in Lake Svět, for example, has fallen by 98 centimetres. High temperatures are also causing water to evaporate more quickly.

The Czech government is expected to address the 2027 budget, upcoming elections and measures to tackle worsening drought.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has pledged an extra CZK 4 billion for drought-related measures. If approved, ministers will present plans for implementing them.

World.title: New analysis: Hungary’s government is full steam ahead with adopting the euro
World.content:
Hungary’s new government says it has inherited a significantly worse fiscal position than expected, but argues that its first months in office already point to a change in direction. With the government targeting euro adoption by 2030, reducing the budget deficit and public debt is set to become one of the defining economic challenges of the coming years.

From a 3.7 per cent target to an 8.3 per cent warning

The 2026 budget was originally approved with a deficit target of around 3.7 per cent of GDP. According to the new government’s review, however, the deficit could have reached approximately 8.3 per cent without corrective measures. The Finance Ministry now expects the deficit to be around 7.5 per cent of GDP, while MBH Analysis Centre forecasts a slightly more favourable figure of about 7 per cent.

The government says EU funds and other measures have helped prevent the situation from deteriorating further. The budget review also identified additional pressures, including higher local government, road development and healthcare spending, as well as EU recovery funds previously included in calculations but ultimately inaccessible.

At the same time, stronger forint exchange rates, lower yields and the recovery of EU funding have helped improve the fiscal outlook. The government plans to amend the 2026 budget and set a new deficit target by the end of August. A 2027 budget and medium-term fiscal plan are expected by the end of October.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The deficit could fall substantially in 2027

There are several reasons to expect the deficit to decline next year. Some exceptional expenditures weighing on the 2026 balance will disappear. The so-called “weapon money” payment, for example, is expected to worsen this year’s deficit by roughly half a percentage point of GDP, as reported by Index.

Interest costs could also fall faster than previously anticipated. Lower government bond yields and potential interest-rate cuts would reduce the cost of servicing Hungary’s debt, providing another boost to the budget. Recent figures have offered an early sign of improvement. Finance Minister Kármán András reported a HUF 524 billion (EUR 1.44 billion) budget surplus in July and highlighted a significant reduction in the deficit.

However, he also warned against drawing premature conclusions. Some of July’s improvement resulted from lower-than-planned spending, and certain payments may simply have been postponed rather than eliminated. The real test will therefore be whether fiscal discipline remains in place once these temporary effects disappear.

The 2030 euro target raises the stakes

The government’s ambition to introduce the euro in 2030 gives the fiscal debate a longer-term dimension. If Hungary is to meet the conditions for euro adoption, it will need sustained progress on its deficit and public debt. A single year of improvement will not be enough; the country would need a credible, multi-year fiscal trajectory.

This is why analysts argue that a predictable consolidation plan could be more valuable than a dramatic one-year deficit reduction. Temporary spending cuts or one-off revenues might improve the headline figure, but would not necessarily resolve the underlying structural problem.

A realistic multi-year programme would show investors, businesses and credit-rating agencies how the government intends to reduce the deficit and debt while maintaining economic stability.

Stay up-to-date: Central bank claims meeting euro adoption criteria would benefit Hungary’s entire economy

Wider economic challenges remain

Fiscal consolidation alone will not solve Hungary’s broader economic problems. MBH analysts point to weak external demand, particularly subdued German industrial performance, as a continuing risk. Hungary’s dependence on imported energy also leaves the economy exposed to international oil and gas prices, while geopolitical tensions could add further pressure.

Tax and competitiveness measures, investment decisions and expectations surrounding possible euro adoption will therefore also influence Hungary’s growth prospects. For now, the government can point to early signs of fiscal improvement. But the decisive question is whether these developments mark a lasting change rather than a temporary adjustment.

If the 2030 euro ambition is to become more than a political target, Hungary will need years of consistent fiscal discipline, steadily falling deficits and a credible path for reducing public debt.

World.title: The Sziget Festival at a crossroads: can one of Europe’s biggest festivals be revived?
World.content:
Sziget Festival has survived ownership changes, a pandemic and more than three decades of transformation. But after a financially disappointing 2026 edition, the Budapest event faces perhaps a more fundamental question: what should Sziget actually be in the years ahead?

There is something unusual about discussing the future of Sziget Festival in terms of survival. For decades, the event seemed almost permanent: every August, a corner of Budapest was transformed into a temporary international city, populated by music fans from across Europe and far beyond.

Yet the numbers from 2026 make uncomfortable reading.

According to Economx, this year’s festival attracted around 350,000–360,000 visits, considerably below the organisers’ target of 400,000 and down from approximately 416,000 the previous year. The financial result was also worse than planned.

Last year’s loss was around HUF 2.8 billion (approximately EUR 7.7 million), while the aim for 2026 had been to reduce the deficit to HUF 1.5 billion (around EUR 4.1 million). That target was not achieved.

Why Sziget Festival is struggling

The reasons go beyond whether this year’s line-up was strong enough.

Founder Károly Gerendai, who returned to the business after the departure of foreign owner Superstruct Entertainment, pointed to a four-month delay in preparations and ticket sales. That mattered because historically almost a third of passes had been sold during this early sales period.

International demand also weakened. A stronger Hungarian forint made Budapest more expensive for overseas visitors, while higher travel costs and geopolitical conflicts affected several important markets, including the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Germany, Italy, Israel and Ukraine. Meanwhile, Hungarians accounted for 53% of the 2026 audience.

There is an uncomfortable truth behind these figures. Sziget can no longer rely on being the inexpensive Central European alternative to Western festivals.

Gerendai acknowledged that the enormous price advantage Sziget enjoyed 10 or 20 years ago has diminished. He nevertheless argued that visitors still receive relatively good value because a Sziget pass covers considerably more festival days and programmes than many similarly priced European events.

From Student Island to the Island of Freedom

For international readers, it is worth remembering how far Sziget has travelled.

The festival began in 1993 as Diáksziget, or Student Island, created by Gerendai, musician Péter Müller Sziámi and their collaborators on Óbuda Island in the Danube. The first edition attracted around 43,000 paying visitors and was primarily a Hungarian cultural gathering rather than an international pop spectacle.

It gradually became one of Europe’s largest music and cultural festivals. International stars arrived, visitor numbers multiplied and the event developed its distinctive “Island of Freedom” identity. Crucially, Sziget was never supposed to be only a row of large concerts: theatre, circus, world music, art, community programmes and encounters between nationalities became part of its appeal. The festival itself says visitors from more than 100 nationalities now attend.

That history matters because it may also contain the answer to Sziget’s present difficulties.

The future may depend on becoming more Sziget, not less

Gerendai believes the model built primarily around an impressive list of headliners is no longer sufficient. Instead, the festival’s future could depend on cultural diversity, community experiences and something its competitors cannot easily reproduce: Budapest itself.

As he told Pénzcentrum, few festivals of this scale take place inside a major European capital. Sziget visitors can spend the afternoon exploring Budapest and return to the island for the evening. Turning the festival and the city into one combined travel experience could therefore become one of its strongest international selling points.

That argument feels particularly convincing. Sziget is unlikely to win a permanent bidding war for every superstar against the world’s richest promoters. But no rival can copy Budapest, the Danube or the strange experience of stepping out of an ordinary European capital and into a temporary festival city.

The operational picture is also less bleak than the financial headlines suggest. Pénzcentrum reported that consumer protection authorities inspected nearly 120 catering outlets during the festival. The overall findings were favourable, with most businesses complying with legal and food-safety requirements and minor problems generally corrected quickly. As we wrote earlier, Sziget attendance plunges as founder warns festival must “move forward to break free”

Foreign visitors show why Sziget matters beyond the festival gates

The economic importance of international visitors becomes particularly clear in new figures published after this year’s Sziget Festival. According to a GKI survey of 529 festivalgoers, an average foreign visitor spent HUF 255,000 (around EUR 700) during their trip, compared with HUF 108,000 (around EUR 296) for a Hungarian guest. Even after subtracting the roughly HUF 95,000 (EUR 260) that foreign visitors spent on travel, their expenditure remained substantially higher. Perhaps just as importantly for Sziget’s positioning, only 28% of foreign respondents considered the festival expensive, while 11% actually regarded its prices as low.

If you missed it: Sziget Festival 2026 in numbers: foreigners vs Hungarians, unsatisfied organisers, the festival’s future

The impact also extends well beyond Óbuda Island. Among respondents who do not live in Budapest, 83% spent at least one additional day in the capital or its surroundings outside their time at the festival; 29% stayed for another three to five days, while a further 25% remained for more than five. These visitors spent an average HUF 98,000 (around EUR 268) outside Sziget itself. With the festival estimating that around 58,000 foreign guests attended in 2026, their combined spending amounted to roughly HUF 15 billion (about EUR 41 million). That gives Gerendai’s argument about selling Budapest and Sziget as a combined experience a measurable economic dimension: attracting international festivalgoers does not only fill the island, but also hotels, restaurants and other businesses across the capital.

Sziget Festival will return in 2027 – but the real test starts now

There is no immediate farewell on the horizon. Sziget Festival has already confirmed its return in 2027 as a five-day event, August 10-14, 2027.

The full-price Super Early Bird pass has been set at EUR 299, or EUR 318 including the handling fee. Advance registration has already begun, even before the first artists have been announced.

That is both a statement of confidence and a gamble.

The question is no longer simply whether Sziget can attract a bigger headliner next summer. It is whether the festival can convince a new generation that travelling to Budapest for several days offers something that an arena concert, a weekend festival or an endless stream of online entertainment cannot.

Perhaps the way forward is hidden in Sziget’s own past. The festival became important not because it was merely big, but because it felt different. Its future may depend on rediscovering exactly that.

World.title: Beethoven’s timeless voices to open the VIII. MiraTone Festival in Budapest
World.content:
The VIII. MiraTone Festival and Academy opens on August 22 with a special musical journey through time: at FUGA Budapest Center of Architecture, the V4 String Quartet will perform three of Beethoven’s defining string quartets. The evening not only offers a glimpse into three distinct periods of the composer’s creative life, but also evokes a Hungarian musical event that took place nearly 180 years ago.

MiraTone Festival 2026

Founded by violinist Miranda Liu, the MiraTone Festival and Academy will bring outstanding artists and young talents from the international classical music scene to Budapest for the eighth time between August 22 and 30. Recognized with the EFFE Label by the European Festivals Association for the third time, the 2026 edition presents its richest program to date, with 12 major concerts for audiences to enjoy.

The opening event itself promises a remarkable musical journey. On August 22, the V4 String Quartet will perform three of Beethoven’s string quartets: the C minor Op. 18 No. 4, the E-flat major “Harp” Quartet, and the A minor Op. 132. Heard together, the three works trace three distinct stages of Beethoven’s artistic development, from the dramatic energy of the young composer to one of the mature master’s most profound and personal creations.

Following in the Footsteps of a 179-Year-Old Concert

The evening gains an additional dimension through its connection to Hungarian musical history. The program was inspired by a Beethoven concert held in London in 1847, where the sixteen-year-old Joseph Joachim performed at the invitation of the renowned Beethoven Quartet Society. By then, the Hungarian violinist was already regarded as one of Europe’s greatest young musical talents; he would later become one of the most influential musicians of the 19th century.

The V4 String Quartet now recreates the program of this historic concert in Budapest. Its members—Miranda Liu, Daniel Rumler, Tomáš Krejbich and Bartosz Koziak—bring together the musical cultures of four Visegrád countries, while the ensemble itself represents the region’s cultural cooperation through music.

The concert thus looks both backward and forward: it begins with a historical precedent, yet comes alive through the interpretation of a contemporary international community of musicians. Beethoven’s music contains everything that makes these works so immediate nearly two centuries later—struggle and hope, drama and release, pain and consolation.

The opening concert also establishes the tone for the nine-day MiraTone Festival. This year’s program features works by 27 composers, alongside concerts by international guest artists and hundreds of master classes, chamber music rehearsals and professional programs. World.title: 30 years of UNESCO recognition: fascinating facts about Hungary’s Pannonhalma Archabbey – Photo gallery
World.content:
Pannonhalma Archabbey, one of Hungary’s most remarkable historic and religious sites, marks 30 years on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2026. Founded more than a millennium ago, the Benedictine monastery has witnessed the birth of the Hungarian state, survived wars and political upheavals, and remains a living religious and cultural centre today. Here are some of the stories that make Pannonhalma unique.

UNESCO World Heritage Centre inscribed the Millenary Benedictine Abbey of Pannonhalma and its Natural Environment on the World Heritage List in 1996. The organisation highlighted not only its architecture, but also the extraordinary continuity of a monastic community whose history stretches back more than 1,000 years.

Pannonhalma Archabbey is older than the Kingdom of Hungary

For foreign visitors, perhaps the most striking fact is just how far back Pannonhalma’s story reaches.

Benedictine monks settled on the hill in 996, after being invited by Prince Géza, father of Hungary’s first king, Stephen I. That makes the monastery four years older than the traditional foundation date of the Christian Kingdom of Hungary in 1000.

The historic Pannonhalma Archabbey (Hungary) is listed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Source: Anadolu The historic Pannonhalma Archabbey (Hungary) is listed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Source: Anadolu The historic Pannonhalma Archabbey (Hungary) is listed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Source: Anadolu

The monks played an important role in spreading Christianity and Western European learning in the emerging Hungarian state. According to UNESCO, they founded Hungary’s first school, while the monastic community became an important centre of culture in Central Europe.

This connection with the origins of Hungary is one reason Pannonhalma is more than simply another medieval monastery: its history runs almost parallel to that of the country itself.

A thousand years of architecture can be seen in one place

Pannonhalma did not emerge in its present form at once. Instead, successive generations added to and rebuilt the monastery, leaving behind an unusual mixture of architectural periods.

The oldest surviving parts of the complex date from the early 13th century. Today, visitors can explore the basilica and crypt, medieval cloisters and the monumental 19th-century library. UNESCO considers this succession of architectural styles one of the defining features of the World Heritage site.

Rather than freezing one moment in history, the buildings effectively document how the abbey changed over hundreds of years.

It is still a monastery – not simply a monument

One of the most important aspects of Pannonhalma Archabbey can easily be overlooked by tourists: monks still live here.

The Benedictine community continues its religious life in the same place where monks settled in the 10th century, while education also remains part of the abbey’s mission. UNESCO specifically notes that the complex continues to house both the monastic community and a school.

Visitors may even encounter this living tradition directly. The abbey’s current visitor programme allows guests to attend the community’s midday prayer, subject to the monastery’s schedule, the Pannonhalmi Főapátság official site said.

Its library contains around 400,000 volumes

The vast classical library is one of Pannonhalma’s most recognisable interiors, but its importance goes well beyond appearance.

The Archabbey says its collection contains approximately 400,000 volumes, making it Hungary’s oldest book collection. A surviving document from around 1090 was already listing dozens of codices belonging to the monastery.

Its holdings include medieval manuscripts and early printed works, reflecting the Benedictines’ centuries-old role in preserving and transmitting knowledge.

The library also made international headlines for a rather unexpected reason in 2025. Around 100,000 historic books had to undergo treatment after a serious infestation of drugstore beetles – also known as bread beetles – was discovered. The insects are attracted to starch- and gelatine-based materials used in old bookbinding. Conservators placed books in oxygen-free conditions for several weeks to eliminate the pests. Details – CNN also alerted: beetle infestation destroys Hungary’s oldest library – PHOTOS

If you missed it: Discover the most beautiful libraries of Hungary – PHOTOS

The World Heritage site includes much more than buildings

The official UNESCO designation deliberately includes Pannonhalma’s natural environment.

The monastery sits prominently above the western Hungarian landscape, roughly 20 kilometres from Győr, and its surroundings include gardens, woodland and an arboretum. The abbey says the protected area contains more than a thousand plant species and almost 150 bird species.

The historic Pannonhalma Archabbey (Hungary) is listed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Source: Anadolu

Herbal cultivation also has deep roots here. According to the Archabbey, monks have been involved in healing and cultivating medicinal plants since the monastery’s earliest centuries, while more than 30 varieties of herbs are grown in the present-day herbal garden.

Benedictine wine has also made a comeback

Wine is another link between Pannonhalma’s medieval heritage and its modern life.

Viticulture formed part of the traditional monastic economy, but the abbey’s historic vineyards were largely lost during the 20th century. The Benedictines eventually began rebuilding that tradition by repurchasing former land and planting new vines.

A modern winery was subsequently established, opening to visitors in 2004.

It is an example of how Pannonhalma has avoided becoming a static historical attraction: ancient monastic traditions have instead been adapted to contemporary life.

Why Pannonhalma Archabbey remains unusual after 30 years of UNESCO status

Three decades after receiving World Heritage status, perhaps Pannonhalma’s greatest curiosity is not any individual treasure hidden in its library or basilica.

It is continuity.

The monastery was founded before the Kingdom of Hungary, its monks helped shape the country’s Christian and intellectual culture, and more than a thousand years later the hill is still home to Benedictine religious life, education, books, gardens and winemaking.

Many World Heritage sites preserve what disappeared long ago. Pannonhalma Archabbey is different because much of the tradition UNESCO recognised in 1996 is still alive.
