Its launch in 2030 would more than triple national ammonia capacity and create Kazakhstan’s first industrial-scale urea production, with around 700 permanent jobs.

The integrated model will also increase processing. Around 543,000 tons of ammonia will be used to produce urea and ammonium nitrate, creating greater value from domestic production.

From importer to exporter

Kazakhstan currently has no potassium fertilizer production, despite more than 6.6 billion tons of confirmed potassium salt reserves. Domestic demand of nearly 14,000 tons is therefore fully covered by imports.

The Qazaq Kalium project at the Satimola deposit plans to produce 1.5 million tons of potassium fertilizer annually by 2030. Even if domestic demand rises to 300,000 tons, most of the planned output could be exported.

KazAzot Prime also has significant export potential, with planned annual exports of approximately 470,000 tons of urea and 98,000 tons of ammonium nitrate. Export volumes are expected to use the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR), or the Middle Corridor.

Rising domestic demand

Fertilizer use in Kazakhstan is increasing rapidly, from 679,000 tons in 2023 to 1.8 million tons in 2025. The 2026 target is 2.3 million tons, or up to 73% of scientifically justified demand.

Yet consumption remains below international levels. Kazakhstan applies an estimated 25-35 kilograms per hectare, compared with a global average of 150-160 kilograms. State compensation of up to 60% of fertilizer costs provides additional support for farmers.

A new export opportunity

Developing nitrogen, phosphate and potassium production could help Kazakhstan reduce imports while creating a new, higher-value export industry.

Key indicators will be completion of the planned projects, continued growth in domestic fertilizer use, and Kazakhstan’s ability to reach international markets through the Middle Corridor.

If these plans are implemented, fertilizers could become an important new pillar of Kazakhstan’s chemical industry, supporting food security while strengthening the country’s export portfolio.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Export Growth Signals Shift Toward Stronger Global Market Presence
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s foreign trade entered a stronger phase in January-June, with exports growing faster than imports and non-resource and processed goods gaining ground in major international markets. The key question is whether this represents a temporary improvement in trade performance or a stronger shift in the structure and geography of Kazakhstan’s exports.

Exports outpace imports

In January-June, Kazakhstan’s exports reached $40.3 billion, up 8.6% compared to a year earlier, while imports increased 5.4% to $31.5 billion. Total foreign trade turnover rose 7.2% to $71.8 billion, producing a positive trade balance of around $8.9 billion.

Faster export growth matters because it shows external demand is driving trade expansion more than imports. Exports increased by approximately $3.2 billion compared with the first half of 2025, while the overall trade balance remained firmly positive, reported the Ministry of Trade and Integration on Aug. 18.

Non-resource exports gain momentum

More important, however, is the performance of non-resource and processed goods. Their exports reached $15.2 billion, up 17.6% year on year. This was almost six times faster than the 3% growth in imports of the same category.

Compared with January-June, non-resource and processed-goods exports have nearly doubled, reaching their highest level in the period covered by the available figures. This suggests that export growth is increasingly supported not only by traditional commodities but also by goods with greater processing and industrial value.

New markets strengthen

The geography of this growth is particularly notable. China remained Kazakhstan’s largest export market, receiving approximately $7.51 billion, or 18.6% of total exports. Italy followed with $6.98 billion, while Russia, Türkiye, the Netherlands, France and Uzbekistan were also among the leading destinations.

Türkiye stands out as one of the strongest growth markets. Total exports to Türkiye rose by 94.3%, while exports of non-resource and processed goods nearly doubled, from $950 million to $1.91 billion.

The United Kingdom also recorded rapid growth, with exports increasing 2.7 times to $671.8 million.

China remains a key market

Exports of non-resource and processed goods to China increased 12.1% to $3.67 billion. Together, Türkiye, the United Kingdom and China generated roughly $1.8 billion in additional exports compared with the first half of 2025. Uzbekistan, France, Afghanistan and Hong Kong also recorded significant growth.

The broader geography gives Kazakhstan greater access to Asian, European and regional markets and reduces reliance on any single destination.

Industrial goods drive growth

The commodity mix also points to expanding industrial potential. Copper and copper cathodes accounted for $2.84 billion, uranium for $1.51 billion and ferroalloys for $1.1 billion. Exports of copper and copper products increased by nearly 58%, while copper ores and concentrates rose roughly 43%.

The shift toward higher-value exports is also visible in agriculture. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin described Kazakhstan’s oilseed-processing industry as “a successful example of economic diversification,” noting that export revenue from oilseed products had quadrupled to $963 million in four years.

Agricultural products are gaining ground too. Sunflower oil exports reached $533 million, while animal feed products accounted for $438 million in January-June.

Metals, processed products and agricultural goods are gaining importance alongside established resource exports.

The next challenge: moving up the value chain

The next challenge is to turn export growth into lasting gains in higher-value products. This will depend on investment in processing, logistics, infrastructure and market access.

The key question is whether Kazakhstan can sustain growth in processed exports and expand into new markets. The first half of this year points to a shift toward more diverse and higher-value exports with a wider global reach.

World.title: What to Expect from Kurultai Elections in Kazakhstan This Week
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s citizens will elect the members of the Kurultai, a new unicameral Parliament, on Aug. 23, putting a redesigned parliamentary and electoral system into practice for the first time.

Beyond determining who receives the 145 seats, the vote will offer an early indication of how the new rules affect party competition, political representation and the composition of the legislature.

Kazakhstan’s new constitutional framework took effect on July 1, replacing the former bicameral Parliament, consisting of the Mazhilis (lower house) and Senate (upper house), with a 145-member Kurultai elected for five years through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency. Parties must receive at least 5% of the vote to enter the legislature.

Seven political parties are contesting the election, with 545 candidates registered for the race. According to the Central Election Commission (CEC), women, young people and persons with disabilities account for a combined 43.9% of registered candidates, exceeding the 30% cumulative quota required for these groups on party lists.

First test of a new parliamentary model

One of the changes is the disappearance of single-member constituencies from national parliamentary elections.

Under the previous system, legislation passed through the Mazhilis before moving to the Senate. Under the new model, the Kurultai concentrates legislative consideration, and adopted laws are then sent to the President.

Standing committees will take on a larger role in the process. The Kurultai can establish up to eight permanent committees to conduct preliminary reviews of legislation and other parliamentary work. The new framework also formally defines the parliamentary majority and opposition, with opposition representatives guaranteed certain roles in committee leadership, parliamentary hearings and government question sessions.

The election will also mark a transition for the executive branch. After the new Kurultai is elected, the government must formally submit its resignation. The President then has 10 days to decide whether to accept it.

Speaking to The Astana Times, Rassul Kospanov, a senior researcher at the Center for Regional Analysis at the National Analytical Center, said concentrating legislative authority in one chamber could also increase the prominence of its chairperson.

“I think the role of the speaker will become stronger. Previously, the highest legislative authority was divided between two chambers, and that influence was also divided between two speakers; now, in effect, there will be one much more powerful speaker. Much will depend on who takes the position and whether that person can become a trusted and prominent figure for the public,” he said.

Parties face a different electoral test

The electoral system has changed just as significantly. In the previous Mazhilis, 69 of 98 deputies were elected through party lists and 29 through single-member constituencies. All 145 Kurultai members will now be elected through closed party lists in one nationwide constituency, meaning voters choose a party rather than individual candidates within its list.

The 2023 Mazhilis election provides the most recent benchmark. Six parties crossed the 5% threshold, with Amanat, then ruling party that later merged with Adilet, receiving 53.9% of the party-list vote and securing 40 proportional seats. It also won 22 of the 29 single-member constituencies, giving it 62 of the chamber’s 98 seats overall.

That comparison is limited, however, because the system and the party field have both changed. Single-member constituencies have been abolished at the national level, while Amanat has since merged with the Adilet Party.

Kospanov highlighted one direct consequence of removing constituency races: citizens who are not affiliated with political parties no longer have an independent route to the national legislature.

“With the transition to a single nationwide constituency, it is no longer possible to become a member of Parliament if you are not affiliated with a party. There are ordinary citizens and politically active people who do not see a political party they are prepared to join, but under the previous system they still had the right to run. That channel is now completely closed to them,” he said.

He noted, however, that the distinction was less clear in practice, as many deputies elected from single-member constituencies also had political party affiliations.

Kamila Amurtayeva, an expert consultant at the Center for Institutional Analysis and Reforms at the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development (KIPD), told The Astana Times that the fully proportional system both strengthens political parties and raises the demands placed on them.

“There is a paradox here that both strengthens parties and makes their task more difficult,” she said.

“Formally, their role increases sharply because the entire Kurultai is now formed through them, but at the same time they can no longer compensate for a weak party brand with the popularity of individual single-member candidates. Parties will now have to explain to voters not only who represents them, but why voters need that particular party,” she explained.

According to Amurtayeva, the election can therefore serve as a “stress test” for the party system, showing whether parties have stable electoral constituencies and sufficiently distinct political identities.

Seven parties compete for Kurultai seats

Those distinctions have become more visible over nearly four weeks of campaigning. The Astana Times has followed the race through weekly reviews, from the parties’ initial policy pitches and regional campaigning to the first televised debate, an education-focused debate, and the final campaign week’s focus on the rule of law.

Adilet has campaigned on jobs, housing, infrastructure, healthcare and governance. Aq Jol and Respublica have emphasized entrepreneurship, domestic production and economic reform, with the two competing more directly for business-oriented and economically liberal voters. Auyl has remained focused on agriculture and rural communities, while Baytaq has centered its campaign on environmental protection and sustainable development. The Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) and the People’s Party of Kazakhstan have placed greater emphasis on social policy, labor rights, healthcare and social protection.

Under the new electoral model, those distinctions matter more because every parliamentary seat depends on a party’s nationwide result. The election will therefore provide a clearer measure of which parties have built support around their platforms rather than individual constituency candidates.

Who enters the first Kurultai

The result will also be measured by who ultimately takes the 145 seats.

The 43.9% share of women, young people and persons with disabilities among registered candidates is higher than the statutory 30% cumulative quota. The quota also applies when parties distribute the mandates they win, making the final composition of the Kurultai an important measure of how representation changes under the new system.

Amurtayeva emphasized that the composition of the party factions will therefore matter alongside vote shares and seat totals.

“I would also look at whom the parties actually bring into the Kurultai. Under a fully proportional system, a party has much greater influence over the formation of the deputy corps and therefore bears greater responsibility for its quality. The important indicator will not simply be the percentage of votes or number of seats, but whether the lists renew representation, bring in new professional and social groups, and provide broad regional representation,” she explained.

Kospanov expects some personnel renewal but emphasized that new names should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of an immediate transformation of the political system.

“The renewal will probably be more personal than political, because we are primarily talking about new personnel and new faces. At the same time, many of those described as new faces have simply not served in the Mazhilis or Senate before. A significant number have experience in local maslikhats [local legislative bodies]. For that reason, I would not expect major systemic changes immediately after the election,” he said.

What to watch on Aug. 23

The immediate result will answer several questions about how the new system is taking shape: how many of the seven parties cross the 5% threshold, how the 145 seats are distributed among them and how concentrated or fragmented the first Kurultai becomes.

Turnout will provide another measure of electoral participation, though Amurtayeva highlighted that it should not be treated on its own as an indicator of the quality of political representation.

“High turnout is important for the legitimacy of an election, but by itself it does not tell us about the quality of political representation. The intrigue, in my view, is no longer only whether the voter comes to the polling station, but what the voter does with that vote. These elections are becoming a kind of stress test for the party system itself,” she said.

International observers will provide a separate assessment of how the new electoral framework operates in practice. In an Aug. 13 statement, the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly announced that nearly 80 parliamentarians and staff from around 30 countries would deploy for the election, working with the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) and a delegation from the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe. Their preliminary findings are expected to be presented in Astana on Aug. 24.

Gábor Hajdu, the OSCE special coordinator leading the short-term observers, said the mission would examine how the constitutional and electoral changes are implemented. Lucija Tacer Perlin, head of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly delegation, emphasized that the observers would assess the process without drawing conclusions in advance.

“Our task is not to prejudge how Kazakhstan’s new system will perform, but to examine the process carefully and impartially,” she said.

For Amurtayeva, however, the distinction between the election result and the reform’s broader effect is central to what can realistically be expected from Aug. 23.

“We will know the result of the election quite quickly – the numbers and the names of the deputies – but the result of the reform itself will become clear much later. Roughly a year after the election, it should be possible to see what each party has actually brought into the work of the Kurultai: what issues it advances, whose interests it represents and what changes it has been able to achieve,” she said.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Industrial Growth Reveals Diverging Paths for Manufacturing and Mining
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan’s economy continued to expand in the first seven months of 2026, with investment and manufacturing providing an important source of growth even as mining output declined and exports remained heavily dependent on raw materials.

New data from the Bureau of National Statistics points to a mixed but potentially significant economic pattern. Industrial output reached nearly 40 trillion tenge (US$83.3 billion), while investment in fixed capital rose to 11.5 trillion tenge (US$24.9 billion) and foreign trade turnover reached $71.8 billion in the first half of the year.

Taken together, the figures suggest that Kazakhstan is attracting and directing more capital toward production and infrastructure. However, the structure of exports shows that the country’s external earnings remain strongly concentrated in commodities, particularly crude oil.

Manufacturing offsets decline in mining

Industrial production reached 39.97 trillion tenge (US$83.23 billion) between January and July, increasing by 3% compared with the same period last year. The most important driver was manufacturing. Output in the sector grew by 9% to 18.83 trillion tenge (US$39.2 billion), accounting for 47.1% of Kazakhstan’s total industrial production.

Growth was particularly strong in pharmaceutical production, which increased by 38.5%, followed by fabricated metal products (+35%), chemicals (+26.9%), and machinery, which grew by 22%. Production of rubber and plastic products increased by 18.6%, food production by 13.9%, and other non-metallic mineral products by 9.4%.

At the same time, mining and quarrying declined by 4.4% to 18.42 trillion tenge (US$38.4 billion). Crude oil production fell by 8.9%, while natural gas output declined by 5.5%.

The contrast between the two sectors is important. Kazakhstan’s industrial economy has historically depended heavily on extractive industries, but the latest figures show manufacturing expanding at a time when mining output is falling. Manufacturing also slightly exceeded mining in the value of industrial production during the seven-month period.

This does not mean that Kazakhstan’s economy has moved away from commodities. Instead, it suggests that other parts of the industrial sector are becoming more capable of supporting growth when output in extractive industries weakens.

Growth was also recorded in electricity, gas, steam and air-conditioning supply, which increased by 12.2%, and in water supply, wastewater and waste collection, which rose by 9.5%.

Investment concentrates on industry, infrastructure and construction

Investment in fixed capital reached 11.5 trillion tenge (US$24 billion) between January and July, increasing by 7.7% in comparable prices. Industry received the largest share of investment, accounting for 41.6% of the total. Manufacturing attracted 14.7% of all investment, while mining accounted for 14%.

The composition of spending also shows that investment is focused primarily on physical expansion. Construction and capital repairs of buildings and structures accounted for 62.1% of investment, while 33.6% was directed toward machinery, equipment and transport.

Transport and warehousing received 17% of total investment, followed by real estate operations at 18.6%. Agriculture, forestry and fisheries accounted for 5.7%. The regional distribution, however, was highly uneven. Investment increased by 94.4% in the Ulytau Region, 56.4% in the Zhambyl Region and 37.5% in the Turkistan Region. Growth was also recorded in the Almaty Region (+16.4%), Abai Region (+16.1%), West Kazakhstan (+13.3%), and the Pavlodar Region (+11.9%).

Meanwhile, investment declined by 24.5% in the Zhetysu Region, 14% in Shymkent, 10.4% in the Karagandy Region and 4.5% in the Mangystau Region. Astana accounted for 11.3% of all investment in fixed capital, while Almaty accounted for 10.8%.

Nearly half of all investment came from large and medium-sized enterprises. Companies’ own funds remained the main source of financing, accounting for 67.7%. Budget funds represented 14%, although their volume declined by 32% compared with January-July 2025.

Bank loans financed 5.6% of investment, while other borrowed funds accounted for 12.7%, including 3% from non-residents.

This financing structure suggests that the current investment cycle is being driven primarily by corporate resources rather than direct state spending or foreign borrowing. At the same time, the scale of investment in construction and industrial sectors indicates that much of the spending is aimed at expanding production capacity and physical infrastructure.

Trade growth still depends on commodities

Kazakhstan’s foreign trade turnover reached $71.8 billion in the first half of 2026, increasing by 7.2% year-on-year. Exports grew faster than imports, rising by 8.6% to $40.3 billion. Imports increased by 5.4% to $31.5 billion.

The resulting figures underline Kazakhstan’s continuing ability to generate a substantial trade surplus. However, the composition of exports remains concentrated.

Crude oil and crude petroleum products accounted for 46.5% of total exports. Refined copper and unwrought copper alloys represented 7.1%, copper ores and concentrates 5.1%, radioactive chemical elements and isotopes 3.7%, and ferroalloys 2.7%. Together, these figures show that Kazakhstan’s export performance continues to depend heavily on energy and mineral commodities.

China was the largest destination for Kazakh exports, accounting for 18.6%, followed closely by Italy at 17.3%. Russia accounted for 8.6%, Türkiye 8%, the Netherlands 6.4% and France 5.7%.

On the import side, Russia remained Kazakhstan’s largest supplier, accounting for 30.9%, followed by China at 29.1%. Germany accounted for 4.8%, the United States 4.2%, South Korea 2.5% and Türkiye 2.2%.

Passenger cars and other motor vehicles represented the largest individual category of imports at 3.2%, followed by telephone equipment at 2.7%, medicines and petroleum gases at 2.5% each, and electric generating sets and rotary electrical converters at 2.3%.

Investment is growing faster than economic diversification

The latest data presents two parallel stories about Kazakhstan’s economy. On one side, manufacturing is growing faster than the overall industrial sector and offsetting a decline in mining. Investment is rising, with more than two-fifths directed toward industry, while significant resources are being spent on machinery, equipment, construction and infrastructure.

On the other side, almost half of Kazakhstan’s exports still come from crude oil and petroleum products. Mining remains one of the largest recipients of investment, while the country’s trade performance continues to depend heavily on demand from major external markets for commodities.

If investment in manufacturing, equipment and new production capacity results in a broader range of competitive industries, Kazakhstan could gradually reduce the gap between its growing domestic industrial base and its commodity-heavy export structure. If not, higher investment and manufacturing output may expand the economy without fundamentally changing its dependence on raw-material exports.

World.title: At 25, Shanghai Cooperation Organization Is More Relevant Than Ever
World.content:
By almost any measure, multilateralism is under pressure. Major powers are increasingly divided, conflicts are multiplying, and international institutions struggle to produce agreement on basic security challenges.

Against this backdrop, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, which marks its 25th anniversary this year, offers a different story: while many multilateral frameworks are losing influence, the SCO has expanded, diversified its agenda and become one of the key platforms for dialogue across Eurasia.

Its success is not accidental. The organization has endured because it was built not around ideology or military commitments, but around solving practical security problems. Its strength lies in a simple principle: cooperation does not require countries to agree on everything.

The SCO’s origins illustrate this point. Before the organization was established in 2001, the Shanghai Five mechanism had already transformed relations among China, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Russia. The breakthrough came in 1997, when the five countries signed an agreement on the mutual reduction of military forces in border areas and confidence-building measures. It covered almost 7,500 kilometers of borders and established a zone of reduced military activity extending about 100 kilometers on both sides.

At the time, this was an extraordinary diplomatic achievement. Countries with complicated historical legacies chose cooperation over confrontation. Border regions that might have remained sources of tension gradually became areas of economic cooperation and people-to-people exchanges.

Seen from today’s perspective, when unresolved territorial disputes continue to destabilize regions around the world, the lesson is clear: security problems are easier to prevent than to resolve after they become conflicts.

That success also gave the organization credibility and created the conditions for its expansion. Yet the SCO’s lasting relevance cannot be explained by its history alone.

First of all, its greatest strength is the political culture that has developed within the organization. The so-called Shanghai Spirit emphasizes mutual trust, equality, consultation, respect for diversity and the search for common ground. These are not simply diplomatic slogans. They describe a working method that allows countries with different political systems and sometimes conflicting interests to keep engaging in regular dialogue.

Second, the SCO’s growing importance is also reflected in its role within Eurasia’s security architecture. Although the SCO is not a military alliance, its strategic weight is difficult to overlook. Its membership includes four nuclear-armed states – China, India, Pakistan and Russia, as well as four important space powers – China, India, Iran and Russia – with advanced missile capabilities and significant space-launch and transportation capabilities. This concentration of strategic, technological and military potential gives the organization considerable geopolitical weight.

Third, the SCO has demonstrated a remarkable capacity to evolve. Rather than being confined to its original mandate, the organization has never remained static and continuously adapted its agenda to the changing needs of Eurasia. The SCO began as a mechanism for building confidence and resolving border issues (1996-2001). It then expanded its focus to combating terrorism, extremism and transnational crime (2001-2015). As regional economies became more interconnected, the organization broadened its agenda to include transport connectivity, trade, investment and cultural exchanges (2015-2025).

Today, the SCO is entering another phase: sustainable development is emerging as the organization’s new growth driver. The emphasis is shifting toward practical cooperation in green development, the digital economy, poverty reduction, energy, education, logistics and cross-border connectivity.

This evolution reflects one of the SCO’s defining characteristics: it is a flexible, pragmatic, results-oriented organization. Rather than pursuing ideological alignment, it identifies areas where member states have tangible common interests and develops practical mechanisms for cooperation.

For Kazakhstan, the SCO has a special meaning. As a founding member, Kazakhstan has participated in shaping the organization from its very beginning. For a middle power at the heart of Eurasia, the SCO is an important instrument of international agency, allowing Kazakhstan to contribute to regional security, promote dialogue and advance cooperative development.

Kazakhstan’s role in the SCO also reflects a broader diplomatic approach: engaging constructively with different powers Kazakhstan’s ability to build bridges and connect different perspectives is becoming more prominent.

The SCO’s 25th anniversary, therefore, is more than a milestone. Its history demonstrates that pragmatic multilateralism can work when institutions address real problems, respect differences and remain capable of adapting. The next 25 years will test these principles. The SCO will undoubtedly face disagreements among its members and pressure to respond to a rapidly changing international environment. Its future relevance will depend on whether it can preserve what made it successful in the first place: pragmatism, dialogue and the ability to turn differences into areas of cooperation.

The author is Aliya Mussabekova, the head of the International Security Department at the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies under the President of Kazakhstan.

World.title: A Gal-Media TV station building has burned down in Abkhazia
World.content:
In Abkhazia, a building housing the regional TV company Gal-Media has been destroyed by fire. Without their equipment, journalists now plan to film their reports using smartphones.

The TV company, which serves the predominantly ethnic Georgian Gali district, occupied several rooms in a four-storey building. The fire destroyed the editing room, recording room and studio where the main news bulletins were produced. It also destroyed all the studio equipment, the server room and the entire archive.

Security camera footage helped investigators identify the exact point where the fire started. It broke out near the ceiling, where a layer of soundproofing foam had been installed. Specialists believe an old bundle of electrical wiring may have caused the fire. Although the premises underwent renovations in 2016, workers did not replace this old section of wiring.

Gali district administration head Konstantin Pilia said emergency services were investigating the incident and expected to release their findings in the coming days. Specialists are also assessing the extent of the damage and the cost of repairs and replacement equipment. The district and republican authorities have already begun taking steps to restore the TV station’s operations.

Because of the fire, Gal-Media will continue operating on a limited basis. Journalists will temporarily use their surviving personal smartphones and laptops to prepare reports. This will allow them to publish information on social media. However, the station’s regular analogue broadcasts will be suspended for the time being, Gal-Media head Thea Arshba said.

The Gali district administration is already looking for temporary premises for the TV company’s staff while repairs are under way.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Gal-Media TV station premises destroyed by fire in Abkhazia

World.title: From C5 to C6: how Azerbaijan is reshaping balance of power in Central Asia
World.content:
Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

On 16 November 2025, the five Central Asian states accepted Azerbaijan as a full member of the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State. Eight months later, on 31 July, Ilham Aliyev took his place at the table at an informal summit in Cholpon-Ata not as a guest, but as one of six equal participants.

The format is now officially known as “Central Asia and Azerbaijan”. The term “C6” has already entered expert vocabulary and is being used at conferences.

The change expands Central Asia’s political and economic cooperation to the western shore of the Caspian Sea. It also turns Azerbaijan from an external partner into a full participant in a route connecting the region with Turkey and Europe.

How did the format emerge and why has it expanded?

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed the idea of a consultative mechanism at the UN in September 2017. The first meeting took place in Astana on 15 March 2018. The format’s advantage was its simplicity: without a treaty, permanent secretariat or supranational bodies, the leaders of the five countries could directly discuss borders, water resources, trade and security.

Azerbaijan did not join the process immediately. Ilham Aliyev attended meetings in Dushanbe in 2023, Astana in 2024 and Tashkent in 2025 as an honorary guest. Since the beginning of 2023, he has visited Central Asian countries 16 times, while the region’s leaders have travelled to Azerbaijan 26 times. In 2025, Azerbaijan’s trade with the five Central Asian states grew by 53% to $1.8 billion. Trade among the Central Asian countries themselves reached $10.7 billion in 2024.

Mirziyoyev described Baku’s accession as an opportunity to create a “single space for cooperation” between Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Aliyev, in turn, described the two shores of the Caspian as a “single geopolitical and geoeconomic space”.

The leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan said they supported expanding the format because it would create new opportunities for transit, logistics and energy cooperation.

The Middle Corridor and the Caspian’s role in bringing the region together

The geography offers the clearest explanation for Azerbaijan’s participation in the format. The Middle Corridor links China and Central Asia with Europe: goods travel by rail across Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk, then across the Caspian Sea to Alat, before continuing through Georgia towards Turkey and the Black Sea. Azerbaijan effectively serves as the western gateway to the route.

According to the Kazakh government, freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian route rose by 62% in 2024 to 4.5 million tonnes. Baku says the volume of cargo travelling through the Azerbaijani section of the Middle Corridor has increased by 90% over three years. The authorities plan to raise the capacity of the Port of Alat to 25 million tonnes a year. The World Bank estimates that if countries coordinate border procedures, tariffs, port operations and transport schedules, freight volumes along the corridor could triple by 2030, while delivery times could fall by half.

The plans go beyond container shipping. Proposed electricity and digital cable projects across the Caspian would also bring energy and information flows into the broader agenda of regional cooperation.

The route through Nakhchivan offers new opportunities but remains contentious. The Washington Declaration, signed on 8 August 2025, provides for a transport link through Armenia between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, based on the sovereignty and jurisdiction of the states concerned, as well as the development of the TRIPP mechanism. Baku calls the route the “Zangezur Corridor”.

If implemented, the route could give the Middle Corridor an additional link to Turkey. However, until the parties agree on customs procedures, security arrangements, financing and management mechanisms, it remains a project rather than an operational transport corridor.

What is changing from a geopolitical perspective?

“C6” is a convenient political label, not the official name of an organisation. The format remains a consultative platform based on consensus. It does not involve collective defence commitments or mechanisms to enforce decisions.

For Moscow, this is therefore primarily about competition over logistics and political influence, including through the development of routes that bypass Russia, rather than the emergence of a new military alliance.

Beijing gains an additional route to the west and more stable conditions for transit.

Ankara has an interest in strengthening direct transport links across the Caspian.

The European Union and the US see the format as an opportunity to reduce dependence on routes through Russia and expand access to Central Asia.

The new C6 format should not be confused with the Organisation of Turkic States. The OTS has a treaty-based framework and institutional cooperation among Turkic states. The “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format also includes Tajikistan and focuses less on shared identity than on geography, economic interests and regional cooperation.

Potential opportunities and real constraints

The potential areas for cooperation are quite concrete: common transit tariffs, digital customs procedures, coordinated port and railway schedules, joint investment funds, green energy exports, tourism routes and coordination at international forums. With its ports, financial resources and transport links through the Caucasus and Turkey, Azerbaijan offers Central Asian countries additional routes and opportunities. Baku, in turn, gains more systematic access to the region’s five markets and their economic ties with China.

However, there are also many constraints. The six countries differ in their economic potential, interests in water resources and energy, and priorities in their relations with Russia, China, Turkey and the West. The format has no permanent secretariat or mechanisms to enforce decisions, so implementation of political agreements will depend on intergovernmental coordination.

The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, has yet to be ratified by Iran, while delimiting the seabed requires separate agreements. Falling water levels in the Caspian, the shallowing of ports and the need for costly dredging also increase the environmental and economic costs of transport logistics.

From symbol to concrete projects?

Mirziyoyev has already proposed transforming the format into a “Community of Central Asia” with a rotating secretariat. The next official meeting, scheduled for 8 October 2026 in Avaza, will be one of the first tests of whether these intentions can turn into practical decisions.

Will the six countries agree on common tariffs, digital customs procedures and a stable ferry schedule? Will TRIPP become a fully fledged part of the Middle Corridor without creating new border disputes? Or will the “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format remain a flexible consultative platform, with its informal nature continuing to be its main advantage?

Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

World.title: Convicted former Georgian PM Garibashvili: ‘Authorities left me no choice, I have to fight’
World.content:
Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

Convicted former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili says in a letter published from prison that the authorities arrested him to end his political career. He also says he gave up his legal fight to avoid a confrontation with the authorities.

The former prime minister writes that he received a letter from Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. According to Garibashvili, he confirmed to Mdinaradze that same day that he did not intend to return to politics.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s press office has described Garibashvili’s claims as “complete absurdity”.

“I state with full responsibility that I did everything to avoid confrontation with the [ruling] team and with someone who is dear to me,” Garibashvili wrote.

He says this is why he abandoned his legal challenge and went through the entire process to the end — to avoid, as he put it, harming the interests of the state and the “team”.

“Unfortunately, in response I received a staged dirty provocation, a sea of lies and injustice. Throughout this time, the public heard not a single word from me. I endured this ordeal patiently,” Garibashvili said.

According to Garibashvili, despite the position he had expressed to Mdinaradze, the authorities believed there was still a “1% risk” that he might return to politics in the future.

“To avoid this, they wanted me to face corruption charges and admit guilt,” Garibashvili writes.

According to him, this demand became a “red line” that forced him to take the “most difficult step of my life” — to turn against the authorities.

“I have no other choice. I am forced to start fighting,” the former prime minister said.

On 17 August 2026, Garibashvili made his first public statement from prison. In a Facebook post, he said he had received an ultimatum in a letter sent on the instructions of Bidzina Ivanishvili. He added that he had “no other choice” but to stand against what he described as “evil that insults my dignity”.

“I tried to do everything possible to avoid taking this step, but unfortunately I have no other choice but to confront this evil that insults my dignity. I must confront this ruthless cruelty, oppression and injustice, as well as the dirty plan to destroy me and my family,” Garibashvili wrote.

He also said that Bidzina Ivanishvili and the government bear responsibility for the safety of both himself and his family.

In the letter, Garibashvili says he had remained publicly silent and patiently endured what was happening until now. However, he says the current situation has left him no choice but to begin fighting.

Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

World.title: Armenian prime minister’s wife launches campaign against domestic violence
World.content:
Anna Hakobyan’s campaign against domestic violence

The wife of Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Anna Hakobyan, has announced the launch of a campaign against domestic violence. She received death threats shortly after calling for a public discussion of the issue. However, she continues to actively promote her initiative.

“The first stage will involve drafting comprehensive and effective legislation and discussing it in the National Assembly,” she said.

According to Anna Hakobyan, the Criminal Code should define domestic violence separately as “a distinct and independent crime”. She plans to invite female MPs from the parliament’s two opposition factions to join her initiative. If they do, she believes there is a chance that “parliament will unanimously approve the bill”.

Anna Hakobyan calls for a “family model with no place for violence”

The prime minister’s wife posted a video message on social media in which she said she intended to continue fighting domestic violence. According to Hakobyan, Armenia’s traditional family model, which hides various forms of violence, should give way to a model of a “family with no place for violence, based on mutual love and respect”. She proposes amending the Criminal Code to achieve this goal:

“An individual article should be added to the Code to establish criminal liability for all forms of domestic violence. Alternatively, different chapters of the Code could include provisions covering specific forms of domestic violence, including beatings, psychological abuse, economic abuse, bodily harm, sexual violence and others.”

According to Anna Hakobyan, eradicating violence requires clear, realistic and effective legal mechanisms.

Before presenting the bill to parliament, she initiated discussions with independent experts and female MPs. Together, they plan to examine gaps in the existing legislation. Once the law comes into force, she has promised to launch the initiative’s second stage. This will involve:

organising an awareness campaign;

improving the skills of staff at relevant agencies;

ensuring the effective implementation of the new regulations.

“At the same time, a group of respected experts is preparing a nationwide study to collect the most accurate and comprehensive data possible on the prevalence of domestic violence against women in Armenia,” she said.

What preceded the campaign

This is not the prime minister’s wife’s first post about domestic violence. She has been actively raising the issue on her social media pages. At the end of July, she said she had received threats after a particular post, including threats to kill her.

“I hope the state authorities can prevent such a development, as it would seriously damage the country’s reputation if the prime minister’s wife became a victim of violence,” Hakobyan said.

At the same time, she urged women to overcome their fears and report cases of violence.

The Prosecutor General’s Office took note of her report. The Investigative Committee said it had opened a criminal case under the article on “hooliganism using information and communication technologies”.

“In addition, within the framework of another criminal case concerning public calls for violence, a warrant has been issued for the arrest of one person. The person has been placed on the wanted list,” Investigative Committee spokeswoman Kim Avdalyan said.

Statistics on domestic violence

The Investigative Committee said it opened 1,794 criminal cases related to domestic violence in the first half of 2026:

712 cases carried over from 2025;

1,082 cases opened in 2026.

Authorities sent 204 criminal cases to court and charged 213 people.

Of the 213 defendants in the cases sent to court, 150 were spouses of the victims, 20 were partners, 15 were parents or grandparents, five were brothers or sisters, 16 were children or grandchildren, one was the husband’s sister or brother, and six were sons- or daughters-in-law.

Of the 213 victims, 192 were over 18, while the rest were minors. Of those, 13 were under 12, three were aged 13-14, and five were aged 15-18.

Anna Hakobyan’s campaign against domestic violence

World.title: ‘Work is being carried out to international standards’ — Georgia’s Gelati Monastery Rehabilitation Committee responds to criticism
World.content:
Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati has described reports circulating on social media and in the media about conservation work at the monastery as disinformation.

The committee said the disinformation was harming efforts to restore Gelati.

The Gelati Monastery complex is one of Georgia’s most important medieval cultural and religious monuments. King David IV, known as David the Builder, founded it in 1106.

The complex’s main church is the Cathedral of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary. In medieval Georgia, Gelati was not only a monastery but also an important centre of education and scholarship, home to the renowned Gelati Academy.

Recent reports and assessments have raised concerns about the condition of Gelati. The debate has focused on several issues:

The church’s temporary roof, which critics have called “cellophane”;

The risk of frescoes collapsing;

Mould and condensation inside the church;

The condition of the drainage system;

Plans to install an underfloor heating system;

Cooperation with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure;

The condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

What does the committee say?

The committee rejects claims that the Gelati Cathedral is covered with “cellophane”. According to the committee, the creation of a single temporary covering for the cathedral was one of the main requirements set by the UNESCO World Heritage Centre as early as 2020.

The committee says Georgian and German specialists jointly designed the roof. The authorities approved the project after considering several proposals. The covering uses a high-tech PVC-based material made in Germany specifically for Gelati. According to the committee, the material meets international conservation standards.

The committee also rejects reports of widespread loss of frescoes inside the cathedral. It says all critically damaged areas have been stabilised, while conservation work on the wall paintings is continuing in stages.

The statement also addresses Gelati’s historic drainage system. According to the committee, drainage channels built during the reign of David the Builder stopped functioning in 1510 after Ottoman forces burned the monastery. The committee says archaeological excavations also support this conclusion.

“For centuries, the drainage system was filled with earth, ash and coal,” the committee said.

The committee also responded to criticism over humidity and condensation inside the church. According to the committee, Italian professor Dario Camuffo conducted the study of Gelati’s microclimate. The committee considers him one of the recognised experts in the study of the microclimate of cultural heritage sites.

The committee explained that the problem at Gelati stems from the church’s massive walls, which retain the cold for a long time during winter. In spring, when outdoor temperatures rise and warm air enters the church, condensation can form on the walls and floor.

Camuffo suggested gradually heating the floor as one possible solution. However, the committee stressed that this remains a working hypothesis and requires further research before a final decision.

The committee also clarified the memorandum it signed with the Italian institute Opificio delle Pietre Dure. According to the committee, the “pilot restoration” provided for in the document does not mean conducting experiments at Gelati. Instead, it refers to pilot or trial restoration work, which is standard international practice.

“This is a widely accepted standard for restoring wall paintings. Before treating an entire fresco, conservators test the safety of the proposed conservation methods on a small, less visible area. Only after obtaining a positive result do they begin the full-scale process,” the committee said.

In a significant part of its statement, the committee also responded to critics and addressed allegations about the condition of the mosaics at Gelati.

According to the committee, experts already knew about the poor condition of the mosaics in 1989. The claim is based on an assessment by restorer Carlo Bakuradze at the time, who found that about 85% of the mosaic depicting the Virgin Mary had detached from its base.

The committee also criticised specialists who question the ongoing conservation work and reminded them of their own responsibility for Gelati’s condition in the past.

“It is cynical and hypocritical for people to question the quality of conservation work when, under their direct supervision, extensive water-infiltration problems emerged within just one year at the recently built Bagrati Cathedral — problems that persist to this day,” the statement said. The Temporary Committee for the Rehabilitation of Gelati urged critics not to try to damage the reputation of the ongoing work and to act according to professional ethics.

“We call on those pursuing certain subjective goals and agendas to refrain from attempts to discredit the conservation work carried out under the Gelati rehabilitation programme and deliberately mislead the public. We also call on them to return to the standards of common decency and professional ethics,” the committee said.

The committee concluded by stressing again that the work at the Gelati Monastery complex is unprecedented in scale, involves international experts and meets international conservation standards.

What happened at Gelati?

The main problem at Gelati Monastery is water and dampness, which have damaged the church’s wall paintings and mosaics over time. The situation became particularly serious after restoration work in recent years, including problems with the roof.

The problem became so serious that the UNESCO World Heritage Centre and its advisory bodies issued specific recommendations to Georgia. The authorities changed their approach to the restoration work in response to those recommendations and established the current Rehabilitation Committee.

A ruling by Georgia’s Supreme Court also notes that workers carried out roofing work at Gelati without an adequate expert assessment. The court found that problems with the materials used and the quality of the installation created a real risk of water entering the building.

Restoration of Georgia’s Gelati Monastery

World.title: Suicides in Armenia’s military: the statistics and debate over who should be held responsible
World.content:
Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

In Armenia, debate continues over the causes of military deaths in peacetime and who should bear responsibility. A series of suicides has prompted the latest discussions. The first incident occurred on 21 July. Then, on 13 August, the Defence Ministry reported that it had found the body of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan with a gunshot wound. In both cases, the Investigative Committee said it had opened criminal proceedings under the article on negligent incitement to suicide.

According to the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, this was the 31st military death in Armenia in 2026. However, the Defence Ministry says 11 servicemen have died. Moreover, the ministry’s spokesperson said the number of military deaths had become the subject of various forms of manipulation.

“We often see reports in the press about 30 deaths in the army over the course of a year. But no one says how many of those 30 cases actually occurred in the army, which were related to military service and which were not. Even if the deaths were related to service, were all of them murders and suicides?” Aram Torosyan said, calling for greater precision.

Government bodies and civil society organisations also differ over who should bear responsibility for military deaths. Human rights groups tend to argue that the defence minister and the chief of the General Staff should be held accountable. However, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan does not share this view.

“In my assessment, it is not the case that the chief of the General Staff and the defence minister are failing to make sufficient efforts to address this issue,” Nikol Pashinyan said.

Civil society data differs from official figures

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan, who represents the Vanadzor office of the Helsinki Citizens’ Assembly, said she had seen no positive changes. According to her, the number of military deaths in non-combat situations has not decreased:

“The situation is even worse than in 2025. There were 35 deaths throughout 2025, while there have already been 31 cases in the first eight months of this year.”

She stressed that 10 cases in 2025 were classified as related to military service, while the same number have been recorded in just eight months this year.

Defence Ministry spokesman Aram Torosyan says these claims do not match the official statistics.

“We have recorded 11 deaths this year. Only five of those who died were serving their mandatory military service. Some died from illness, while others died in a mine explosion,” he said.

Torosyan said six of the 11 deaths involved suicide or incitement to suicide, but only three were related to military service.

Commenting on last year’s figures, he stressed that there were no cases of murder in the army in 2025.

Causes of suicides in the army

The authorities have not released details about the death of serviceman Grigor Zakaryan. However, the prime minister said that 85-90% of suicides in the army result from:

gambling addiction and the debts it causes;

personal and family problems;

servicemen falling asleep while on duty, which can lead to conflicts with fellow soldiers.

“If a serviceman on duty at a border post falls asleep, he puts other people’s lives at risk. Soldiers then begin to treat the person who fell asleep at the post negatively, and he becomes isolated. After returning from combat duty, psychological pressure can also follow. We should not place all the blame on the army leadership. I am responsible for the fact that we have still not found a solution to this problem,” Pashinyan said.

Human rights activist Nazeli Movsesyan believes that the first two causes mentioned by the prime minister have nothing to do with the army. At the same time, she believes authorities can eliminate the third factor by taking systemic measures:

“Why does a serviceman fall asleep while on duty? Are there enough personnel to ensure that everyone gets enough rest and does not feel the need to sleep while on duty?”

Prime minister’s statements and dismissals

On the day the soldier died, Nikol Pashinyan told reporters that the government had discussed the situation and decided to make dismissals. He announced personnel changes in the Military Police and the Defence Ministry’s Department of Moral and Psychological Support:

“We will analyse in detail why our efforts in this area are not producing the desired results and draw conclusions. Yes, there must be individual accountability.”

The same day, reports emerged that Military Police chief Ashot Zakaryan had submitted his resignation. Today, the president dismissed Zakaryan from the post he had held for six years. In another decree, Major General Aram Hovhannisyan was appointed to replace him. From 2023 to 2025, he served as deputy interior minister and police chief.

There are no specific details yet about personnel changes in the Department of Moral and Psychological Support.

In recent days, the Defence Ministry has reported consultations on organising psychological support in the armed forces. To review a report on the psychological assistance provided to the military, the defence minister met professors from Yerevan State University’s Research Centre for Psychology. The ministry is also holding discussions with conscript sergeants and officers serving on duty at military posts.

“The agenda includes issues related to preventing hazing and eliminating inappropriate behaviour in the army,” the ministry said.

Comment

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan believes:

“The army’s top command, led by Suren Papikyan, must give the public a detailed explanation of the series of deaths.

Has anyone from the army’s top command visited the military unit to establish the circumstances of the soldier’s death and find out what was happening there? I strongly doubt it.

Papikyan did not even visit the military unit in the village of Azat when 15 servicemen died.

On 19 January 2023, a fire broke out in the engineering and sapper company’s premises in the village of Azat, killing 15 servicemen. Three others suffered burns of varying severity.

Then, as now, Nikol Pashinyan spoke on Papikyan’s behalf. He named those responsible and accountable. But he did not explain what the Military Police had to do with the death.

If Pashinyan knows more about the situation in the army and at military units, why is Papikyan still the defence minister?”

Suicides in Armenia’s army: statistics

World.title: White House: China is using Georgia to circumvent US tariffs
World.content:
US tariffs on China

According to a White House report titled The Great Transshipment Scam, China is using third countries, including Georgia, to circumvent US tariffs.

The Trump administration’s report names 40 countries and territories as participants in China’s “shadow shipping network”. The White House says these countries may have helped China circumvent US trade restrictions by transshipping and processing goods destined for the US.

The report divides the economies into three categories:

The first category includes countries and trading blocs that receive significant volumes of China-linked goods but have diversified industrial markets. The White House places Canada, the European Union, India, Israel, Japan, Mexico, South Korea and Taiwan in this group.

The second category includes countries with significant economic integration with China. According to the report, these are Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Turkey and Vietnam.

The third category includes China’s “secondary targets”. The White House considers this group to include relatively small economies such as Georgia, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Argentina, Switzerland, Panama, Colombia, Chile, Cambodia and the United Arab Emirates.

According to the report, rerouting Chinese goods through third countries is one of the mechanisms companies use to avoid US tariffs on Chinese imports.

The White House published the report as part of the broader trade policy of the US administration. One of its main goals is to tighten enforcement of restrictions on imports from China and prevent companies from circumventing tariffs through third countries.

In 2025, Georgia imported $1.98 billion worth of goods from China, while its exports to the US amounted to just $120 million.

The value of goods imported from China into Georgia was significantly higher than the value of Georgian exports to the US. According to 2025 data, ferroalloys accounted for the largest category of goods imported from China into Georgia.

During the same period, Georgia’s main exports to the US included power-generating equipment and passenger cars.

Trade data show that Chinese imports account for a significant share of Georgia’s trade with China, while Georgian exports to the US remain relatively small.

US President Donald Trump began imposing and gradually increasing tariffs on Chinese goods in February 2025. By April 2025, the rate had reached 145%. Beijing responded with similar measures, imposing a 125% tariff on US products.

Following talks in May that year, the US cut the newly imposed tariffs from 145% to 30%, while China reduced its tariffs from 125% to 10%. However, other tariffs introduced before 2025 remained in place.

According to data published by the US Congress, various tariffs on Chinese goods are currently in effect under several US laws. Some target China directly, while others apply to specific economic sectors and also affect Chinese goods.

US tariffs on China

World.title: Deportation, ‘international wanted list’ mark new escalation in Baku-Moscow tensions
World.content:
Escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations

Two developments on 17 August highlighted the continuing fragility of relations between Baku and Moscow. Russia deported Bakhtiyar Hasanov, chairman of the Azerbaijani National-Cultural Autonomy in Moscow, to Azerbaijan. Azerbaijan, in turn, placed three Russian citizens on an international wanted list: Moscow 24 TV presenter Ivan Knyazev, political consultant and media expert Semyon Uralov, and journalist and adviser to the Russian transport minister Alexei Chadayev.

The fact that the two developments occurred on the same day may at first suggest that they were reciprocal measures. However, the process that culminated in Hasanov’s deportation had begun well before 17 August, with his case under consideration for at least several months. Therefore, while there is no public evidence of a direct causal link between the two decisions, both developments fit into the broader pattern of the prolonged deterioration in Azerbaijani-Russian relations.

Deportation of Bakhtiyar Hasanov

According to open sources, Bakhtiyar Hasanov was detained in Russia in June 2026 and placed in a temporary detention centre for foreign nationals. He appealed against the decision to deport him, but the court rejected his appeal.

According to sources, Hasanov’s Russian citizenship was revoked in September 2025. In autumn 2025, the Agentstvo media outlet established that Hasanov’s passport, issued in 2019, was listed as invalid in a Russian government database. Hasanov himself denied at the time that he had been stripped of his citizenship.

One of the key questions is the legal basis on which his citizenship was revoked. Open sources provide no complete or unequivocal explanation for the decision.

The case also carries political significance because of Hasanov’s status. For many years, he cooperated with official Moscow bodies dealing with diaspora and interethnic relations and served on public councils. His deportation is therefore also being viewed as part of a broader trend of pressure on the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia.

Growing pressure on the diaspora

Since the summer of 2025, several prominent members of the Azerbaijani diaspora in Russia have been stripped of their citizenship, detained or expelled from the country. The names of Arshad Khankishiyev, Elshan Ibrahimov and Javid Rzayev have been mentioned in this context.

Russian nationalist and Kremlin-aligned media have largely portrayed these measures as part of efforts to combat illegal migration, alleged links to criminal groups and security concerns. However, final court rulings on all the allegations made against these individuals are not publicly available.

This process took on a more overtly political dimension following an operation targeting Azerbaijani families in Yekaterinburg in June 2025. The deaths of the Safarov brothers during the operation prompted a sharp reaction from Baku. Moscow linked the operation to an investigation into crimes committed many years earlier, while the Azerbaijani side focused on reports of violence and torture against those detained.

Since then, the issue of the diaspora has gradually moved beyond the social and cultural sphere and become one of the instruments of political pressure in relations between the two countries.

Baku’s charges against three Russian citizens

On 17 August, Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office said that Ivan Knyazev, Semyon Uralov and Alexei Chadayev had been placed on a wanted list as part of a criminal investigation.

The investigation relates to programmes published on Uralov’s YouTube channel on 14 July and 13 August. According to the Azerbaijani authorities, the broadcasts contained calls for the violent overthrow of the country’s constitutional order, violations of its territorial integrity, terrorist activity and incitement of ethnic hatred.

The criminal case is being investigated under Articles 214-2, 281.2 and 283.2.1 of Azerbaijan’s Criminal Code. A court ordered the three men to be detained in absentia.

Excerpts from the broadcasts published by Azerbaijani media include remarks about a possible military operation against Baku, military pressure on Azerbaijan from the Caspian Sea and the use of physical violence against the country’s leadership. However, the Prosecutor General’s Office has not published full transcripts of the broadcasts, expert assessments or all the episodes on which the charges are based.

What do Uralov and Chadayev say?

The accused reject Baku’s allegations. Alexei Chadayev denied inciting ethnic hatred, saying that his criticism was directed not against the Azerbaijani people but against the country’s political leadership.

Semyon Uralov, for his part, described the Azerbaijani authorities’ decision as politically motivated. In subsequent Telegram posts, he continued to sharply criticise the political systems of post-Soviet countries, including the Azerbaijani authorities.

The response indicates that the case has moved beyond the legal sphere and become part of the broader information confrontation between the two countries.

‘International wanted list’ does not mean automatic arrest

The term “international wanted list”, used by Azerbaijani media, does not mean that a wanted person will automatically be arrested in another country.

Even if Interpol issues a Red Notice, it does not constitute an international arrest warrant. Each country decides whether to detain a wanted person in accordance with its own laws. In addition, Interpol’s constitution prohibits the organisation from intervening in matters of a political, military, religious or racial character.

The outcome of Baku’s request will therefore depend on the legal evidence submitted, as well as on how other countries assess the case — as a criminal prosecution or as a continuation of the political confrontation.

Ukraine factor

The latest escalation in Azerbaijani-Russian relations comes against the backdrop of the growing prominence of the Ukraine issue.

On 6 August, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov made his first official visit to Kyiv since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and visited Irpin. Azerbaijan reiterated its support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders. The two sides also discussed the possibility of supplying Azerbaijani gas to Ukraine.

Against this political backdrop, former Ukrainian President Viktor Yushchenko visited Baku on 16–17 August and met Ilham Aliyev. The presentation to Aliyev of a certificate naming him an honorary citizen of Irpin could be perceived in Moscow as a symbolic political gesture.

There is no evidence confirming a direct link between these developments and Hasanov’s deportation. However, the Azerbaijani leadership’s increasingly open articulation of a position on Ukraine that differs from Moscow’s fits into the broader picture of growing discontent in Russian political circles.

New mechanisms of mutual pressure

One notable change in relations between Baku and Moscow over the past two years has been the increasingly active use of law-enforcement and administrative mechanisms in the context of their political confrontation.

Russia has applied citizenship and migration laws, as well as criminal legislation, against members of the Azerbaijani diaspora. Azerbaijan, in turn, has used criminal prosecution mechanisms against individuals linked to Russian media over statements that Baku regards as posing a threat to the country.

This does not in itself mean that the legal arguments put forward by either side are unfounded. However, the fact that such legal measures are being taken against the backdrop of political crises in bilateral relations inevitably raises questions about their selective application and possible use for political purposes.

Where are relations heading?

At this stage, a complete political rupture between Azerbaijan and Russia appears unlikely. The two countries have significant mutual interests in areas including trade, transport, logistics and regional security.

At the same time, a return to the previous level of relations also appears difficult. Instead, an emerging model seems to be characterised by political mistrust alongside continued, limited cooperation.

Azerbaijanis living in Russia, as well as diaspora organisations maintaining social ties between the two countries, could find themselves particularly vulnerable in this confrontation. The use of diaspora representatives as instruments in an interstate dispute, particularly when accompanied by ethnic rhetoric, increases the risk that tensions could extend beyond diplomatic relations and affect relations between the two societies.

The events of 17 August therefore have broader significance than two separate legal decisions. They point to the emergence of a new model of relations in which Baku and Moscow, while continuing to cooperate, are increasingly making use of political and legal means to exert pressure on one another.

World.title: Evergrande founder sentenced to life in prison by Chinese court
World.content:
Chinese property developer Hui Ka Yan, founder of the Evergrande real estate group, has been sentenced to life in prison with the companies fined a total of $US2.3 billion ($3.2 billion), by a court in the southern city of Shenzhen.

The decision marks a milestone in Evergrande's saga after it collapsed with more than $US300 billion ($420 billion) in liabilities when Chinese authorities cracked down on excessive borrowing in the real estate industry in 2020.

That triggered a crunch among many developers and brought on a downturn in the property market that has weighed on the broader economy ever since.

The Shenzhen Intermediate People's Court convicted Hui, also known as Xu Jiayin, and Evergrande of large-scale financial fraud in inflating the group's assets and concealing its liabilities.

Evergrande was fined $1.85 billion in addition to Hui's sentence. (Reuters: Aly Song)

In a statement, the court said Hui also abused his position in orchestrating financial fraud and misappropriating company assets.

Hui had faced eight charges including misuse of funds and illegally taking public deposits.

It also sentenced several other senior Evergrande executives to prison terms of up to 18 years on charges including illegally taking public deposits and fraud, the court said.

Evergrande group was fined 8.82 billion yuan ($1.85 billion) and Evergrande Real Estate Group was fined 7 billion yuan ($1.45 billion), the court said in a statement.

Hui pleaded guilty in April to various charges including illegal absorption of public deposits, fraud and bribery after he was arrested in China.

China Evergrande, founded in 1996, defaulted on its debts in 2021.

China now suffers from an oversupply of modern properties. (Reuters: Aly Song)

It was the world's most heavily indebted real estate developer before it was ordered to liquidate its assets.

China's fix for property crisis rewards marathon runners Local governments in China are offering marathon runners, AI experts and tennis players subsidies to purchase unwanted properties amid a lingering real estate downturn.

Authorities in Hong Kong and mainland China earlier said their investigations found Evergrande had manipulated its financial data.

Tactics used included prematurely booking revenue from property sales before completion and delivery of the apartments to buyers.

Revenues were overstated by roughly $US80 billion ($112 billion) over 2019 and 2020, they said.

The Chinese property market in 2026 is undergoing a deep structural shift from speculative hyper-growth into a permanent "stable contraction".

The Chinese real estate industry is struggling with an oversupply of inventory, while adjusting to a new economic reality where real estate is no longer China's primary engine of wealth.

World.title: At least 100 dead after gold mine collapses in Central African Republic
World.content:
The death toll from a gold mine collapse in a western part of Central African Republic (CAR) has risen to more than 100 as the desperate search for survivors continues.

The low-tech, artisanal gold mine collapsed in the village of Zamboye in the Nana-Mambere prefecture earlier this week.

Zamboye youth council member Bertrand Be Yangué said people remained missing and others were trapped under the rubble.

"Finding them alive would be a miracle," he said.

" We are saddened and heartbroken to see young men and women perish after coming to the mines to save their families from despair. "

An investigation to identify the victims and those responsible for operating the site is underway, the prosecutor at the Baboua sub-prefecture court said in a statement.

The investigation will seek to establish what caused the collapse and any potential criminal liability.

Footage of the incident showed hundreds of people gathered near the mine prior to the collapse.

The crowd scattered as a wall of dirt flowed down the rocky terrain towards a group of people gathered below.

Miners, mostly young men and women covered in mud, attempted to pull survivors from the pit while dozens of others were scattered around the expansive site, some shouting for help.

AP

World.title: Judge finds 'fundamental defect' in police taser investigation
World.content:
A judge has brought an end to a criminal prosecution against two police officers who had been accused of criminally restraining and assaulting a prisoner at a Far North Queensland watch house.

Senior constables Andrew David Couchman, 54, and Ulrich Weiss, 45, were charged with criminal offences after they allegedly capsicum sprayed, tasered and forcibly restrained Charlton Bong, then aged 23, at the Mareeba watch house in January 2024.

Queensland Police Service's Ethical Standards Command investigated the alleged incident and charged the senior constables with offences including assault and deprivation of liberty.

However, both officers applied to the District Court in Cairns for a permanent stay of the charges last week, arguing they could not be assured of a fair trial.

Andrew David Couchman (right), pictured earlier this month with his lawyers, including barrister David Jones KC (far left). (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

At a hearing last Thursday, lawyers for senior constables Couchman and Weiss told the court the case against the officers had been "contaminated" when an Ethical Standards Command investigator inserted a paragraph into the alleged victim's sworn statement.

Today, Judge Dean Morzone KC handed down his decision to grant the permanent stay, acknowledging a court's power to do so was "reserved for … exceptional, extreme cases".

Detective Senior Sergeant Kim Cavell drafted a statement in Mr Bong's name, including a paragraph asserting that he did not consent to being tasered, sprayed or restrained, the court heard.

Mr Bong could not read or write, and Detective Senior Sergeant Cavell told him the statement "was compiled from what he had previously told her", Judge Morzone said.

Andrew David Couchman (right) allegedly tasered Charlton Bong, who was experiencing mental health issues. (ABC Far North: Conor Byrne)

However, it had been established in evidence at a pre-trial hearing that Mr Bong had not used those words and did not know what the word "consent" meant.

Judge Morzone said Mr Bong was the "only witness who can speak personally to the central issue" and the way his evidence was gathered had "produced a fundamental defect" that "no ruling or direction available to a trial judge can cure".

"That continuation of proceedings would result in unacceptable unfairness to each applicant and that it would be incompatible with the integrity of this court's processes," he said.

"Nothing in these reasons should be understood as a finding as to the merits of the underlying conduct, nor is this order framed to punish or to censure the investigating officer.

"The order reflects only the court's conclusion that a trial on this indictment cannot now be a fair one and the court should not lend its processes to it."

Left alone in cell

The Crown argued there was significant public interest in the case proceeding.

In May, Mr Bong gave evidence at a pre-trial hearing, telling the court voices in his head were telling him the "world was ending" and to punch and spit at the officers.

The court heard after he was tasered, Mr Bong was restrained and left alone in a padded cell in a prone state for more than two hours.

Charlton Bong was called to give evidence at a pre-trial hearing in May. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

Judge Morzone said the Crown case relied on "the state of mind of a cognitively and emotionally vulnerable witness" who adopted an account from investigators "upon a false representation and without comprehension".

Senior constables Couchman and Weiss had been listed to stand trial next month, but that trial has now been delisted.

"Each of the defendants are discharged from their bail undertakings, and we will work out what goes from there," Judge Morzone said.

The court heard the case could be listed for a mention on a future date.
