Union backs officers' return

Queensland Police Union general president Shane Prior said the ruling "brings to an end more than two years of enormous professional and personal stress for those officers".

Senior constables Couchman and Weiss were not in court for today's hearing, which their lawyers joined by video link.

However, Mr Prior spoke with the officers shortly after the decision was handed down.

"Both these officers will be back at work in the near future, I expect, and today is a day of great relief for them as they can now mix with their families without the stress that has been hanging over their heads," Mr Prior said.

Shane Prior said the officers would be supported in returning to work. (ABC News)

Mr Prior said he still had confidence in Ethical Standards Command but said the judge's findings about the integrity of the investigation "cannot be ignored".

"I fully expect that to be examined at length by Ethical Standards Command or any other agency, including the CCC."

The union provided the officers with legal and welfare support while they were charged, and Mr Prior said they would receive further help to make a safe return to work.

The Queensland Police Service has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Liberals accuse government of backdown on aged care program
World.content:
The Commonwealth program helping older people with shopping, transport and meals on wheels will be extended until 2029, but the government has flagged its intention to make the program permanent beyond that.

The Commonwealth Home Support Program (CHSP) provides low-level support to 830,000 seniors to help them live at home.

As part of major changes to the aged care sector, the program was due to be abolished in mid-2027 and rolled into the new Support at Home program. The new program is designed to provide a coordinated budget for more complex care, but critics have argued that the changes would make service delivery more expensive and less efficient.

Providers, including local councils, had also withdrawn services because of the uncertainty surrounding the program's future.

Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said the government was now also beginning consultation with a view to permanently keeping CHSP separate from Support at Home.

"We believe the CHSP should remain a standalone program," he said.

Mr Rae said it was important for the government to be looking at how it could use early intervention services like CHSP to take pressure off the rest of the ever-growing aged care system, which faces a shortage of beds and long waitlists.

He hoped the operators that had stopped providing services would return now they had certainty.

The program is designed to take pressure off the aged care system. (ABC News: Glyn Jones)

Health Minister Mark Butler said the CHSP program would require reform, though, because there was some overlap between it and the Support at Home program.

"There are differences in co-contribution arrangements that will have to be sorted," he said.

Under CHSP, participants are expected to contribute varying amounts to the cost of their care, if they can afford to.

"Simple services like house cleaning and meals might cost a few dollars. More complex services like some home modifications will cost much more," according to the department's website.

Under Support at Home, depending on someone's pensioner status and the type of care they require, they contribute between 5 and 80 per cent of costs.

Anne Ruston says cutting community support would have been "reckless". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

'Overwhelming' evidence for decision

A Senate inquiry earlier this year recommended CHSP be kept as a separate block-funded program, and Shadow Aged Care Minister Anne Ruston said the decision was an "embarrassing" backdown given the mounting evidence.

"This is an embarrassing, overdue backdown from Labor in the face of overwhelming evidence that abolishing community support would have been reckless for the 835,000 older Australians who rely on this program," she said.

"Labor has left this decision until the last minute, just as they have done repeatedly throughout their chaotic aged care reforms."

The announcement was welcomed by provider body Ageing Australia, which had been pushing for the program to remain separate, given Support at Home was "not yet delivering for older people".

Council on the Ageing chief executive Patricia Sparrow agreed it was important the program was extended.

"The task now is making sure the Commonwealth Home Support Program, Support at Home and the broader aged care system work together so older Australians don't fall through the cracks, get caught between program boundaries or face unnecessary barriers as their needs change," she said.

" It's good that this gives people, including providers like local councils, certainty about the future of the program. "

The Greens have welcomed the change. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Greens leader Larissa Waters also labelled the decision a "massive win".

"It is outrageous that Labor thought that older Australians should have their lives uprooted and future thrown into uncertainty," she said.

The government did not reveal the cost of extending the program but said it was not a savings measure.

World.title: Lambie sparks veterans debate as Labor strikes deals
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

An impassioned Jacqui Lambie struggled to get the words out as she shared details about the medical battle behind her five-month absence from Parliament House.

Six months ago, her vagina started to prolapse and three months later, she told the Senate, it took her "bladder with it" and required surgery. Lambie said it was directly linked to her back injuries from her time serving in the army.

After hearing the story of female veteran Kate, who waited three years before she could find a gynaecologist "happy with the low prices [the Department of Veterans' Affairs] pay", Lambie took matters into her own hands.

Lambie says it's part of a broader issue with how the department treats female veterans and their health.

"I would like to ask the prime minister, minister [Richard] Marles, and minister [Matt] Keogh what they would do if their penises were hanging by a thread, and what they would do if treatment for that injury directly connected to their military service was denied by the Department of Veterans' Affairs," she said.

Loading...

Lambie used the speech to draw focus on the government's contentious proposed $5000 cap on veterans' allied health spending, which covers everything from chiropractors to physiotherapy.

The cap was announced in the budget and is aimed at tackling dodgy providers. It doesn't come into effect until next year and the government argues that veterans will still be able to apply for more funding where it is clinically indicated.

But veterans are sceptical about the department's ability to administer the cap. Lambie's intervention came as the Coalition used Question Time to exploit the rift between the veterans' affairs minister and former defence personnel on the matter.

Keogh had initially knocked back a request to meet with The Coalition of Veterans' Voice, which is campaigning against the cap. After pressure was applied, he conceded he'd "got it wrong" and sat down with them.

He was later accused of rolling his eyes and crossing his arms during the meeting, a characterisation he rejected. The Coalition jumped on claims Keogh had disrespected veterans and called for him to be sacked.

Everything must go

Lambie's speech cut through in a week where there was a lot going on. A smorgasbord of deals saw the prime minister get a trio of inconvenient bills off his plate.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

It was, as David Speers wrote this morning, a week of rare cooperation between the government and the opposition. After striking an agreement with the Greens on negative gearing, the capital gains tax, and environment laws it was now the Coalition's turn.

A bipartisan deal was struck on gambling advertising, which will result in the establishment of an opt-out register for online wagering ads. How that would work, well, that's anyone's guess right now.

The overhaul will be reviewed in three years' time, well after the next election. The debate was emotive across all sides of politics, especially for those who arrived in parliament at the same time as the late Labor MP Peta Murphy. She chaired the inquiry that led to the landmark report that called for online advertising and inducements to be banned completely.

Her husband, Rod Glover, this week wrote on LinkedIn to say the reforms were limited due to the "considerable power of the gambling industry, major sporting codes and media organisations".

Loading...

Albanese was also willing to give the Coalition another win on the so-called "widow's tax" — an issue the opposition plucked from David Pocock to champion.

The government says it was always going to patch up the unintended loophole left behind in its changes to negative gearing that removed the grandfathering arrangements in the case of inheritance or where a property was transferred by death or divorce. But the fix was in the tranche of legislation it pushed out to later in the year.

Given nobody objected to its draft changes, Albanese said he it took him a "millisecond" to give the green light to put it on the fast-track after Angus Taylor issued an ultimatum to do so or else the Coalition would hold up the overhaul to the National Disability Insurance Scheme.

Hanson continues to loom large

As much as this week was about the differentiation between what the major parties can achieve by cooperating and what One Nation is promising in protest, Pauline Hanson still hung heavy over debate.

Her declaration that cash-strapped Australians struggling with the cost of living should be able to access their superannuation early was easy morning television fodder — and a fight for Jim Chalmers to jump on.

The treasurer's office is in the much-coveted blue carpeted ministerial wing. So, it's always curious to find him at the House of Representatives doors where reporters with cameras lay in wait to ask backbench MPs questions about the news of the day as they roll into work.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers wants to have a fight on superannuation. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

He declared the next election would be a referendum on super. It's a fight he's been wanting to have. And it's a fight that got quickly personal when Labor sent text messages to supporters taking aim at Hanson and Liberal senator Andrew Bragg (who also isn't shy in his opinions on super), while asking for a donation to the party.

Hanson said the treasurer was "full of sh**" while Bragg called him an "absolute loser".

Meanwhile, a fight is also brewing over the tobacco excise. One Nation thinks it can wipe out the booming tobacco black market by cutting almost $30 off the cost of a packet of cigarettes — or slashing the excise by 75 per cent.

"The only way we can deal with the criminality, the mafia that also underwrites so many other drugs, is to bring back the price of legal cigarettes to the same realm as where illegal ones are," Barnaby Joyce told ABC's Radio National Breakfast.

To one-up One Nation, the Coalition is now reportedly considering an 80 per cent cut. The government on the other hand doesn't want to get in the "habit of engaging in price competition with organised crime" and sees this as an enforcement issue.

Loading

After the deals, comes the fight

With a meeting of the national cabinet on the agenda for next week, the prime minister will be gearing up for another round of tense negotiations.

From the GST carve-up to the NDIS and data centres, there is no shortage of fights the premiers could pick. Likewise, the prime minister will have a bone to pick with everyone but New South Wales over the national gun buyback scheme. Several state treasurers this week essentially told the ABC: "thanks, but no thanks".

But hey, at least he won't be talking about melons.

World.title: Dr Who, Star Wars and the manosphere: 'Geek culture' revealed as pipeline to misogyny
World.content:
The manosphere can operate like a vortex, pulling in the uncertain young men who are often lost and seeking self improvement.

Flynn Martin is one who says he was radicalised by the manosphere.

He was 20 years old. A uni student. A self-professed doomscroller.

But once the anti-women algorithm infiltrated his social media, it took just months for the hobby content creator to become another online prophet of misogyny.

A video Flynn Martin posted about being a "straight white male" went viral in 2022. (Supplied)

In late 2022, he posted a controversial video of himself ranting on social media.

It was deliberately provocative, he tells 7.30 — "rage bait" for more "clicks and views".

From the front seat of his car, he rhetorically asks: "Is it actually OK being a straight white male?"

Then he turns his focus on women.

"It's all pretty convenient when they say men are only good for 'that, that and that' … but as soon as they open their little f***ing useless mouths, I don't want to f***ing hear it."

The videos went viral. The backlash was swift. But Flynn says — at the time — he did not care.

"When you become so intoxicated by the idea of garnering as much attention as possible … you don't have a regard for what you're saying," he says.

The 'inescapable' manosphere vortex

Flynn says he had become convinced the world was rigged against "straight white men" and women were to blame.

Flynn Martin suffered severe public backlash after his viral video in 2022. (ABC News)

"I was the perfect example for someone who can be exposed and susceptible to that content," he tells 7.30.

Two years out of school, isolated through COVID and a year into a film degree, he was, in his words, "super lost and confused".

Flynn felt his frustration boiling over into anger because he did not know what he was meant to do, or where he was going in life.

"That was when all this manosphere content just started flooding my algorithm," he says.

" It did feel inescapable … once it started showing up, it didn't stop. It was just there, just always there. "

The clips he was seeing bombarded him with followed a familiar formula, peddled by prominent anti-feminists.

Flynn says the manosphere content he was exposed to on social media fuelled his insecurities and internalised self-hatred. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)

They ranged from alpha-male self-improvement and get-rich advice to pseudo-scientific claims that women are inferior and "can't come to logical conclusions".

Flynn says he barely noticed the effect such content had on his mindset but admits it changed the way he thought.

"You just become so insecure that it becomes a lot of internalised self-hatred … and that can very easily spew out into misogyny, taking that self-insecurity and self-hatred and taking it out on other people," he says.

"It just started spewing out into how you speak and what you talk about with people."

He says it did not take long until he had adopted the language of the manosphere as his own.

The manosphere has gone mainstream

Flynn's experience is mirrored by admissions made by several other young men in new research documenting pathways into the manosphere.

A team from Queensland University of Technology, Deakin University and Dublin City University interviewed more than 50 men across Australia and Ireland who had spent time in its online communities.

While the work is ongoing, clear patterns are emerging. The manosphere, they say, has gone mainstream — no longer a fringe society or a niche that men must seek out.

"Anyone going online … will very quickly encounter it," Professor Michael Flood, who was part of the research team, tells 7.30.

Professor Michael Flood has been mapping the pipeline to the manosphere in new research. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Professor Flood has spent more than 30 years studying men, masculinity and gender-based violence and says anti-feminist groups have existed for centuries.

"What's shifted is that they've now moved online and proliferated and expanded in troubling ways," he says.

"And there have also been really significant changes in how people come to the manosphere.

"It's very easy to go down those rabbit holes."

Troubling testimonies

What starts as a search for advice on self-improvement can often lead young men down the manosphere. (Supplied: Adobe Stock)

To protect the men's identities, the researchers gave them pseudonyms.

Some described the draw to online anti-women spaces as the chance to live out a "power fantasy".

Henry* was 15 when he developed a habit centred around "hate".

He told researchers "it was fun" to talk about how much he despised women, and at one stage, the now-28-year-old saw it as a competition.

"I'd post something hateful, see someone double down and take it further, and I'd think: how can I take that even further, to just be the most vile person posting right now?" he told the researchers.

Others echoed that experience.

"There's something about … at least some part of every teenage boy which is going to just wanna [do] the politically incorrect … you're gonna see how far you can take things, just to see how far you can take things," said Sebastian*, 19.

Brandon*, 33, said manosphere content was "hilariously confronting", telling researchers "you get numbed to it the more time you spend getting bombarded with stuff".

Andrew Tate is a leading influencer in the manosphere. His content promotes an 'alpha male' lifestyle and tips on how to coerce women. (Reuters: Inquam Photos/Octav Ganea)

Professor Flood says in many cases the men did not go looking for manosphere content but it still found them.

"They were looking for information on fitness or financial advice or sexual success. And as part of that, encountered influencers who were next to the manosphere, or bleeding into the manosphere," he says.

In Lachlan's* case he found Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures while looking for guidance his father never gave, "like how to relate to [women] and how to impress them," the 24-year-old said in an interview.

Sebastian*, 19, says he went to social media looking for fitness advice and ended up in a manosphere rabbit hole, driven by desires to appeal to women.

"There's also the stuff that's really easy to fall into, which is like, 'Do these three exercises to make your shoulders bigger, to become more attractive to women'," he said.

'Geek culture' an easy entry point

Others were exposed or pulled in through otherwise harmless hobbies and special interests, from fandoms for sci-fi series to gaming forums.

"As a person who held certain geeky interests, you must be wary of the kind of content you consumed, as you would inevitably be directed towards manosphere content in the process of consuming it," Professor Flood says.

"These groups broadly aligned with the interests of young men and boys and often centred on 'geek culture', including gym content creators, Doctor Who fan forums, Star Wars and sci-fi fan fiction communities, soccer fan pages, online atheist content creators and gaming forums," he says.

The decision to cast Jodie Whittaker as the first female actor to play Doctor Who sparked an outcry among some male fans online. (BBC)

Frankie*, 18, was pouring through Doctor Who forums and came across blogs decrying the show's choice to cast a woman — Jodie Whittaker — as the lead character: "That was what introduced me to the male toxicity side of the fandoms," he told researchers.

"[The show's] writing and quality is used as a Trojan horse to criticise things that some people don't find politically aligning with their views … there are people who just flat out say, 'I didn't like it because it was progressive and a woman was the character,'" he said.

Nick*, 22, was looking for reviews of Star Wars and found "a lot of the content is centred around the same couple of people, and a lot of them are these, like, manosphere, right-wing activists".

Professor Flood says some men encountered manosphere content in spaces where there were "debates over wokeness".

"'Disney's gone woke', or 'this franchise has gone woke' … and those debates sometimes led participants into more explicitly anti-women content," he said.

For Jan*, 21, "it was probably Minecraft", he admits, watching YouTube videos about the game which eventually led him to more politically-driven content.

Brandon* said "one of the guys who was in my World of Warcraft guild at the time was just talking about it … and I'm like, 'oh, f*** it, alright, I'll have a look'".

Leaving the manosphere

Carolyn Robinson, who founded a domestic violence prevention charity, says the findings correlate with the experience of survivors.

Carolyn Robinson is the founder of the charity Beyond DV and says the manosphere is having a detrimental impact on progress made in preventing domestic violence. (ABC News: Scott Kyle )

"There is certainly a link with the messaging that is coming through the manosphere — not all gender inequality is going to lead to domestic and family violence, but all domestic and family violence starts with gender inequality," Ms Robinson tells 7.30.

She worries the manosphere is undermining years of work in the prevention space, especially for younger men.

"These male influencers online — they are role models to young people," she says..

"And if these men are saying that to dominate a woman, to tell her what her role is, is acceptable, and if they hear it enough, they may be more likely to say, 'Well, this is the behaviour that I should be showing."

After Flynn posted his video and it went viral, severe public backlash and a mental health episode led to a break from social media.

He says that absence pulled him out of the manosphere.

"I can clearly see where I was wrong," he tells 7.30.

"Even though it's a really disgraceful video, I think I still hold a lot of empathy for myself in that period because I can just clearly see that that's someone who's struggling and doesn't really know what they're talking about."

Flynn Martin is still creating content but now he is focusing on helping other young men avoid the pull and pitfalls of the manosphere. (ABC News: Daniel Fermer)

Flynn has since been diagnosed with bipolar disorder and says treatment helped.

"I was just having really in-depth conversations with so many mental health professionals. And I was lucky enough to have access to two really, really supporting and understanding parents," he says.

"And also a really, really solid group of friends who were really just helping me throughout that whole time."

He is now back creating content and trying to figure out how he can help other young men avoid the pitfalls of the manosphere.

"I think if you already are in that space and you're kind of deep within it, maybe you're going to have to learn the hard way like I did," he says.

"But if you're kind of in those early stages and starting to form those things, I feel like the best thing that I could say is, all the answers that you're looking for aren't there."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Rape trial of competitive bull rider Clay Hall hears closing arguments
World.content:
The trial of competitive bull rider Clay Benjamin Hall, who is charged with the alleged rape of a teenage girl, has heard closing arguments from the prosecution and defence.

Warning: This article contains details of alleged sexual assault that some readers may find distressing.

The court was told Mr Hall met the girl, who was in her late teens at the time, on a street in Warwick, about 160 kilometres south-west of Brisbane, in the early hours of October 2021.

Prosecutors allege Mr Hall, now 26, raped the teenager after she offered to show him a shortcut to the Warwick Showgrounds.

The court heard the girl had been drinking and had attended a house party with people she did not know before meeting Mr Hall.

Mr Hall was in Warwick to watch his brother compete at the Warwick Rodeo.

The court heard he was not competing because of an injury and had also been drinking before walking to a service station to buy food in the early hours of the morning.

Crown says case centres on consent

In her closing address, Crown prosecutor Samantha O'Rourke told the jury the key issue in the trial was whether the girl had consented.

"He [Mr Hall] had struck out at the rodeo and he wanted sex, when she didn't, he did it anyway," Ms O'Rourke said.

Clay Benjamin Hall has pleaded not guilty to two counts of rape. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Ms O'Rourke said Mr Hall introduced himself to the girl, showed her his Instagram page and was then offered to be shown a shortcut back to the rodeo grounds.

"There was no kissing, no hand holding, nothing romantic in the build-up," Ms O'Rourke said.

The prosecutor told the jury the pair walked past the girl's home and through a gap in a fence towards the showgrounds before Mr Hall sexually propositioned her.

Ms O'Rourke said instead of outright saying no, the girl said she needed to pee as a "subtle non confrontational way" to rebuff Mr Hall.

Ms O'Rourke told the court that Mr Hall remained persistent.

"Every woman's deep-seated fear became [the girl's] reality," she said.

She said Mr Hall raped the girl against a tree, both vaginally and anally.

Defence says consent was given

Defence barrister David Jones KC told the jury it was not in dispute that Mr Hall and the girl had vaginal sex but rejected the allegation that anal penetration had occurred.

The jury was shown a recorded police interview conducted with Mr Hall in 2023, about two years after the alleged incident, where he said he propositioned the girl and initially received no response.

"She kinda didn't say anything, she was just quiet, and I said that's alright I can leave," Mr Hall said.

"She said, 'Nah it's alright.' I said we can do something or I can leave.

"When she said yes, we started to touch each other."

The trial has been heard at Warwick District Court. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

The court heard Mr Hall tell police he asked the girl to bend over against a tree before they had sex. He said the encounter lasted about 10 to 15 seconds before she began crying.

"We started, then she started crying and I did stop," Mr Hall said.

"I said, 'What's wrong? She said, 'I don't know.' I said, 'OK, I'm going to go back to the rodeo grounds.'

"So, I walked off one way, and she walked off in the other direction."

Mr Jones said the police investigation was incomplete because while the girl was tested for alcohol, recording a blood alcohol concentration below 0.1, she was not drug tested while in hospital.

Boxing trainer called

The court also heard evidence from the girl's boxing trainer, who cannot be identified for legal reasons, who said she called several times on the night of the alleged incident.

"She was in tears really bad," the trainer said.

"I asked if she is OK; she said she had been raped."

The trainer said they remained on the phone with the girl before locating her and driving her to hospital.

"I found her sitting under a streetlight with her knees tucked up crying," the trainer said.

"I helped her up, she cried on my shoulder. I asked her if she wants to go the hospital or to the police. She said hospital."

The trainer was questioned about several phone calls the girl made earlier in the night, including while she was walking with Mr Hall and during discussions.

The trainer said the phone was muffled as though the girl was holding it by her side and could hear her talking with a man before the call hung up.

The trainer also told the court the girl had said she had a "significant sexual encounter" while she was at the house party earlier in the evening.

The girl said she could not recall the encounter, telling the trainer about it and did not mention it to the police.

Mr Jones said this cast doubt over the reliability of her testimony.

The prosecution told the jury the fact the girl had called the trainer several times while she was with Mr Hall was the "the most compelling" evidence in the case.

"She tries to call someone who can help her, who can hear what's happening," Ms O'Rourke said.

"But it doesn't work, this man catches what she's doing and so she's left on her own."

World.title: Sex crimes detectives told of drug use in Sydney Swans hotel room
World.content:
Detectives investigating a sexual assault scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans have been told players paid female adult entertainers to consume drugs off their bodies.

Several adult entertainers are understood to have joined players at Melbourne's Pullman Hotel after being hired in the hours after the Swans' win against Essendon on Sunday night.

On Wednesday, the Swans stood down five players for the rest of the AFL season — vice captain Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, James Jordan, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey — for breaching club standards for drinking and bringing women to the hotel.

That came as a separate police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the hotel expanded with detectives flying to NSW yesterday.

Multiple senior police sources have told the ABC they understand an arrangement was reached in a hotel room for players to pay extra to take drugs, believed to be cocaine, from the women's breasts and buttocks.

It is not clear how many or which players allegedly participated.

Police are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Police were called to the Pullman Hotel in East Melbourne on Monday morning. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

It is understood the woman was seen leaving the hotel room in a distressed state with a Triple Zero (000) call made to police soon after.

Police were seen gathering evidence from the hotel on Monday.

Sex crimes detectives have since taken over the investigation, with the alleged victim having made a formal statement to police.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

At a press conference at midday yesterday, Swans officials confirmed none of the five players had been formally interviewed as yet.

Chief executive Matthew Pavlich referred questions about whether the players had been drug tested to investigators, saying: "That matter is for police."

Loading...

However, law enforcement sources dismissed that claim, saying police did not have the powers to drug test the players in this investigation as they were not "doing an activity where it is illegal to be under the influence".

Those activities typically include driving or operating heavy machinery.

"To say it's part of the police investigation, it's definitely not. They [the Swans] are just protecting themselves," one senior police source said.

Late on Wednesday night, the players issued an apology to everyone involved in the scandal after being slapped with season-ending bans for breaching club behavioural standards.

The Sydney Swans, the AFL and the national anti-doping organisation, Sporting Integrity Australia, have all been contacted for comment.

World.title: Former minister on verge of tears over sacking, realisation she was ‘used’ by a friend
World.content:
A former NSW cabinet minister has told a major corruption inquiry she was “disgusted” by the thought of being used in a plot orchestrated by a disgraced developer to drive outspoken building commissioner David Chandler from office. Eleni Petinos, the minister for fair trading and small business in the Perrottet government, told the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Thursday of repeated attempts by several Liberal Party operatives to undermine Chandler, including senior political staffer Chris Spence. A defiant Petinos told the corruption watchdog she now realises Spence, a close friend and the chief of staff to then-planning minister Anthony Roberts, had used her to try to have Chandler removed. Eleni Petinos leaves the commission on Thursday. Ben Symons “Frankly, even the little I knew coming into here today is enough to leave me disgusted and to feel like personal relationships were leant on in a highly improper way, and that’s not someone that you would call a friend,” she said.



The corruption watchdog on Thursday heard the first details of a smear campaign against Chandler, including false claims he would take money in brown paper bags, had received a $10,000 deposit in his bank account, and showed favourable treatment to some companies. Related Article Operation Rosny Catholic Schools NSW boss wiped his iPhone and iPad after Hunters Hill Hotel catch-up The ICAC alleges the campaign was part of a co-ordinated effort by fugitive developer Jean Nassif to undermine Chandler and prevent him from policing substandard building projects by his Toplace development firm. Chandler had been a regular thorn in the side for Nassif and his company. After nearly a month investigating illegal donations claims, Operation Rosny has turned its focus towards a fresh set of allegations involving a $2 million bribe from Nassif to Liberal Party operatives Christian Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet, the brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet. The commission previously heard phone taps in which Nassif says he was promised Chandler would be removed from his taxpayer-funded role policing substandard developments across Sydney.



Petinos said Charles Perrottet had sought to sow doubts over Chandler’s suitability for the role during a phone call in early 2022, after she had been promoted to cabinet amid the fallout from Gladys Berejiklian’s resignation as premier. She said Charles Perrottet had warned she would have her “hands full” with Chandler because he was “dodgy” and a bully. Cassandra Lawry leaves the ICAC on Thursday. Peter Rae She also recalled Spence repeatedly mentioned the existence of a video of Chandler in which the building commissioner complains about building certification issues. The ICAC heard earlier on Thursday Spence had shown the video to Petinos’ chief of staff, Cassandra Lawry, during a meeting at Parliament House, and said it could help her “get rid of” Chandler.



Petinos was responsible for the portfolio in which Chandler was employed and would have held significant say over his future. Spence is a former MP who was forced to resign from the Liberal Party in 2014 during a previous inquiry codenamed Operation Spicer. He was later found to have been involved in a scheme to disguise political donations from banned donors. Petinos said it was now clear Spence wanted Chandler gone. “I don’t understand why,” she said.



“He was a senior person in that government, his minister was very senior, and so it had not occurred to me that there was the possibility of any improper external influence.” She said she respected the building commissioner and had no doubts about his experience or commitment to cleaning up the industry, but said he could sometimes “go rogue”. Petinos was sacked over bullying allegations in July 2022. She appeared on the verge of tears on Thursday while recounting the phone call in which Dominic Perrottet told her she “had to go”. “I thought there was something very strange at play for Dominic to take the action that he did so swiftly, so coldly, and without the opportunity to even put me in front of a camera,” Petinos said.



“He was very, very cold. He was immovable.” Chandler resigned as building commissioner that same month, citing concerns about Petinos and her office. He was later talked into coming back following overtures by the premier and others. Lawry told the ICAC she also “started to wonder” what Spence’s true motivations were in raising the Chandler video with her in May 2022. Asked by counsel assisting the commission Dr Peggy Dwyer, SC, whether she felt she was being set up, Lawry replied: “I did.” The ICAC has not named Spence as a person of interest in its Operation Rosny inquiry. It has not accused Petinos, Lawry or Dominic Perrottet of any wrongdoing.



Dwyer also asked Petinos about evidence given by former Anthony Roberts staffer Dylan Whitelaw. He told the ICAC last month Spence was frustrated Petinos had “effed up” the chance to use the video against Chandler. NSW Reformers member Dylan Whitelaw at the ICAC. Edwina Pickles “I’m delighted I ‘effed it up’,” Petinos told Dwyer. She said Spence’s approaches were “so subtle they did not seem out of context until they have been strung together with the benefit of hindsight”. The commission previously heard phone taps in which Nassif claimed to have significant influence over the previous Coalition government. It is examining whether Chandler’s resignation in mid-2022 was the result of work for which Nassif had paid Charles Perrottet and others. Petinos said Nassif, who is now hiding in Lebanon, was one of the first developers Chandler raised with her when she became minister.

World.title: CBA, News Corp close ranks around ‘new friends’ Matt Comyn and Laura Jayes
World.content:
NationalCBD Opinion CBA, News Corp close ranks around ‘new friends’ Matt Comyn and Laura Jayes John Buckley CBD columnist August 20, 2026 — 5:38pm

August 20, 2026 — 5:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Corporate communications often comes down to the art of semantics. Nowhere is that semantic precision more critical than at the market’s biggest companies, where an errant word can move a share price. So the fact Commonwealth Bank Chief Executive Matt Comyn’s media offsider refused to deny that he has a personal relationship with high-profile News24 broadcaster Laura Jayes piqued our interest. Commonwealth Bank of Australia CEO Matt Comyn. Sitthixay Ditthavong The relationship, which we don’t yet know how to characterise, was first reported by The Australian Financial Review on Wednesday night, a day after CBD revealed Comyn has been separated from his wife for “some time”. The bank said the couple was working through the terms privately. The Financial Review reported Comyn and Jayes had been seen around Bondi and gone on holiday together. It immediately lit up group chats in business and media circles, and landed as the Commonwealth Bank boss sat with journalists for the bank’s annual media dinner on Wednesday night.



But when we sent questions about Comyn’s relationship with Jayes to the bank’s flack on Thursday morning, it was crickets until the afternoon. Then a simple “no comment”. The lack of response to our questions over at News Corp Australia also raised our eyebrows. The Murdoch-controlled media giant owns News24, formerly Sky News Australia, where Jayes hosts the network’s morning political program, AM Agenda. Laura Jayes pictured in 2019 at the Bellvue Hill home of Lachlan and Sarah Murdoch for Christmas drinks. James Alcock A handful of the company’s leadership team didn’t know anything about Jayes’ ties with Comyn beyond what they’d read the night before, we’re told. But even then, they weren’t surprised to learn the pair could be Sydney’s newest power couple – or power friends! Spokespeople for News Corp Australia and News24, who are usually pretty quick to tell us when what we’re hearing is “horsesh-t”, to borrow from the Holt Street vernacular, didn’t even pick up the phone.



But something tells us it won’t be long before we learn more. There are already questions simmering in media circles about how Jayes will manage the perception of a conflict of interest, to the extent she needs to cover the bank or its engagement with the Albanese government in her day job. Investors, meanwhile, tend to be alert when a CEO is going through a divorce. Related Article Opinion

CBD Commonwealth Bank boss Matt Comyn enters his bachelor era John Buckley CBD columnist Still, the pair could well be Sydney’s most eligible bachelor and bachelorette. So if it turns out they are in a relationship, good luck to them. Sydney Swans call for backup The Sydney Swans have a de facto crisis expert on its board in Brian Tyson, the chairman of SEC Newgate. So it was little surprise to learn the Swans had retained Tyson’s firm to help answer the phones from journalists as the club remains engulfed in scandal.



SEC Newgate was brought in to help on Tuesday, CBD hears, but the firm is not expected to work with the club long-term. By Thursday, the club was still reckoning with the fallout of a Victoria Police investigation into an allegation of sexual assault. Just a day earlier, the club announced the suspensions of Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon on Wednesday for unrelated breaches of the club’s behavioural standards at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel on Monday morning. Given the crisis has led front pages and news bulletins across the country all week, we can only imagine the phones at Swans HQ have been ringing off the hook. Tyson is no stranger to high-stakes crises and financial transactions. Over the years, Newgate has advised several big Australian corporates on all manner of work, including in Canberra. Among the firm’s known clients, at least as disclosed to the lobbyists register, are Westpac, Toyota, American Express, Ebay, Domain, and AI giant Anthropic. Kellie Sloane’s lullaby



NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane has done a pretty good job of pretending the party’s living ICAC nightmare is not really happening. And it was more of the same at its Coogee campaign launch at the beachside Intercontinental Hotel on Wednesday evening, CBD hears, where a decent number of people turned up for a special guest appearance from the opposition leader herself. The Libs reckon it was a sellout crowd. NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane addresses a Coogee campaign launch. But if the scene report from inside the room is anything to go by, it was a pretty sedate affair. We were sent a photo of a guy in attendance appearing to nod off. When we alerted the party and Sloane’s office to this, they understandably wanted receipts, which we dutifully provided but have decided to omit from this column for privacy reasons. In response, a spokeswoman for Sloane argued the man pictured – who stood with his arms crossed, chin down, eyes closed – may just have “closed his eyes for a second”. Fair enough – he may have just dropped in after a long day at work.



The party’s candidate for Coogee is Carolyn Martyn. Sloane addressed the room. But funnily enough, so did senior Liberal MP Chris Rath. This is the same Rath who the ICAC confirmed this month was integral in helping Jeremy Greenwood, and Jean-Claude and Charles Perrottet avoid attending a parliamentary inquiry, as this masthead reported last week. World.title: Broken Hill Gold blows White Dam hunt wide open in SA
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Broken Hill Gold blows White Dam hunt wide open in SA Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor August 20, 2026 — 5:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Broken Hill Gold has emerged from its recent rebranding from PacGold, with its sights firmly fixed on White Dam. The company has blown open a much bigger exploration front at its 100 per cent-owned project, 80km east of Broken Hill in South Australia, with the Icebreaker discovery pointing to resource growth and triggering a hunt for deeper gold-copper riches across a swag bag of near-mine targets. Icebreaker, previously the White Dam North prospect, has revealed what could be a significant mineralised system sitting beneath White Dam’s shallow oxide gold. Drilling hit 20m grading 2.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 0.5 per cent copper from 58m, including 6m at 7.5g/t gold and 1.2 per cent copper. Another hole returned 10m at 3.4g/t gold and 0.7 per cent copper from 54m. The discovery lies within a magnetic anomaly that extends up to 1km and remains open in all directions. An aerial view of the White Dam gold project in South Australia, owned by Broken Hill Gold, the recently rebranded PacGold Limited. Hannaford and Vertigo produced 200,000 and 100,000 ounces respectively. However, one of the few deep holes beneath Hannaford hit 29m at 0.7g/t gold from 315m and remains open along strike and down dip. The Vertigo Fault between the pits remains untested at depth. Elsewhere, old workings are throwing up plenty of smoke. Mary Mine returned 16m at 0.9g/t gold and 2.2 per cent copper, Green and Gold Mine delivered 36m at 1.0g/t gold and 0.3 per cent copper and the Wilkins prospect hit 9m at 0.9g/t gold and 0.5 per cent copper. Surface samples peaked at 13 per cent copper at Mary.



‘With our large ground position, we have multiple areas and new targets to start expanding our exploration programmes.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes The Rolling prospect, 800m north of Hannaford and on the same magnetic feature as Icebreaker, returned 4m at 2.7g/t gold from 34m, including 1m at 8.0g/t. Hannaford North, White Dam East, Hannaford Northeast and Vertigo West add to the near-mine pipeline. The Wadnaminga prospect, 80km southwest, adds a 700m undeveloped lode around old workings that produced 19,962 ounces at 37.88g/t gold. Together, a review of historical exploration data has put more than 50 prospects in the frame, several of which share characteristics with Icebreaker, Vertigo and Hannaford and are generally untested below 80m. Icebreaker has turned the White Dam exploration thesis on its head. Its sulphide-hosted gold-copper discovery points towards iron-oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) mineralisation, a deposit family capable of forming very large orebodies.



White Dam sits within the underexplored Curnamona Province of eastern South Australia, where oxide gold caps can overlie primary gold-copper sulphides linked to structural feeder zones. Classified as an iron-poor IOCG end member, its deeper copper-gold potential has never been systematically tested, with previous explorers overwhelmingly focused on shallow oxide gold for heap leaching. Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “The Curnamona province is becoming some of the most prized exploration ground in Australia with major companies now focusing on acquiring and exploring in the region primarily for IOCG and large metasediment-hosted copper-gold systems.” The company is now backing that conviction with more than 30,000m of drilling over 18 months, alongside electrical and magnetic geophysics and geochemistry. Near-mine drilling applications are in, regional heritage clearances are scheduled and a large slice of its recent capital raising will fund the regional push and data reprocessing. Drilling at Icebreaker is now moving towards an updated and upgraded oxide resource in the fourth quarter, with Vertigo North Extended and Hannaford also planned for August-September. Open-pit optimisation and mine planning will follow. Those resource upgrades and mine plans form one half of Broken Hill Gold’s two-pronged strategy. White Dam already hosts 4.6 million tonnes at 0.7g/t gold for 102,000 ounces, backed by existing pits, heap-leach infrastructure and an operational gold extraction plant.



Acquired in late 2025, the operation has already produced doré from historical heap material, with fresh open-pit ore the next prize and smaller oxide discoveries offering potential satellite feed. The plan is to use that production platform to generate cash and help bankroll the bigger exploration hunt. The prize at depth could be considerably bigger. Just 40km north, Havilah Resources’ Kalkaroo hosts 1.1 million tonnes of copper and 3.1 million ounces of gold, while North Portia and Mutooroo provide further evidence of sizeable copper-gold systems across the Curnamona. Following its North Queensland demerger, the Icebreaker discovery is a game-changer for Broken Hill Gold at its flagship project and across its wider Curnamona ground. With open-pit mining offering cashflow while it chases the gold-copper elephants earlier explorers barely tested, the company has a clear run at writing a whole new chapter for the old White Dam mine. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Putin’s blood oil profits untouched by Australia’s toothless sanctions
World.content:
Australia has become an international outlier by allowing fuel made from Russian crude oil to enter the country, a parliament inquiry has found, urging the federal government to close loopholes that allow Moscow to profit from imports through third countries. A damning report into the effectiveness of Australia’s sanctions regime also found not a single person has been prosecuted for breaching Russia-related sanctions since Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Australia is inadvertently helping to fund Vladimir Putin’s war machine. The cross-party Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade References Committee, tabled on Thursday, called on the government to urgently tighten the laws and better align Australia’s approach with the European Union, Britain and other allies. Among 11 recommendations, it urged the banning of Russian blended oils and other products, including timber, that can be transformed in third countries before being legally imported.



The report says Australia should also identify all Russian assets subject to sanctions and consider giving agencies more resources to investigate, freeze and seize them. Related Article Exclusive

Russia-Ukraine war ‘Blood money’ claims over Russian commodity used in thousands of Australian houses The committee, chaired by Liberal senator Jess Collins, acknowledged that seizing sovereign Russian assets carried legal and financial risks, but argued Australia should nevertheless examine the option. “The case for seizing and repurposing Russian assets is strong,” the report found, noting that “immense sums” would be required to ensure the European Union’s security if Russia emerged victorious. “Supporting Ukraine to prevent a Russian victory instead is an economically sound alternative.”



As revealed in several reports by this masthead last year in its Blood Oil series, Russian crude continues to be shipped to countries such as India, refined into petrol, diesel and other products, and then sold into Australia. The committee found Australia had become “the largest single-country importer of oil products refined from Russian crude oil”. That trade has flourished as Australia has become increasingly dependent on imported refined fuel after the closure of five domestic refineries. Refined petroleum imports more than doubled from $19.9 billion in 2014 to $48.5 billion in 2024, while crude oil imports fell to $8 billion. The US-led strikes on Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in February also forced Australia into panic-buying Asian fuel, inadvertently exposing its supply chain to laundered, sanctioned Russian oil.



The committee warned Russia was continuing to benefit even when its oil was transformed overseas before reaching Australian shores. It urged the government to stop allowing the complexity of global fuel markets to become an excuse for delay, warning against “sanctions policy paralysis”. “It goes without saying that EU and UK jurisdictions were faced with the same challenges Australia may be weighing now, arguably greater challenges due to their geographical proximity and reliance on Russian oil,” it said. The report also exposed the limited enforcement muscle behind Australia’s sanctions regime. The Australian Sanctions Office had just 27.7 full-time equivalent staff at the end of January, of which only seven work on sanctions compliance and monitoring. The committee said the absence of prosecutions was unlikely to mean sanctions were not being evaded. “It is unlikely that this lack of prosecution is due to a complete absence of sanctions evasion on Australian soil,” it said, warning evasion may have gone undetected or detected breaches may not have been prosecuted.



DFAT confirmed it had not sought additional resources for the office. The office also has no investigatory powers and must refer suspected breaches to the Australian Federal Police. But Labor members of the committee, led by Senator Raff Ciccone, said the government did not accept many aspects of the characterisation by Coalition senators of the effectiveness of sanctions against Russia. Related Article Blood Oil Warnings over Russian ‘blood oil’ as Asian fuel imports increase “Labor senators take particular issue with the report’s assertion that it is reasonable to conclude that ‘evasion has either taken place undetected, or that instances have been detected but not prosecuted’,” he said. “The claim that the Australian Sanctions Office and Australian Federal Police are unaware of sanctions evasion, or aware but have failed to act, is baseless, and ignores evidence presented in the committee’s own report.”



The report said sanctions were only as effective as their enforcement, and warned sophisticated evasion techniques were evolving through third countries, offshore companies and complex supply chains. The committee heard more than 70 per cent of Russian crude delivered each month was being carried by using a so-called shadow fleet of tankers to move oil beyond the reach of Western sanctions. DFAT described the fleet as the “most clear example” of sanctions circumvention. The report said the sanctions remained “sound in principle” but needed to evolve as Russia developed new ways to evade them.

World.title: This WA politician ‘challenged’ the deputy speaker to remove him from parliament. He was suspended
World.content:
PoliticsWAWA Parliament This WA politician ‘challenged’ the deputy speaker to remove him from parliament. He was suspended Michael Philipps August 20, 2026 — 5:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian Greens MLC Sophie McNeill has lashed a Nationals MP who was suspended from parliament as a “a gutless coward” who just wants attention. And Central Wheatbelt MLA Lachlan Hunter himself took aim at Labor after being suspended for four days, claiming the Cook government had used its absolute majority to “shut down a member of the opposition”. Nationals MP Lachlan Hunter. Premier Roger Cook said the speaker had suspended the Nationals MP for four days over his conduct and behaviour, accusing Hunter of lacking the maturity to “respect the institution”. Hunter was cautioned three times during question time on Wednesday, before interjecting several times during private members’ business to raise the issue of a “pro-Palestine” meeting held at parliament on Tuesday evening.



The event Hunter was referring to was the “Wall of Tears” – a visual display of the names of 18,000 children who have been confirmed to have been killed in Gaza from October 2023 until the middle of last year. The exhibition was displayed by the Perth Doctors for Palestine group, made up of more than 100 Perth doctors, with the assistance of the Parliamentary Friends of Palestine group. WA Greens MLC Sophie McNeill. Holly Thompson McNeill, along with WA Labor MLA Dave Kelly, helped facilitate the event. Addressing the chamber on Thursday, Speaker Stephen Price said Hunter’s responses went beyond mere noncompliance and amounted to direct challenges to the authority of the chair.



“When reminded how many calls to order he had received, he effectively challenged the deputy speaker to remove him from the chamber,” Price said. Related Article Political donations Who’s funding WA’s parties ahead of the Secret Harbour byelection? “Taken together, I am satisfied that the member’s conduct constituted a persistent and wilful disregard for the authority of the chair for the purposes of standing order 42.” Price moved that the member for Central Wheatbelt be suspended from service of the assembly. “As this is the second occasion within a year on which the member has been named, the suspension will be for four sitting days, including the remainder of today,” Price said.



The motion was carried 27 to 12. Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, McNeill said she was a proud co-convenor of Parliamentary Friends of Palestine. She then turned the blowtorch on Hunter for his comments on the event. “Lachlan Hunter is a gutless coward who wouldn’t dare repeat what he said outside of parliament,” she said. “He’s a disgusting, cowardly little man who is using the deaths of 18,000 children to try and get a bit of attention because he’s worried about One Nation taking his seat at the next election. “I think Lachlan … clearly is just a complete shithead.”



Speaking to media outside Parliament House on Thursday, Hunter claimed he had been kicked out for addressing “very serious issues like antisemitism”. Related Article WA Parliament What’s on voters’ minds as the first votes are cast in the battle for Secret Harbour? “So, if the deputy speaker didn’t call me out yesterday and kick me out of the parliament, then why is the speaker now intervening today to kick me out of the state parliament on this very, very serious issue?” he asked. “The deputy speaker, on a number of occasions, asked me to remain relevant to the opposition’s own motion on vulnerable people. “Well, I ask the Labor Party if they think that the Jewish community in Western Australia are not some of the most vulnerable people in our state.



“I will accuse the speaker, the deputy speaker, and every single acting speaker in this parliament for being totally biased, and I have called it out, and we’ve called it out as an opposition, time and time again.” Speaking to media, Cook said he believed Hunter’s suspension was “an important part of making sure that we restore the rules and the respect of the chamber”. “Let’s be very, very clear on this. This has nothing to do with the subject matter [Hunter] raised,” Cook said. “What he chose to do was simply to run loose with the rules of the chamber, to be disrespectful to the deputy speaker. “She was in the chair at the time, and he was talking over, being disrespectful and rude. And there are rules around that. It has nothing to do with the debate itself.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Broken Hill Gold blows White Dam hunt wide open in SA
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Broken Hill Gold blows White Dam hunt wide open in SA Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor August 20, 2026 — 5:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Broken Hill Gold has emerged from its recent rebranding from PacGold, with its sights firmly fixed on White Dam. The company has blown open a much bigger exploration front at its 100 per cent-owned project, 80km east of Broken Hill in South Australia, with the Icebreaker discovery pointing to resource growth and triggering a hunt for deeper gold-copper riches across a swag bag of near-mine targets. Icebreaker, previously the White Dam North prospect, has revealed what could be a significant mineralised system sitting beneath White Dam’s shallow oxide gold. Drilling hit 20m grading 2.5 grams per tonne (g/t) gold and 0.5 per cent copper from 58m, including 6m at 7.5g/t gold and 1.2 per cent copper. Another hole returned 10m at 3.4g/t gold and 0.7 per cent copper from 54m. The discovery lies within a magnetic anomaly that extends up to 1km and remains open in all directions. An aerial view of the White Dam gold project in South Australia, owned by Broken Hill Gold, the recently rebranded PacGold Limited. Hannaford and Vertigo produced 200,000 and 100,000 ounces respectively. However, one of the few deep holes beneath Hannaford hit 29m at 0.7g/t gold from 315m and remains open along strike and down dip. The Vertigo Fault between the pits remains untested at depth. Elsewhere, old workings are throwing up plenty of smoke. Mary Mine returned 16m at 0.9g/t gold and 2.2 per cent copper, Green and Gold Mine delivered 36m at 1.0g/t gold and 0.3 per cent copper and the Wilkins prospect hit 9m at 0.9g/t gold and 0.5 per cent copper. Surface samples peaked at 13 per cent copper at Mary.



‘With our large ground position, we have multiple areas and new targets to start expanding our exploration programmes.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes The Rolling prospect, 800m north of Hannaford and on the same magnetic feature as Icebreaker, returned 4m at 2.7g/t gold from 34m, including 1m at 8.0g/t. Hannaford North, White Dam East, Hannaford Northeast and Vertigo West add to the near-mine pipeline. The Wadnaminga prospect, 80km southwest, adds a 700m undeveloped lode around old workings that produced 19,962 ounces at 37.88g/t gold. Together, a review of historical exploration data has put more than 50 prospects in the frame, several of which share characteristics with Icebreaker, Vertigo and Hannaford and are generally untested below 80m. Icebreaker has turned the White Dam exploration thesis on its head. Its sulphide-hosted gold-copper discovery points towards iron-oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) mineralisation, a deposit family capable of forming very large orebodies.



White Dam sits within the underexplored Curnamona Province of eastern South Australia, where oxide gold caps can overlie primary gold-copper sulphides linked to structural feeder zones. Classified as an iron-poor IOCG end member, its deeper copper-gold potential has never been systematically tested, with previous explorers overwhelmingly focused on shallow oxide gold for heap leaching. Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “The Curnamona province is becoming some of the most prized exploration ground in Australia with major companies now focusing on acquiring and exploring in the region primarily for IOCG and large metasediment-hosted copper-gold systems.” The company is now backing that conviction with more than 30,000m of drilling over 18 months, alongside electrical and magnetic geophysics and geochemistry. Near-mine drilling applications are in, regional heritage clearances are scheduled and a large slice of its recent capital raising will fund the regional push and data reprocessing. Drilling at Icebreaker is now moving towards an updated and upgraded oxide resource in the fourth quarter, with Vertigo North Extended and Hannaford also planned for August-September. Open-pit optimisation and mine planning will follow. Those resource upgrades and mine plans form one half of Broken Hill Gold’s two-pronged strategy. White Dam already hosts 4.6 million tonnes at 0.7g/t gold for 102,000 ounces, backed by existing pits, heap-leach infrastructure and an operational gold extraction plant.



Acquired in late 2025, the operation has already produced doré from historical heap material, with fresh open-pit ore the next prize and smaller oxide discoveries offering potential satellite feed. The plan is to use that production platform to generate cash and help bankroll the bigger exploration hunt. The prize at depth could be considerably bigger. Just 40km north, Havilah Resources’ Kalkaroo hosts 1.1 million tonnes of copper and 3.1 million ounces of gold, while North Portia and Mutooroo provide further evidence of sizeable copper-gold systems across the Curnamona. Following its North Queensland demerger, the Icebreaker discovery is a game-changer for Broken Hill Gold at its flagship project and across its wider Curnamona ground. With open-pit mining offering cashflow while it chases the gold-copper elephants earlier explorers barely tested, the company has a clear run at writing a whole new chapter for the old White Dam mine. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Putin’s blood oil profits untouched by Australia’s toothless sanctions
World.content:
Australia has become an international outlier by allowing fuel made from Russian crude oil to enter the country, a parliament inquiry has found, urging the federal government to close loopholes that allow Moscow to profit from imports through third countries. A damning report into the effectiveness of Australia’s sanctions regime also found not a single person has been prosecuted for breaching Russia-related sanctions since Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Australia is inadvertently helping to fund Vladimir Putin’s war machine. The cross-party Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade References Committee, tabled on Thursday, called on the government to urgently tighten the laws and better align Australia’s approach with the European Union, Britain and other allies. Among 11 recommendations, it urged the banning of Russian blended oils and other products, including timber, that can be transformed in third countries before being legally imported.



The report says Australia should also identify all Russian assets subject to sanctions and consider giving agencies more resources to investigate, freeze and seize them. Related Article Exclusive

Russia-Ukraine war ‘Blood money’ claims over Russian commodity used in thousands of Australian houses The committee, chaired by Liberal senator Jess Collins, acknowledged that seizing sovereign Russian assets carried legal and financial risks, but argued Australia should nevertheless examine the option. “The case for seizing and repurposing Russian assets is strong,” the report found, noting that “immense sums” would be required to ensure the European Union’s security if Russia emerged victorious. “Supporting Ukraine to prevent a Russian victory instead is an economically sound alternative.”



As revealed in several reports by this masthead last year in its Blood Oil series, Russian crude continues to be shipped to countries such as India, refined into petrol, diesel and other products, and then sold into Australia. The committee found Australia had become “the largest single-country importer of oil products refined from Russian crude oil”. That trade has flourished as Australia has become increasingly dependent on imported refined fuel after the closure of five domestic refineries. Refined petroleum imports more than doubled from $19.9 billion in 2014 to $48.5 billion in 2024, while crude oil imports fell to $8 billion. The US-led strikes on Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in February also forced Australia into panic-buying Asian fuel, inadvertently exposing its supply chain to laundered, sanctioned Russian oil.



The committee warned Russia was continuing to benefit even when its oil was transformed overseas before reaching Australian shores. It urged the government to stop allowing the complexity of global fuel markets to become an excuse for delay, warning against “sanctions policy paralysis”. “It goes without saying that EU and UK jurisdictions were faced with the same challenges Australia may be weighing now, arguably greater challenges due to their geographical proximity and reliance on Russian oil,” it said. The report also exposed the limited enforcement muscle behind Australia’s sanctions regime. The Australian Sanctions Office had just 27.7 full-time equivalent staff at the end of January, of which only seven work on sanctions compliance and monitoring. The committee said the absence of prosecutions was unlikely to mean sanctions were not being evaded. “It is unlikely that this lack of prosecution is due to a complete absence of sanctions evasion on Australian soil,” it said, warning evasion may have gone undetected or detected breaches may not have been prosecuted.



DFAT confirmed it had not sought additional resources for the office. The office also has no investigatory powers and must refer suspected breaches to the Australian Federal Police. But Labor members of the committee, led by Senator Raff Ciccone, said the government did not accept many aspects of the characterisation by Coalition senators of the effectiveness of sanctions against Russia. Related Article Blood Oil Warnings over Russian ‘blood oil’ as Asian fuel imports increase “Labor senators take particular issue with the report’s assertion that it is reasonable to conclude that ‘evasion has either taken place undetected, or that instances have been detected but not prosecuted’,” he said. “The claim that the Australian Sanctions Office and Australian Federal Police are unaware of sanctions evasion, or aware but have failed to act, is baseless, and ignores evidence presented in the committee’s own report.”



The report said sanctions were only as effective as their enforcement, and warned sophisticated evasion techniques were evolving through third countries, offshore companies and complex supply chains. The committee heard more than 70 per cent of Russian crude delivered each month was being carried by using a so-called shadow fleet of tankers to move oil beyond the reach of Western sanctions. DFAT described the fleet as the “most clear example” of sanctions circumvention. The report said the sanctions remained “sound in principle” but needed to evolve as Russia developed new ways to evade them.

World.title: This WA politician ‘challenged’ the deputy speaker to remove him from parliament. He was suspended
World.content:
PoliticsWAWA Parliament This WA politician ‘challenged’ the deputy speaker to remove him from parliament. He was suspended Michael Philipps August 20, 2026 — 5:13pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian Greens MLC Sophie McNeill has lashed a Nationals MP who was suspended from parliament as a “a gutless coward” who just wants attention. And Central Wheatbelt MLA Lachlan Hunter himself took aim at Labor after being suspended for four days, claiming the Cook government had used its absolute majority to “shut down a member of the opposition”. Nationals MP Lachlan Hunter. Premier Roger Cook said the speaker had suspended the Nationals MP for four days over his conduct and behaviour, accusing Hunter of lacking the maturity to “respect the institution”. Hunter was cautioned three times during question time on Wednesday, before interjecting several times during private members’ business to raise the issue of a “pro-Palestine” meeting held at parliament on Tuesday evening.



The event Hunter was referring to was the “Wall of Tears” – a visual display of the names of 18,000 children who have been confirmed to have been killed in Gaza from October 2023 until the middle of last year. The exhibition was displayed by the Perth Doctors for Palestine group, made up of more than 100 Perth doctors, with the assistance of the Parliamentary Friends of Palestine group. WA Greens MLC Sophie McNeill. Holly Thompson McNeill, along with WA Labor MLA Dave Kelly, helped facilitate the event. Addressing the chamber on Thursday, Speaker Stephen Price said Hunter’s responses went beyond mere noncompliance and amounted to direct challenges to the authority of the chair.



“When reminded how many calls to order he had received, he effectively challenged the deputy speaker to remove him from the chamber,” Price said. Related Article Political donations Who’s funding WA’s parties ahead of the Secret Harbour byelection? “Taken together, I am satisfied that the member’s conduct constituted a persistent and wilful disregard for the authority of the chair for the purposes of standing order 42.” Price moved that the member for Central Wheatbelt be suspended from service of the assembly. “As this is the second occasion within a year on which the member has been named, the suspension will be for four sitting days, including the remainder of today,” Price said.



The motion was carried 27 to 12. Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, McNeill said she was a proud co-convenor of Parliamentary Friends of Palestine. She then turned the blowtorch on Hunter for his comments on the event. “Lachlan Hunter is a gutless coward who wouldn’t dare repeat what he said outside of parliament,” she said. “He’s a disgusting, cowardly little man who is using the deaths of 18,000 children to try and get a bit of attention because he’s worried about One Nation taking his seat at the next election. “I think Lachlan … clearly is just a complete shithead.”



Speaking to media outside Parliament House on Thursday, Hunter claimed he had been kicked out for addressing “very serious issues like antisemitism”. Related Article WA Parliament What’s on voters’ minds as the first votes are cast in the battle for Secret Harbour? “So, if the deputy speaker didn’t call me out yesterday and kick me out of the parliament, then why is the speaker now intervening today to kick me out of the state parliament on this very, very serious issue?” he asked. “The deputy speaker, on a number of occasions, asked me to remain relevant to the opposition’s own motion on vulnerable people. “Well, I ask the Labor Party if they think that the Jewish community in Western Australia are not some of the most vulnerable people in our state.



“I will accuse the speaker, the deputy speaker, and every single acting speaker in this parliament for being totally biased, and I have called it out, and we’ve called it out as an opposition, time and time again.” Speaking to media, Cook said he believed Hunter’s suspension was “an important part of making sure that we restore the rules and the respect of the chamber”. “Let’s be very, very clear on this. This has nothing to do with the subject matter [Hunter] raised,” Cook said. “What he chose to do was simply to run loose with the rules of the chamber, to be disrespectful to the deputy speaker. “She was in the chair at the time, and he was talking over, being disrespectful and rude. And there are rules around that. It has nothing to do with the debate itself.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Wellington residents march on parliament in bid to get rising water bills lowered
World.content:
Hundreds gather in Wellington to protest new Tiaki Wai bills Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Some Wellington residents are fed up and stressed by the prospect of rising water bills as they marched on parliament in a bid to get the organisation to lower costs.

And a former Wellington mayor-turned MP, who turned out to the protest, admitted his was among councils which could have invested more in water infrastructure in previous years.

About 300 people turned up in central Wellington on Thursday to raise concerns about their water bills in a cost of living crisis, as part of the Stop Tiaki Wai group.

Water bills were increasing by 13.3 per cent on average across the region this year, and were projected to reach over $6000 per year in a decade.

A sign at Thursday's protest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Lower Hutt resident AJ said that's shocking.

"The people are fed up, you can't get blood out of a stone can you?"

She said her first water bill was about $500 for the quarter.

"I came out here today, because the cost of living is through the roof, and this is just one more bill that people have to find money to pay - and people can't find that money anymore."

Mary Head, an Upper Hutt resident and pensioner, said she's frustrated about the way her water bills were being calculated.

"There's only my husband and I at home, and the amount of water we use, is negligible to say a family - and yet we are paying the same or more of a family of six or eight," she said.

Mary Head at the protest. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Tiaki Wai said in its first years' of operation, the way water services would be calculated was taken from councils' rates bills.

In Upper Hutt, Porirua and Lower Hutt water bills were being calculated through a combination of a fixed rate and property value.

In Wellington city, most people's bills were based on property valuation, board chairperson Will Peet recently told RNZ.

The entity has said it wants to move to a single-pricing model in the future, as well as install water meters.

But Head said the indicative costs Tiaki Wai had put out for that so far - at half-a billion dollars for the programme - were ridiculous.

Protest organiser Guy Nunns admitted he can't actually stop Tiaki Wai - which was set up under the government's Local Water Done Well policy.

Protest organiser Guy Nunns. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Nunns said he would be paying his bill this year - but suggested he would encourage people to not pay their bills if the costs don't change.

That's not something Wellington City Councillor Karl Tiefenbacher, who was among the crowd at parliament, agreed with.

"I don't think that really works. To be fair I am against the fact we have no rates cap on top of Tiaki Wai - I think that's the issue."

He asked what the point of rates caps against councils were, if there was none against water entities.

"I think water is the biggest issue we have. I think this protest actually represents what is wrong with our society at the moment, and that's that it's becoming unaffordable."

When asked whether he thought spending was needed to upgrade failing pipes and water plants, Nunns said "no one" was happy with the current state of infrastructure.

Attendees at the protest on Thursday. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"We have always paid for water infrastructure in our rates, people have not necessarily understood that, they'll be understanding it now - but at $2200 a year, and until recently I was the sole occupant of the property, that's not realistic."

New Zealand First MP and former Wellington city councillor and mayor Andy Foster was also at the protest.

He was asked whether the council he led between 2019 and 2022 did enough to invest in pipes during its years in power.

He said his council set in motion more investment and was heading in the direction of a CCO for infrastructure, but also said more could have been done.

"We were going to fix it, so long term, yes, there was under-investment in infrastructure, but that is true of pretty-well every council in the country."

Tiaki Wai said it needed to spend $25 billion dollars across three decades to fix the regions old failing water treatment plants and pipes.

Stop Tiaki Wai protest attendee, Bridie McGill with her sign. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Officials said there's a major crisis point at Seaview, where a crucial outfall pipe was leaking into the harbour and the Waiwhetū stream.

They also said about 100 kilometres of pipe at the point needed to be replaced each year.

In a recent interview with RNZ, Brewster urged anyone facing hardship to contact the organisation, saying Tiaki Wai had policies in place to help those who were really struggling to pay bills.

But he said debt collection would have to be pursued for those who were refusing to pay for no reason.

"If you are refusing to pay the bill and not contacting us then we, we would unfortunately, we would have to pursue that.

"Because at the end of the day there is an obligation to pay the bill, if nobody pays their bill we've got no money to fix the system."

Attendees march to Parliament. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He said on Thursday, he respected the rights of Wellingtonians to join the protest and express their views.

But he urged the protesters to respect those working at Tiaki Wai trying to upgrade the region's infrastructure.
